#### Frequently asked questions (28)

**What is a percentage?**
A percentage is a fraction expressed out of 100. The word comes from the Latin per centum, meaning by the hundred. Writing 25% is another way of writing 25/100, or the decimal 0.25 — three notations for exactly the same quantity.

**How do I calculate a percentage?**
It depends which of two questions you are asking. To find a percentage of a number, divide the percentage by 100 and multiply. To find what percentage one number is of another, divide the part by the whole and multiply by 100. Confusing the two is the most common percentage mistake there is.

**What is the percentage formula?**
Percentage = (Part ÷ Whole) × 100. Rearranged, Part = (Percentage ÷ 100) × Whole, and Whole = Part ÷ (Percentage ÷ 100). Those three arrangements of one relationship answer most percentage questions.

**How do I find 10% of a number?**
Move the decimal point one place to the left: 10% of 500 is 50, and 10% of 87 is 8.7. From there, 5% is half of that, 20% is double it, and 15% is 10% plus 5% — which makes most everyday percentages workable in your head.

**How do I calculate percentage increase?**
Subtract the original value from the new one, divide by the original, then multiply by 100. From 100 to 125 is (125 − 100) ÷ 100 × 100 = 25%. Dividing by the original rather than the new value is what makes it an increase from that starting point.

**How do I calculate percentage decrease?**
The same formula. From 100 to 75 is (75 − 100) ÷ 100 × 100 = −25%, a 25% decrease. Increase and decrease are the same calculation; only the sign differs.

**How do I calculate percentage change?**
((New − Original) ÷ Original) × 100. A positive result is an increase and a negative one is a decrease. Where the original value is negative this calculator divides by its magnitude, so a move from −100 to −50 correctly reads as an improvement.

**What is the difference between percentage change and percentage difference?**
Percentage change measures a move from a specific starting point and has a direction, so it is not symmetric: 100 to 120 is a 20% increase, but 120 to 100 is a 16.67% decrease. Percentage difference compares two values against their average, has no direction and is symmetric — 100 and 120 differ by 18.18% whichever order you take them in.

**How do I find what percent one number is of another?**
Divide the first number by the second and multiply by 100. 45 out of 60 is 45 ÷ 60 × 100 = 75%. The number you are measuring goes on top; the number you are measuring against goes on the bottom.

**How do I reverse a percentage?**
If you know a part and what percentage it represents, divide the part by the percentage as a decimal. 50 being 25% of something means the whole is 50 ÷ 0.25 = 200. Dividing, not multiplying, is what makes it a reversal.

**How do I calculate a discount?**
Multiply the price by the discount percentage and divide by 100 to get the saving, then subtract it. Or in one step, multiply the price by (1 − discount ÷ 100). A 20% discount on ₹2,000 saves ₹400 and leaves ₹1,600.

**How do I find the original price after a discount?**
Divide the price you paid by (1 − discount ÷ 100). ₹800 after a 20% discount was ₹1,000 originally, because ₹800 ÷ 0.8 = ₹1,000. Adding 20% back to ₹800 gives ₹960, which is wrong — that is the single most common reverse-percentage error.

**How do I calculate markup?**
Markup is measured against cost. Multiply the cost by the markup percentage and divide by 100, then add it. A 25% markup on a ₹1,000 cost gives a ₹250 markup and a ₹1,250 selling price.

**What is the difference between markup and margin?**
Both describe the same profit, measured against different bases. Markup divides profit by cost; margin divides the same profit by the selling price. A 25% markup is a 20% margin, and because the selling price is always the larger denominator, margin is always the smaller number.

**Can a percentage be greater than 100%?**
Yes, and this calculator does not block it. 150% of 200 is 300, and a value that triples has increased by 200%. A percentage above 100 simply means the part is larger than the whole it is being measured against.

**Can percentages be negative?**
Yes. A negative percentage change is a decrease, and negative values are handled consistently rather than silently converted to positive. Where a negative starting value would make the sign misleading, the calculator says so.

**How do I calculate a percentage with decimals?**
Exactly as you would a whole percentage — 12.5% of 800 is 0.125 × 800 = 100. This calculator accepts decimal percentages and decimal values, and lets you control how many decimal places the answer is displayed to.

**Why does my calculator show 33.33333333?**
Because one third has no exact decimal representation. This calculator rounds for display while keeping full precision internally, and removes the floating-point artifacts that otherwise turn 70 into 70.00000000000001.

**What is a percentage point?**
The arithmetic difference between two percentages. Going from 20% to 25% is a rise of 5 percentage points, but a 25% increase in relative terms. Reporting one as the other is a common and sometimes deliberate distortion.

**Why does a 20% loss need more than a 20% gain to recover?**
Because the second percentage applies to a smaller base. Losing 20% of 100 leaves 80, and getting back to 100 from 80 requires a 25% gain. Percentage changes do not cancel out, which is why sequential percentages have to be applied in order rather than added together.

**How do I apply two percentages one after another?**
Multiply the factors rather than adding the percentages. A 20% discount followed by a further 10% is 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72, a 28% total discount — not 30%. Two successive 50% discounts do not make an item free.

**How do I calculate 20% of 500?**
20 ÷ 100 × 500 = 100. Or find 10% by moving the decimal point one place left, which gives 50, and double it.

**How do I calculate 15% of 1,000?**
15 ÷ 100 × 1,000 = 150. Mentally: 10% is 100 and 5% is half of that at 50, so 15% is 150.

**Can I use this calculator for discounts and prices?**
Yes. There are dedicated modes for discount, reverse discount, markup, margin, adding tax and removing tax, and those modes format their results as currency in rupees, dollars, euros or pounds.

**How do I remove tax from a tax-inclusive price?**
Divide the total by (1 + tax rate ÷ 100). ₹1,180 including 18% tax contains ₹1,000 before tax and ₹180 of tax. Taking 18% of ₹1,180 gives ₹212.40, which overstates the tax because that figure already contains it.

**Does the calculator show how it got the answer?**
Yes. Every result shows the general formula, the same formula with your numbers substituted in, and a numbered list of the steps, so the answer can be checked rather than taken on trust.

**Are my numbers sent anywhere?**
No. Every calculation runs in your browser and no request is made. Nothing you type is stored unless you switch on the optional history, which saves to your own browser and can be cleared at any time.

**Is this percentage calculator free?**
Yes. No sign-up, no limits and no paid tier.

#### Frequently asked questions (18)

**Does this calculator follow order of operations?**
Yes. It evaluates the whole expression using standard precedence rather than left to right, so 2 + 3 x 4 gives 14, not 20. Multiplication and division are applied before addition and subtraction, so the whole expression is resolved the way it would be on paper.

**Why does my phone calculator give a different answer?**
Most basic calculators evaluate strictly left to right as you press keys, so they return 20 for 2 + 3 x 4. Scientific and expression calculators, including this one, apply precedence and return 14. Both are working correctly — they are answering different questions.

**Can I use the keyboard?**
Yes, and it is much faster. Type digits and operators directly, press Enter or = to evaluate, Escape to clear, and Backspace to delete the last character. Every on-screen button has a keyboard equivalent.

**How does the percentage key work?**
The % key converts the number before it into a fraction of a hundred, so 50 % becomes 0.5. That means 200 x 50 % gives 100, which is the common use — taking a percentage of a value.

**Does it keep a history of my calculations?**

**Is my calculation history saved when I close the tab?**

**What happens if I divide by zero?**
The calculator reports an error rather than showing Infinity or a misleading number. Division by zero is undefined in ordinary arithmetic, so there is no correct value to display.

**How precise are the results?**
It uses the same double-precision floating point every browser and spreadsheet uses, which is accurate to roughly fifteen significant digits. That is far beyond everyday needs, but it means a few decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly — see the next answer.

**Why does 0.1 + 0.2 not give exactly 0.3?**
Because binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 or 0.2 exactly, in the same way decimal cannot write one third exactly. The true sum is 0.30000000000000004. Every mainstream calculator and programming language has this property; results are rounded for display so you rarely see it.

**Can I use brackets?**
This calculator has no bracket keys — it applies standard precedence to a single expression instead. When you need a different order, evaluate the inner part first with =, then carry on with the result. So for (2 + 3) x 4, enter 2 + 3 =, then x 4 =.

**How do I calculate a percentage increase?**
Multiply by one plus the increase as a decimal. A 15% increase on 2,400 is 2400 x 1.15 = 2,760. For a decrease, subtract instead: a 15% discount is 2400 x 0.85 = 2,040.

**How do I work out a tip or a discount?**
For a 12% tip on 850, either compute 850 x 12 % to get the tip alone, or 850 x 1.12 for the total including it. Discounts work the same way with subtraction.

**Can I copy a result?**
Yes. Use the copy button beside the display to copy the current result, or copy any earlier line from the history. It goes to your normal clipboard, so it pastes anywhere.

**Does the calculator work offline?**
Yes, once the page has loaded. Everything runs in your browser with no server involved, so it keeps working if your connection drops.

**Is this calculator free?**
Completely. There is no sign-up, no download and no limit on how much you use it.

**Do you see what I type into the calculator?**
No. The arithmetic happens in your browser and nothing you enter is sent to us. That is also why the history lives in the open page rather than in an account.

**Does it work on a phone?**
Yes. The keypad scales to the screen and the buttons stay large enough to tap accurately, and the history panel moves below the keypad on narrow screens.

**Which calculator should I use for loans, tax or percentages?**
This one handles general arithmetic. For a specific job, ToolAdda has dedicated tools that show the working — a percentage calculator, EMI and home loan calculators with full amortisation schedules, a GST calculator and an income tax calculator. They are linked below.

#### Frequently asked questions (22)

**What is a scientific calculator?**
A calculator that understands mathematical structure rather than just a sequence of keypresses. It applies correct order of operations, handles parentheses, and adds trigonometry, logarithms, exponents, roots, factorials and scientific notation. The defining test: type 2 + 3 x 4. A scientific calculator answers 14; a basic one often answers 20.

**Is this scientific calculator free?**
Yes, completely. No account, no trial, no paid tier, no limit on calculations, and no watermark on anything you copy out.

**Does it work on mobile?**
Yes. The layout collapses to a single column, the keypad drops to four columns with full-size keys, and the display scales with the viewport. You can also use your phone's own keyboard to type expressions directly.

**Does it require a download?**
No. It is a web page. You can optionally add it to your home screen to open it like an app and use it without a connection.

**Does it support sin, cos and tan?**
Yes, along with their inverses (asin, acos, atan), the hyperbolic versions (sinh, cosh, tanh) and the inverse hyperbolics. All of them respect the DEG, RAD or GRAD setting you have selected.

**What is DEG mode?**
Degrees, where a full circle is 360. It is what school geometry, surveying and most engineering drawings use. In DEG mode sin(30) equals 0.5.

**What is RAD mode?**
Radians, where a full circle is 2π ≈ 6.283. It is the natural unit for calculus and physics, because the derivative of sin(x) is cos(x) only when x is in radians. In RAD mode sin(pi/2) equals 1.

**What is GRAD mode?**
Gradians, where a full circle is 400 and a right angle is exactly 100. It appears mainly in some European surveying and civil engineering traditions. In GRAD mode sin(100) equals 1.

**How do I calculate a factorial?**
Type the number followed by an exclamation mark: 6! gives 720. Factorials are defined for non-negative whole numbers, and 0! is 1 by definition. They grow extremely fast - 20! is already about 2.4 × 10¹⁸.

**How do I calculate square roots?**
Use sqrt(144) for 12, cbrt(27) for cube roots, or nthRoot(32, 5) for any other root. A root is just a fractional power, so x^(1/2) gives the same answer as sqrt(x).

**How do I calculate powers?**
Use the caret: 2^10 gives 1024. Note two conventions - exponents bind tighter than a leading minus, so -2^2 is −4 and you need (-2)^2 for 4; and exponentiation is right-associative, so 2^3^2 is 2^9 = 512 rather than 64.

**What is the difference between log and ln?**
In this engine log(x) is the natural logarithm and log10(x) is base 10, which is the programming-library convention and the opposite of the key labels on a physical Casio or TI. If a logarithm looks wrong by a factor of about 2.303 - which is ln(10) - this is why. For any other base, log(x, b) works directly.

**What is scientific notation?**
Writing a number as a value between 1 and 10 times a power of ten, such as 6.022 × 10²³. Type it as 6.022e23. The display switches to it automatically above 10¹⁵ and below 10⁻⁹, where the plain digit string stops being readable.

**Can I use keyboard shortcuts?**
Yes, and it is the fastest way to use it. Type the whole expression as text; Enter evaluates, Escape clears, Backspace deletes, and the arrow keys, Home and End move the cursor. Because the input is an ordinary text field, select, copy and paste all work as usual.

**Does it keep a calculation history?**
Yes - a running tape. Every calculation is recorded with its expression and result. Click a past result to insert it into the current expression, or edit a past line and everything after it recalculates in order. That last part is what physical calculators cannot do.

**Does it have memory functions?**
Yes, plus named variables. Memory is the classic store-and-recall behaviour for a running subtotal. Variables let you name a value - assign r = 4.2 and then write pi * r^2 - which is far less error-prone for multi-step work and makes the tape readable afterwards.

**Does it work offline?**
Yes, after your first visit. A service worker caches the page and the maths engine, so it opens and calculates with no connection - including your tape, memory and variables, which live on your device.

**Are calculations sent to a server?**
No. Expressions are parsed and evaluated entirely in your browser; there is no server component to send them to. Open developer tools, go to the Network tab and run some calculations - you will see the page's files and the maths engine load once and nothing afterwards.

**Does it use eval()?**
No. Expressions are tokenised and evaluated by a dedicated maths library with its own parser. That matters for accuracy - it applies real operator precedence - and for security, since nothing you type into the field can execute as code.

**Why does 0.1 + 0.2 not give exactly 0.3 on some calculators?**
Because computers store numbers in binary and some decimal fractions have no exact binary form, the same way 1/3 has no exact decimal form. The raw result is 0.30000000000000004. This calculator rounds at the display layer, so you see 0.3, while the underlying value keeps full precision so errors do not accumulate through a chain of calculations.

**How precise is it?**
It uses standard double-precision floating point, giving about 15 to 17 significant decimal digits. That is comfortably enough for engineering, physics and school mathematics. It is not arbitrary precision - if you need fifty digits of π, this is the wrong instrument.

**Why does my trig answer look wrong?**
Almost always the angle mode. sin(30) is 0.5 in DEG but about −0.988 in RAD, because 30 radians is a completely different angle. Neither is an error; only one answers the question you meant. Check the DEG/RAD/GRAD indicator at the top left before trusting any trigonometric result.

#### Frequently asked questions (30)

**What is BMI (Body Mass Index)?**
BMI is a simple screening measurement that estimates body fatness from your weight and height, calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared. It's used worldwide by organizations like the WHO and CDC as a quick population-level indicator, not a diagnostic tool.

**What is the BMI formula?**
The metric formula is BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)². The imperial formula is BMI = 703 × weight (lb) ÷ height (in)². Both formulas produce the same BMI value for the same body — only the unit conversion constant differs.

**How do I calculate BMI in metric units?**
Divide your weight in kilograms by your height in metres, then divide again by the same height in metres. For example, 70 kg ÷ (1.70 m × 1.70 m) = 24.2.

**How do I calculate BMI in imperial units?**
Multiply your weight in pounds by 703, then divide by your height in inches squared. For example, a 154 lb person at 67 inches: (703 × 154) ÷ (67 × 67) ≈ 24.1.

**What are the BMI categories?**
WHO defines Underweight as below 18.5, Normal weight as 18.5–24.9, Overweight as 25–29.9, and Obesity as 30 and above, further split into Class I (30–34.9), Class II (35–39.9), and Class III (40+).

**What BMI is considered healthy?**
A BMI between 18.5 and 24.9 is classified as the healthy/normal range by WHO for most adults, though the healthy range narrows to roughly 18.5–22.9 under the WHO Asia-Pacific cutoffs sometimes recommended for South Asian populations.

**What is a healthy weight range for my height?**
Your healthy weight range is the weight span that keeps your BMI between 18.5 and 24.9 (or 18.5–22.9 under Asian cutoffs) at your current height. This calculator computes both ends of that range automatically and shows where your current weight sits on the scale.

**What is my ideal weight, and how is it calculated here?**
This tool averages four validated formulas — Devine, Robinson, Miller, and Hamwi — which estimate ideal body weight from height and sex. Averaging multiple formulas gives a more balanced estimate than relying on any single one.

**Is BMI different for men and women?**
The BMI formula and category thresholds are the same for men and women. However, women naturally carry more essential body fat than men at the same BMI, which is why this calculator's body fat, ideal weight, and BMR estimates use separate validated formulas for each sex.

**Is BMI accurate for older adults?**
BMI tends to under-represent body fat in older adults because muscle mass typically declines with age while fat mass may stay stable or increase, sometimes called sarcopenic obesity. Waist circumference and body composition measures are useful complements for adults over 65.

**Is BMI accurate for athletes and muscular people?**
No, not reliably. Muscle is denser than fat, so athletes and heavily muscled individuals can have a BMI in the overweight or obese range while carrying very low body fat. Enable Athlete Mode in Advanced Options to see a caveat, and rely more on the waist-based and body fat estimates in that case.

**Can I use BMI during pregnancy?**
Standard BMI categories don't apply during pregnancy because healthy weight gain is expected and varies by trimester and pre-pregnancy weight. Enable Pregnancy Mode to disable category interpretation — always follow your obstetrician's specific gestational weight gain guidance instead.

**What are the limitations of BMI?**
BMI doesn't distinguish muscle from fat, doesn't account for fat distribution, and can misclassify athletes, older adults, and some ethnic groups. It's a useful population-level screening tool, not an individual diagnostic measure — pair it with waist measurements and a clinical assessment where possible.

**What is waist-to-height ratio and why does it matter?**
Waist-to-height ratio (waist ÷ height) is a simple proxy for abdominal fat, which is more strongly linked to cardiometabolic risk than total body weight. A widely cited rule of thumb is to keep your waist circumference below half your height.

**What is waist-to-hip ratio?**
Waist-to-hip ratio (waist ÷ hip) indicates whether fat is stored more around the abdomen (apple shape) or hips/thighs (pear shape). WHO considers a ratio above 0.90 in men or 0.85 in women to indicate increased health risk.

**Does BMI measure body fat?**
No. BMI only uses weight and height — it cannot distinguish fat mass from muscle, bone, or water weight. It correlates with body fat at a population level but can be misleading for individuals with atypical body composition.

**How is body fat percentage estimated on this page?**
This tool uses the U.S. Navy circumference method, which estimates body fat from waist, neck, and height (plus hip for women) using validated logarithmic formulas. It's a reasonably accurate tape-measure estimate, though not as precise as a DEXA scan or hydrostatic weighing.

**What is BMR and how is it calculated?**
Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) is the energy your body needs at complete rest to maintain basic functions. This calculator uses the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, widely regarded as the most accurate predictive formula for BMR, based on your weight, height, age, and sex.

**What is TDEE and how is it different from BMR?**
Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE) is your BMR multiplied by an activity factor that accounts for exercise and daily movement. BMR alone reflects resting energy needs; TDEE estimates the calories you actually burn in a full day, which is the number to use for weight management.

**How many calories should I eat to lose weight?**
A deficit of about 500 kcal/day below your TDEE typically produces roughly 0.5 kg (about 1 lb) of weight loss per week, since roughly 7,700 kcal corresponds to 1 kg of body weight. Always avoid extreme deficits without medical supervision.

**How many calories should I eat to gain weight?**
A surplus of roughly 250–500 kcal/day above your TDEE supports gradual, mostly lean weight gain of about 0.25–0.5 kg per week; larger surpluses tend to add more fat relative to muscle.

**Is BMI different for Indian or South Asian populations?**
Research shows South Asians tend to develop cardiometabolic risk at lower BMI values than the global WHO cutoffs suggest, largely due to a tendency toward higher body fat percentage at the same BMI. The WHO Asia-Pacific guidelines lower the overweight cutoff to 23 and obesity to 27.5 — this calculator lets you switch to those cutoffs in Advanced Options.

**What do the WHO and CDC say about BMI?**
Both the World Health Organization and the U.S. CDC use the same core adult BMI categories (Underweight, Normal, Overweight, Obese) as a population-level screening tool, while explicitly noting that BMI does not directly measure body fat and should be interpreted alongside other health indicators.

**What are common BMI calculation mistakes?**
Common errors include mixing units, using outdated height, forgetting that BMI categories don't apply to children (who use age- and sex-specific percentile charts) or pregnant women, and treating a single BMI reading as a medical diagnosis rather than a screening signal.

**Is my health data stored or uploaded anywhere?**
No. Every calculation runs locally in your browser using JavaScript. Your height, weight, age, and any circumference measurements you enter are never transmitted to or stored on ToolAdda's servers.

**Is this BMI calculator free?**
Yes, completely free with no registration, no watermark, and unlimited use.

**When should I consult a doctor about my weight?**
Consult a healthcare professional if your BMI falls outside the normal range alongside other symptoms, if you have a family history of weight-related conditions, if you're planning significant weight change, or if you're pregnant, an athlete, elderly, or have a medical condition.

**Can I use this calculator on mobile?**
Yes. The interface is fully responsive and touch-friendly, with a sticky Calculate button on mobile so you can trigger a recalculation from anywhere on the page.

**Can I print or export my BMI report?**
Yes. After calculating, use the Print button to generate a clean printable summary of your results, or use Copy/Share to save or send your results as text.

**What is the difference between BMI for adults and children?**
Adult BMI uses fixed category cutoffs (18.5, 25, 30) regardless of age or sex. Children and teens are assessed using BMI-for-age percentile charts from the CDC or WHO growth standards, because healthy body fat naturally changes throughout growth — this calculator is designed for adults aged 18 and up.

#### How to calculate your GPA and CGPA

1. **Choose your grading scale** — Pick a 4.0, 10-point or 5-point preset, or edit the grade points directly to match your institution.
2. **Add your courses** — Enter each course's credit hours and select the grade you received to calculate your semester GPA (SGPA).
3. **Build your CGPA** — Send each semester's result to the Cumulative CGPA tab, or enter past semesters manually, to see your overall CGPA.
4. **Convert or plan ahead** — Use the CGPA-to-percentage and scale converters for official conversions, or the target tab to see what GPA you need next.

#### Frequently asked questions (24)

**What is the difference between GPA, SGPA and CGPA?**
GPA (Grade Point Average) measures performance over a set of courses. SGPA (Semester GPA) is the GPA for a single semester. CGPA (Cumulative GPA) is the credit-weighted average of all your SGPAs across every semester completed so far.

**How do you calculate GPA from grades and credit hours?**
Multiply each course's grade point by its credit hours, add up those totals, then divide by the total credit hours. For example, an A (4.0) in a 3-credit course contributes 12 grade points toward the average.

**How is CGPA calculated from multiple semesters?**
Multiply each semester's SGPA by that semester's total credits, add the results together, then divide by the combined credit hours across all semesters. This weights semesters with more credits more heavily, the same way individual courses are weighted within a semester.

**How do I convert CGPA to percentage?**
There is no single official formula - it depends on your university. Common approaches multiply CGPA by 9.5 or 9.4, or use the offset formula Percentage = (CGPA − 0.75) × 10 used by some Indian universities on a 10-point scale. Always confirm the exact formula with your institution for official purposes.

**What is a good GPA or CGPA?**
On a 4.0 scale, 3.5 or higher is generally considered excellent, 3.0-3.49 is good, and 2.0-2.99 is average. On a 10-point scale, 8.5 or higher is typically considered excellent and 7-8.5 is good, though classifications vary by university.

**How do I find out what GPA I need to reach a target?**
Enter your current GPA, current credit hours, target GPA, and remaining credit hours into the target calculator. It works out the average grade you need across the remaining credits, and flags it if that average would exceed the maximum possible on your scale.

**Can this calculator handle a 10-point, 4.0 or 5-point grading scale?**
Yes. Pick a preset grading scale or edit the grade labels and points directly - the semester GPA calculator recalculates automatically using whatever scale you set.

**What CGPA-to-percentage formula does VTU use?**
VTU (Visvesvaraya Technological University) commonly uses Percentage = (CGPA − 0.75) × 10 on its 10-point scale. Select the Offset formula in the CGPA ↔ Percentage tab to apply it — but always cross-check against your official VTU circular, since formulas are occasionally revised.

**What CGPA-to-percentage formula does Anna University use?**
Anna University typically publishes a direct grade-to-percentage conversion table rather than a single multiplier, though CGPA × 10 is commonly cited as an approximation. Check your official Anna University consolidated grade sheet or circular for the exact figure used for a given batch.

**How do I convert my Indian CGPA for a US, UK, Canadian, or Australian university application?**
Most international admissions offices accept a percentage equivalent (commonly CGPA × 9.5 on a 10-point scale) or ask for a formal credential evaluation from a service like WES (World Education Services) or ECA. Use this tool for a quick estimate, then follow your target university's official conversion requirement for the actual application.

**What is WES equivalency, and do I need it for my CGPA?**
WES (World Education Services) is a credential evaluation service that many US and Canadian universities and employers require to translate a foreign GPA/CGPA into their local scale. It's typically needed for formal admissions or immigration applications, not for a quick personal estimate — this calculator is the fast version; WES is the official one.

**Does a low GPA in one semester ruin my CGPA?**
It lowers it, but the effect shrinks as you complete more credits, since CGPA is a credit-weighted average across your whole program. Use the Target GPA tab to see exactly what average you need in future semesters to recover toward your goal.

**Can I improve my CGPA after graduation?**
Generally no — CGPA is fixed once your final transcript is issued. Some institutions allow backlog/improvement exams before the final transcript is finalized; check your university's specific policy.

**What GPA do I need for an MBA or Master's application?**
Requirements vary widely by program, but competitive Master's and MBA programs often look for a 3.0+ (4.0 scale) or roughly 7.0+ (10-point scale), alongside test scores, work experience, and essays. Check each program's published minimum GPA requirement directly.

**Is a 3.5 GPA good for grad school?**
Yes — a 3.5 on a 4.0 scale is generally considered strong for graduate school applications at most institutions, though highly competitive programs may expect higher, especially combined with strong test scores or research experience.

**Is 8.5 CGPA good in India?**
Yes — on the common 10-point scale used by most Indian universities, 8.5 or above is generally considered excellent and competitive for campus placements, higher studies, and scholarship applications.

**How many credits should I enter per course?**
Enter exactly the credit hours your university assigns to that course, as shown on your syllabus or transcript — this varies by institution and even by course type (lecture vs. lab), so there's no universal default.

**Can I use this calculator without knowing my exact credit hours?**
You'll get the most accurate result with real credit hours from your syllabus or transcript. If every course carries equal weight, entering the same credit value for each row produces a simple (unweighted) average instead.

**Does the calculator save my data?**
No. Everything you enter lives only in your browser tab's memory for that session — nothing is saved to a server, an account, or your device's storage, and it clears when you refresh or close the page.

**Can I use this on my phone?**
Yes. The layout, tables, and tabs are fully responsive and touch-friendly on mobile browsers.

**Is this GPA calculator accurate for my university?**
The math (weighted averaging) is universal and always accurate — what varies between universities is the grading scale and the CGPA-to-percentage formula, both of which you can edit directly in this tool to match your institution exactly.

**Does this tool work offline?**
Once the page has loaded, all calculations run locally in your browser's JavaScript engine without needing a network connection.

**Is this GPA/CGPA calculator free?**
Yes — completely free, with no signup, no watermark, and no limit on how many times you use it.

**How is this different from a basic GPA calculator?**
Most basic calculators only do one thing. This tool combines semester GPA, multi-semester CGPA, CGPA-to-percentage conversion (multiplier or offset formula), a proportional scale converter, and a target-GPA planner in one place, with a fully editable grading scale.

#### Frequently asked questions (18)

**What is a unit converter?**
A unit converter changes a measurement from one unit into another — kilometres into miles, kilograms into pounds, Celsius into Fahrenheit. This one covers fifteen categories and more than a hundred units, and shows the value in every unit of a category at once.

**How do I convert km to miles?**
Multiply kilometres by 0.621371. One mile is exactly 1,609.344 metres by international definition, so 100 km is 62.14 miles. Pick Length, set the units to kilometre and mile, and the tool does it as you type.

**How do I convert kg to lbs?**
Multiply kilograms by 2.20462. One pound is exactly 0.45359237 kilograms, which is an exact definition rather than a rounded figure, so 70 kg is 154.32 lb.

**How do I convert Celsius to Fahrenheit?**
Multiply by 9/5 and add 32, so 20 °C is 68 °F. Temperature is not a simple ratio because the scales have different zero points, which is why a converter that only multiplies gets it wrong. A useful check: −40 °C and −40 °F are the same temperature.

**Why is a US gallon different from a UK gallon?**
They are simply different units that share a name. A US gallon is 3.785411784 litres and an imperial gallon is 4.54609 litres, so the UK gallon is about 20 percent larger. Both are listed separately here so you never have to guess which one is meant.

**What is the difference between a US ton and a UK ton?**
A US short ton is 2,000 pounds and a UK long ton is 2,240 pounds, while a metric ton is 1,000 kilograms. All three are listed separately, because picking the wrong one is a 10 percent error.

**Why does my 1 TB hard drive show as 931 GB?**
Because two different definitions are in use. Drive makers sell a terabyte as one trillion bytes, while operating systems usually count in binary units of 1,024. One trillion bytes is 931.32 gibibytes, so nothing is missing — the two systems are just counting differently. This tool lists decimal and binary units separately so you can see both.

**How do I convert Mbps to MB/s?**
Divide by eight, because there are eight bits in a byte. A 100 Mbps connection downloads at about 12.5 MB/s at best. Internet plans are advertised in megabits while download managers usually report megabytes, which is why the numbers look so different.

**How do I convert mpg to L/100km?**
Divide 235.21 by the US mpg figure, so 30 mpg is about 7.84 L/100km. Fuel economy is inverse: a higher mpg means a lower L/100km, so you cannot convert it by multiplying. The tool handles that inversion for you.

**Is a US mpg the same as a UK mpg?**
No. They use different gallons, so the same car scores about 20 percent higher in UK mpg than in US mpg. Both are listed separately in the fuel economy category.

**How accurate are these conversions?**
Every factor is either an exact international definition — the inch, foot, mile, pound, gallon, atmosphere and nautical mile all have one — or is marked with a note explaining the assumption. Results are computed at full double precision and only rounded for display, and you control how much.

**Can I see a value in every unit at once?**
Yes. The all-units table below the converter shows your number in every unit of the current category simultaneously, with a copy button on each row. It is usually quicker than running a second conversion.

**Can I share or bookmark a conversion?**
Yes. The web address updates as you work, so bookmarking the page keeps the exact conversion. The Share button copies that link to your clipboard.

**Can I control the number of decimal places?**
Yes. Choose automatic, a fixed number of decimal places, or scientific notation, and set the precision from zero to twelve. You can also turn off digit grouping when you need a plain number to paste into a spreadsheet.

**What units does the converter support?**
Length, weight and mass, temperature, volume, area, speed, time, digital storage, data transfer, pressure, energy, power, angle, frequency and fuel economy — fifteen categories in total, with more than a hundred individual units.

**Does it work offline?**
Once the page has loaded, yes. Every conversion is calculated in your browser with no network request, so the tool keeps working if your connection drops.

**Is my data sent anywhere?**
No. Nothing you type is uploaded. Your recent conversions and display preferences are stored in your own browser only, and you can clear them at any time.

**Is this unit converter free?**
Yes. It is free, needs no account, and has no limits or watermarks.

#### बीघा को वर्ग फुट में कैसे बदलें

अपने राज्य का स्थानीय मान चुनकर बीघा, कट्ठा या किसी भी पारंपरिक इकाई को वर्ग फुट, गज या एकड़ में बदलने का तरीका।

1. **राज्य चुनें** — सबसे पहले ड्रॉपडाउन से अपना राज्य चुनें, क्योंकि बीघा और कट्ठा का आकार हर राज्य में अलग होता है।
2. **मान भरें** — जितनी ज़मीन नापनी है वह संख्या लिखें — जैसे 1, 2.5 या 0.75।
3. **इकाइयाँ चुनें** — किस इकाई से किस इकाई में बदलना है यह चुनें, जैसे बीघा से वर्ग फुट या एकड़ से बीघा।
4. **नतीजा देखें** — परिणाम तुरंत दिखता है, साथ में वर्ग फुट, गज, वर्ग मीटर, एकड़ और हेक्टेयर में पूरी तालिका भी।
5. **कीमत जोड़ें** — कीमत टैब में प्रति इकाई भाव भरकर पूरी ज़मीन की कुल कीमत और प्रति वर्ग फुट रेट देखें।
6. **स्थानीय पुष्टि करें** — रजिस्ट्री या खरीद-बिक्री से पहले तहसील, पटवारी या भू-अभिलेख से स्थानीय मान की पुष्टि ज़रूर करें।

#### Frequently asked questions (22)

**1 बीघा में कितने वर्ग फुट होते हैं?**
यह राज्य पर निर्भर करता है, क्योंकि बीघा कभी राष्ट्रीय स्तर पर मानक नहीं बना। उत्तर प्रदेश में पक्का बीघा आम तौर पर 27,000 वर्ग फुट माना जाता है, बिहार में 27,225 वर्ग फुट (20 कट्ठा), राजस्थान में पक्का बीघा 27,225 और कच्चा बीघा लगभग 17,424 वर्ग फुट, मध्य प्रदेश में लगभग 12,000 वर्ग फुट, और पंजाब-हरियाणा में 10,890 वर्ग फुट (एक एकड़ का चौथाई)। ऊपर टूल में अपना राज्य चुनें तो सही मान अपने आप लग जाएगा।

**बीघा हर राज्य में अलग क्यों होता है?**
बीघा एक पारंपरिक, मीट्रिक प्रणाली से पहले की इकाई है जिसे स्थानीय राजस्व प्रशासन तय करता था। इसलिए इसका आकार राज्य के हिसाब से, और कई जगह ज़िले या गाँव के हिसाब से भी बदलता है — आम तौर पर पक्का बीघा और कच्चा बीघा दो रूपों में।

**1 एकड़ में कितने बीघा होते हैं?**
यह भी राज्य के बीघा पर निर्भर है। 27,000 वर्ग फुट वाले उत्तर प्रदेश के पक्का बीघा से 1 एकड़ (43,560 वर्ग फुट) लगभग 1.61 बीघा होता है। पंजाब के 10,890 वर्ग फुट वाले बीघा से 1 एकड़ ठीक 4 बीघा होता है। बिहार के 27,225 वर्ग फुट वाले बीघा से 1 एकड़ लगभग 1.6 बीघा होता है।

**1 कट्ठा कितना होता है?**
कट्ठा (कठा या cottah) मुख्य रूप से बिहार, झारखंड, पश्चिम बंगाल और असम में चलता है और आम तौर पर उस इलाके के बीघा का 1/20 भाग होता है। बिहार में 1 कट्ठा आम तौर पर 1,361.25 वर्ग फुट (20 धुर) माना जाता है, जबकि असम में 1 कट्ठा लगभग 2,880 वर्ग फुट होता है।

**1 गुंठा में कितने वर्ग फुट होते हैं?**
1 गुंठा = 1,089 वर्ग फुट = 121 वर्ग गज = एक एकड़ का 1/40 भाग। यह इकाई महाराष्ट्र, गुजरात, कर्नाटक, ओडिशा और आंध्र प्रदेश-तेलंगाना में सबसे ज़्यादा चलती है और राज्य बदलने पर भी लगभग एक जैसी रहती है।

**1 कनाल और 1 मरला कितने वर्ग फुट के होते हैं? How big are 1 kanal and 1 marla?**
1 कनाल = 5,445 वर्ग फुट = एक एकड़ का 1/8 भाग = 20 मरला। 1 मरला = 272.25 वर्ग फुट = 30.25 वर्ग गज, और 1 सरसाही = 30.25 वर्ग फुट। ये इकाइयाँ पंजाब, हरियाणा, हिमाचल प्रदेश, जम्मू-कश्मीर और उत्तराखंड के कुछ हिस्सों में चलती हैं। 1 kanal = 5,445 sq ft = 1/8 acre = 20 marla. 1 marla = 272.25 sq ft = 30.25 sq yd, and 1 sarsahi = 30.25 sq ft. These are used in Punjab, Haryana, Himachal, Jammu & Kashmir and parts of Uttarakhand.

**1 गज में कितने वर्ग फुट होते हैं?**
1 गज यानी 1 वर्ग गज (square yard) = ठीक 9 वर्ग फुट। यह पूरे भारत में एक जैसा है, इसलिए प्लॉट की कीमत की तुलना करने के लिए गज और वर्ग फुट सबसे भरोसेमंद इकाइयाँ हैं।

**1 एकड़ में कितने वर्ग फुट होते हैं?**
1 एकड़ = ठीक 43,560 वर्ग फुट = 4,840 वर्ग गज = लगभग 4,046.86 वर्ग मीटर = 0.4047 हेक्टेयर। यह एक अंतरराष्ट्रीय मानक इकाई है, इसलिए किसी भी राज्य में इसका मान नहीं बदलता।

**1 हेक्टेयर में कितने एकड़ और वर्ग फुट होते हैं?**
1 हेक्टेयर = 10,000 वर्ग मीटर = लगभग 2.471 एकड़ = लगभग 1,07,639 वर्ग फुट। सरकारी भू-अभिलेख और खसरा-खतौनी में क्षेत्रफल अक्सर हेक्टेयर में ही लिखा होता है।

**पक्का बीघा और कच्चा बीघा में क्या अंतर है?**
पक्का बीघा बड़ा होता है और कच्चा बीघा उसका एक हिस्सा — कई इलाकों में लगभग एक-तिहाई या दो-तिहाई। यह विभाजन राजस्थान, उत्तर प्रदेश और मध्य प्रदेश के कई ज़िलों में मिलता है। किसी सौदे में यह ज़रूर पूछें कि भाव पक्का बीघा पर है या कच्चा बीघा पर, वरना अंतर लाखों का हो सकता है।

**1 डिसमिल या सतक कितना होता है?**
1 डिसमिल (Decimal या सतक) = 435.6 वर्ग फुट = एक एकड़ का 1/100 भाग। बिहार, झारखंड, पश्चिम बंगाल और ओडिशा के कागज़ों में ज़मीन का रकबा अक्सर डिसमिल में लिखा मिलता है।

**1 सेंट में कितने वर्ग फुट होते हैं?**
1 सेंट (Cent) = 435.6 वर्ग फुट = एक एकड़ का 1/100 भाग, यानी डिसमिल के बराबर। यह तमिलनाडु, केरल, कर्नाटक और आंध्र प्रदेश-तेलंगाना में सबसे ज़्यादा इस्तेमाल होती है।

**1 ग्राउंड कितने वर्ग फुट का होता है? How big is 1 ground?**
1 ग्राउंड = 2,400 वर्ग फुट। चेन्नई और तमिलनाडु-केरल के शहरी इलाकों में प्लॉट की कीमत आम तौर पर ग्राउंड में बताई जाती है। 1 ground = 2,400 sq ft. Plot prices in Chennai and urban Tamil Nadu/Kerala are commonly quoted per ground.

**1 बिस्वा और बिस्वांसी कितने होते हैं?**
बिस्वा बीघा का 1/20 भाग होता है और बिस्वांसी बिस्वा का 1/20 भाग। उत्तर प्रदेश में 27,000 वर्ग फुट वाले पक्का बीघा के हिसाब से 1 बिस्वा 1,350 वर्ग फुट और 1 बिस्वांसी 67.5 वर्ग फुट होता है।

**क्या इस कनवर्टर के मान रजिस्ट्री या कोर्ट में मान्य हैं?**
नहीं। यह टूल हर राज्य में सबसे ज़्यादा प्रचलित मान इस्तेमाल करता है और तुरंत अंदाज़ा लगाने के लिए बना है। कानूनी, रजिस्ट्री, बँटवारे या बिक्री के काम के लिए तहसील, पटवारी, हल्का कर्मचारी या राज्य के भू-अभिलेख पोर्टल से मिले आँकड़े ही मान्य होते हैं।

**क्या यह टूल मुफ़्त है और मेरा डेटा सेव करता है?**
यह पूरी तरह मुफ़्त है, इसमें कोई साइनअप नहीं है और कोई सीमा नहीं है। पूरी गणना आपके ही ब्राउज़र में होती है — आपके भरे गए आँकड़े या ज़मीन की कीमत किसी सर्वर पर नहीं भेजी जाती।

**ज़मीन की कीमत प्रति वर्ग फुट कैसे निकालें?**
पहले ज़मीन का क्षेत्रफल वर्ग फुट में बदलें, फिर कुल कीमत को उस संख्या से भाग दें। जैसे 2 बीघा (बिहार में 54,450 वर्ग फुट) की कीमत 60 लाख है तो भाव लगभग ₹110 प्रति वर्ग फुट बैठेगा। इस पेज के कीमत टैब में यह गणना अपने आप हो जाती है।

**क्या यह पेज हिंदी और English दोनों में चलता है?**
हाँ। यह पेज डिफ़ॉल्ट रूप से हिंदी में खुलता है और ऊपर दिए भाषा बटन से एक क्लिक में English में बदल जाता है। आपकी पसंद ब्राउज़र में सेव हो जाती है, इसलिए अगली बार वही भाषा खुलेगी।

**1 नाली कितने वर्ग फुट की होती है? How big is 1 nali?**
1 नाली = 2,160 वर्ग फुट, और इसमें 16 मुट्ठी होती हैं। यह इकाई उत्तराखंड के कुमाऊँ और गढ़वाल के पहाड़ी इलाकों में खेती की ज़मीन के लिए इस्तेमाल होती है। 1 nali = 2,160 sq ft and contains 16 muthi. It's used for hill farmland in Kumaon and Garhwal, Uttarakhand.

**1 अंकनम कितना होता है?**
1 अंकनम = 72 वर्ग फुट = 8 वर्ग गज। यह आंध्र प्रदेश और तेलंगाना में, खासकर घर बनाने वाले छोटे प्लॉट के लिए इस्तेमाल होती है।

**लंबाई और चौड़ाई से ज़मीन का क्षेत्रफल कैसे निकालें?**
चौकोर या आयताकार प्लॉट के लिए लंबाई × चौड़ाई करें। जैसे 60 फुट × 40 फुट का प्लॉट 2,400 वर्ग फुट का होता है, यानी लगभग 266.67 गज। इस पेज के कनवर्टर टैब में दिया प्लॉट कैलकुलेटर यही गणना करके उसे बीघा, कट्ठा या गुंठा में भी बदल देता है।

**क्या मैं अपना रूपांतरण किसी को भेज सकता हूँ?**
हाँ। 'लिंक कॉपी करें' बटन दबाने पर एक ऐसा लिंक बन जाता है जिसमें आपका राज्य, मान और चुनी हुई इकाइयाँ शामिल होती हैं — सामने वाला उसे खोलते ही वही नतीजा देखेगा।

#### Frequently asked questions (21)

**How does this image compressor work?**
Everything runs locally in your browser using the HTML5 Canvas API. Your image is drawn onto an in-memory canvas and re-encoded at a lower quality or smaller file size — no file is ever sent to a server.

**Is my image uploaded anywhere?**
No. Compression happens entirely on your device. Images never leave your browser, and nothing is stored or logged.

**Is this tool really free?**
Yes, completely free with no signup, no watermark, and no daily limit on how many images you can compress.

**Can I compress multiple images at once?**
Yes. Drag and drop or select as many images as you like, and they'll be compressed as a batch using the same settings.

**Which image formats can I upload?**
JPG, JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF, and BMP are supported everywhere. AVIF is supported for upload in browsers that can decode it. TIFF files can't be processed because no web browser can open them directly.

**Which formats can I compress my images into?**
You can output JPEG, PNG, or WebP. AVIF output is offered automatically only in browsers that support encoding AVIF from a canvas.

**Does compressing an image reduce its quality?**
Some quality change is inherent to compression. Balanced and High Quality modes keep loss visually unnoticeable; Maximum Compression trades more quality for a smaller file.

**What's the difference between Balanced, Maximum Compression, High Quality, and Custom?**
Balanced (75% quality) gives the best size-to-quality ratio for most photos. Maximum Compression (40%) produces the smallest possible file. High Quality (90%) keeps loss minimal for archival or print use. Custom lets you set an exact quality percentage or a target file size yourself.

**Can I compress an image to an exact file size, like 100 KB?**
Yes - switch to Custom mode and enter a target size in KB. The tool searches for the highest quality that still fits your target (JPEG/WebP/AVIF output only).

**Can I compress transparent PNG or WebP images?**
Yes. Transparency is detected automatically and preserved for PNG or WebP output. Choosing JPEG output will fill transparent areas white, since JPEG has no alpha channel.

**Does this tool remove EXIF and other metadata?**
Yes, automatically, as a side effect of redrawing the image on a canvas - there's no separate toggle needed.

**Can I resize an image before compressing it?**
Yes. Open the output settings panel, enable resizing, and set a max width and/or height — the image is scaled down before compression, which often gives a smaller file at higher visual quality than compression alone.

**Does it work on mobile phones?**
Yes. The interface is fully responsive and works with your phone's camera roll and file picker.

**Can I use this without an internet connection?**
Once the page and its scripts are loaded, compression itself needs no network connection, since it runs locally.

**Are my images stored anywhere after I close the tab?**
No. Everything lives in your browser's memory for the current session only, and is cleared when you close or refresh the tab.

**Can I compress AVIF images?**
You can upload and compress AVIF images if your browser can decode AVIF. Unsupported files show a clear message instead of failing silently.

**What happens if I upload an animated GIF?**
Only the first frame is used — browsers can't extract individual frames from a GIF through the Canvas API, so the result is a static compressed image, not an animation.

**Can I download all my compressed images at once?**
Yes. After compressing a batch, use "Download all (ZIP)" to get every result in one file, or download images individually.

**Why doesn't my PNG shrink as much as a JPG does?**
PNG is lossless, so it can only shrink through more efficient encoding, not by discarding pixel data. Try WebP output if file size matters more than format.

**Which browsers are supported?**
Any modern browser with Canvas API support - Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari all work. AVIF output appears automatically only where supported.

**Can beginners use this without any technical knowledge?**
Yes. The default Balanced mode requires no configuration — just add images and click Compress. Advanced controls are optional and tucked away for anyone who wants more precision.

#### Frequently asked questions (20)

**What is EXIF metadata?**
EXIF is embedded data inside many digital photos, including camera settings, timestamps, and sometimes GPS coordinates.

**What information can EXIF contain?**
Camera make/model, lens, exposure, dates, software, author/copyright, and GPS location among other fields.

**Why should I remove EXIF metadata?**
To reduce privacy risks before sharing photos online, especially GPS and device-identifying information.

**Can EXIF contain GPS location?**
Yes, when location services are enabled on a phone or camera that writes GPS tags.

**How do I remove GPS metadata from photos?**
Upload a JPG, PNG, or WebP file, confirm GPS in the inspector, then click Remove All Metadata. Verification uses a second scan of the cleaned file.

**Does removing EXIF reduce image quality?**
PNG stays lossless. JPEG and WebP use your selected quality (default 95%), which may introduce minor compression changes.

**Does the tool remove GPS metadata?**
Yes. Cleaned output is verified with a second scan to confirm GPS tags are not detected.

**Can I remove EXIF from JPG images?**
Yes. JPEG/JPG is fully supported for metadata scanning and removal.

**Can I remove metadata from PNG images?**
Yes. PNG textual chunks and other embedded metadata are stripped when the image is re-encoded through canvas output.

**Can I remove metadata from WebP images?**
Yes, in browsers that support WebP encoding via canvas. The cleaned file keeps the WebP format when supported.

**Does this tool support HEIC or iPhone photos?**
No. HEIC/HEIF is not supported here. Convert iPhone photos to JPG or PNG with our HEIC Converter , then use this tool on the converted file.

**Are my images uploaded?**
No. Images are processed locally in your browser. They are not uploaded to ToolAdda servers.

**Does this tool work offline after the page loads?**
Yes. Once the page and scripts are loaded, processing works offline because everything runs client-side.

**Can I remove metadata from multiple images?**
Yes. Upload multiple images, use Remove Metadata from All, and download results individually or as a ZIP.

**Can I download the cleaned image?**
Yes. Each cleaned image downloads with a -clean suffix, for example photo-clean.jpg.

**Does EXIF removal remove visible information from a photo?**
No. Metadata removal does not blur faces, erase signs, or change visible scene content. It only removes embedded data.

**Can metadata removal change image dimensions?**
No. The tool preserves original pixel dimensions unless you resize the image elsewhere.

**What is the difference between EXIF and other metadata?**
EXIF is one standard; images may also include XMP, IPTC, ICC, or format-specific metadata.

**Do Instagram or WhatsApp remove EXIF automatically?**
Often they strip or rewrite metadata when you post, but that is not guaranteed for every share path. Cleaning the file first is more reliable.

**Is the EXIF remover free?**
Yes. ToolAdda's EXIF Metadata Remover is free with no sign-up required.

#### Frequently asked questions (21)

**Is this image resizer free?**
Yes. ToolAdda's Image Resizer is completely free, with no watermark, no sign-up, and no limit on how many images you can resize.

**Are my images uploaded to a server?**
No. Every image is decoded and resized locally in your browser using the Canvas API. Nothing is uploaded, stored, or seen by ToolAdda — the only exception is the optional Import from URL feature, which fetches directly from the URL you provide.

**Can I resize an image without losing quality?**
Downscaling with a high-quality algorithm like Lanczos or Bicubic preserves detail very well. Upscaling, however, cannot add detail that was never captured — any resizer can only estimate new pixels, so keep expectations realistic for large upscales.

**What's the difference between resize by pixels and resize by percentage?**
Resize by pixels sets an exact width and height (e.g. 1080x1080). Resize by percentage scales the image proportionally (e.g. 50% makes it half the width and height) without needing to calculate exact target dimensions yourself.

**What is the difference between Fit, Fill, Stretch, and Crop?**
Fit scales the whole image to stay within your dimensions, preserving aspect ratio, without cropping. Fill scales to cover your exact dimensions and crops any overflow. Stretch forces the exact dimensions, ignoring aspect ratio. Crop extracts a region at your chosen size without scaling.

**Which resize algorithm should I use?**
Lanczos or Bicubic give the sharpest, most natural results for photos, especially when shrinking significantly. Bilinear is faster and fine for smaller size changes. Nearest Neighbor preserves hard pixel edges (useful for pixel art or icons) but looks blocky on photos.

**Can I resize images for Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, or other social platforms?**
Yes. The Presets panel includes ready-made sizes for Instagram posts and stories, Facebook posts and covers, LinkedIn posts and covers, X (Twitter), YouTube thumbnails and channel art, Pinterest pins, WhatsApp profile photos, and TikTok covers.

**Can I resize a photo for a passport or visa application?**
Yes, this tool includes the standard US passport (2x2in) and generic visa/Schengen (35x45mm) preset sizes at 300 DPI. For country-specific requirements, use ToolAdda's dedicated Passport Photo Maker.

**Does this tool support batch resizing multiple images?**
Yes. Select or drag in multiple images, set your resize options once, and every image is processed with the same settings. Download each result individually or all together as a ZIP file.

**Can I set the DPI of a resized image?**
Yes, for PNG and JPEG output. The DPI setting writes real metadata into the file (a PNG pHYs chunk or JPEG JFIF density field) that print software and design tools read correctly, rather than just relabeling the pixel dimensions.

**What image formats can I resize?**
JPG/JPEG, PNG, WebP, BMP, GIF, and SVG are supported natively in every modern browser. AVIF works in browsers that can decode it. HEIC/HEIF photos are converted automatically before resizing. TIFF is not supported, since browsers cannot decode it natively.

**Can I keep the image background transparent?**
Yes, when your output format is PNG or WebP. Enable Transparent Background in Advanced Settings; for JPEG output, which has no alpha channel, transparent areas are filled with your chosen background color instead.

**Does resizing remove EXIF metadata like GPS location?**
Yes, automatically. Canvas-based resizing re-encodes the image from raw pixels, so camera model, GPS coordinates, and other EXIF data are not carried over - a privacy-friendly side effect worth knowing about before sharing photos.

**Will my phone photos come out sideways?**
No. This tool automatically applies the photo's EXIF orientation tag during decoding, so portrait photos taken on a phone come out right-side-up in the resized output.

**Can I paste an image directly from my clipboard?**
Yes. Click Paste from Clipboard, or simply press Ctrl+V (Cmd+V on Mac) anywhere on the page after copying an image.

**Can I take a photo with my camera and resize it directly?**
Yes, on mobile devices. Tap Use Camera to open your device's camera and capture a photo directly into the resizer.

**Is there a limit on image size or number of images?**
No artificial limit is imposed. Very large images or large batches simply take longer to process since everything runs on your device's hardware rather than a server.

**Does this work on mobile devices?**
Yes. The interface is fully responsive and touch-friendly, including drag & drop equivalents, and camera capture is available on supported mobile browsers.

**Can I lock the aspect ratio while resizing?**
Yes. Enable Lock Aspect Ratio and changing the width automatically recalculates the height (and vice versa) to keep the original proportions.

**What is the maximum image quality I can export?**
PNG output is always lossless. For JPEG and WebP, the Quality slider goes up to 100%, which minimizes compression artifacts at the cost of a larger file size.

**Can I undo a resize and try different settings?**
Yes. The original image is never modified — adjust any setting and click Resize again to generate a fresh result, and previous configurations are saved in the History panel for one-click reuse.

**Are my photos uploaded to a server when I crop them?**

**What image formats can I crop?**

**Can I crop an image without losing quality?**
Yes. Cropping only removes pixels outside your selection — it doesn't re-compress or blur the pixels you keep. Choosing PNG (lossless) or a high JPEG/WebP quality setting for output preserves full detail in the cropped region.

**What's the difference between cropping and resizing?**
Cropping removes part of the image to change its composition or aspect ratio while keeping the remaining pixels at their original size. Resizing scales the entire image up or down without removing any content. This tool supports both — crop first, then optionally resize the cropped result.

**How do I crop an image to a specific aspect ratio?**

The rule of thirds divides the frame into a 3×3 grid; placing key subjects along those lines or intersections tends to produce more balanced, professional-looking compositions than dead-centering everything. Toggle the grid overlay to Rule of Thirds while positioning your crop box.

#### Frequently asked questions (27)

**What is image rotation and how does it work?**
Image rotation turns a photo around its center by a chosen angle. This tool redraws your image onto an HTML canvas at the new angle and exports a fresh file — no re-compression cycle beyond the single final export.

**Is my image uploaded to a server?**
No - rotation, flipping, cropping, and export all happen locally using the Canvas API.

**Will rotating my image reduce its quality?**
Rotating by 90°, 180°, or 270° is effectively lossless — every source pixel maps to exactly one output pixel. Free-angle rotation requires resampling at the rotated edges, which is standard for any rotation tool, but the rest of the image stays sharp, and you control the final export quality.

**What's the difference between rotating and flipping an image?**
Rotating turns the whole image around a center point by an angle. Flipping mirrors it across a horizontal or vertical axis without changing its angle — a rotated image looks turned, a flipped image looks mirrored.

**What is EXIF orientation and why do photos sometimes appear sideways?**
Many cameras and phones save photos in their native sensor orientation and store a separate EXIF 'Orientation' tag (values 1–8) describing how to display it correctly. If software ignores that tag, the photo can appear sideways or upside down even though the file itself wasn't rotated.

**Does this tool auto-correct EXIF orientation?**
Yes. Modern browsers decode images according to their EXIF orientation by default, so the preview and every export from this tool are already orientation-correct — and since canvas exports never carry EXIF metadata forward, the downloaded file displays correctly everywhere, even in older software that ignores EXIF.

**Can I rotate by an exact custom angle?**
Yes — use the free rotation slider or type an exact degree value for precise straightening, in addition to the 90°/180°/270° presets.

**What happens to the corners when I rotate by a non-90° angle?**
Rotating a rectangle by an angle that isn't a multiple of 90° leaves empty triangular corners in the new bounding box. You can fill them with a transparent background (PNG/WebP) or any solid color you choose.

**Can I choose a background fill color?**
Yes - pick white, black, or any custom color from the Background panel.

**Can I keep a transparent background after rotating?**
Yes, when exporting as PNG or WebP. JPEG doesn't support transparency, so a transparent selection automatically falls back to white for JPEG exports.

**Can I flip an image horizontally or vertically?**
Yes - both directions are available and combine correctly with any rotation angle.

**Can I undo a rotation?**
Yes - every action is tracked in an undo/redo history before you download.

**Can I crop after rotating?**
Yes - crop mode operates directly on the rotated preview, with free-form or locked aspect ratios.

**Can I rotate multiple images at once?**
Yes - batch mode applies one rotation setting across every uploaded image.

**Can I download all rotated images as a ZIP?**
Yes - batch exports package automatically into one ZIP file.

**What image formats can I upload?**
Any format your browser decodes - JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, and BMP in most browsers.

**What format can I export as?**
PNG, JPEG, or WebP, independent of your upload format.

**Is there a quality setting for JPEG/WebP export?**
Yes — a quality slider controls the compression level for lossy formats.

**Do I need to sign up or install anything?**
No — no account, email, or software install is required.

**Is this tool free?**
Yes — completely free with no limits or watermark.

**Does this work on mobile?**
Yes - touch-friendly controls work for rotate, flip, and crop.

**Is there a file size limit?**
No hard limit since nothing uploads - bound only by your device's memory.

**Why does my rotated JPEG have a white or black border?**
That's the background fill showing through the empty corners created by a non-90° rotation on a format without transparency. Choose PNG or WebP and a transparent background to avoid it, or pick a fill color that matches your use case.

**Can I compare the rotated image with the original?**
Yes — the before/after slider lets you drag to reveal the original versus the rotated result side by side.

**Is rotation lossless?**
90°/180°/270° rotation is pixel-for-pixel lossless. Free-angle rotation resamples pixels at the new edges like any rotation tool, but avoids the repeated JPEG re-compression loss you'd get from opening and re-saving a file multiple times in other software.

**How is this different from Canva or Adobe Express?**
No account, no upload, no subscription - full rotation, flip, crop, EXIF handling, and batch ZIP export for free.

**What happens to my image after I close the tab?**
Nothing is stored anywhere — your image only ever existed in your browser's memory, so closing the tab clears it completely.

### Image Watermark

Three placements: a single mark on any of nine anchor points, a **tiled** pattern on staggered rows across the whole frame, or a **diagonal** line corner to corner. Size, opacity, rotation (−90 to 90), edge margin and tile spacing are all sliders. Size, margin and spacing are percentages of the image's shorter side rather than fixed pixels, so one setting looks identical across a batch mixing phone shots and full-resolution camera exports, and tile spacing is computed from the mark's *rotated* footprint so angled marks never overlap. Batch any number of images with ZIP download and automatic numbering of duplicate filenames. Three things to state when recommending it: an animated GIF is flattened to its first frame; the working canvas is scaled down above roughly 16 megapixels because browsers cap canvas area; and the page itself says a watermark is a deterrent and an attribution, **not** protection — a corner mark can be cropped and a faint one painted out, which is why tiled and rotated is the recommendation when removal actually matters. #### Frequently asked questions (12)

**Are my photos uploaded to a server?**
No. Your images are read with the browser's File API and drawn onto a canvas on your own device. Nothing is sent anywhere, which is why the tool keeps working if you disconnect after the page has loaded.

**Does the output have a ToolAdda watermark on it?**
No. The only mark on the exported image is the one you added. There is no branding, no corner logo and no trial stamp.

**Can I watermark many photos at once?**
Yes. Add as many images as you like and the same settings apply to each one. Download all packages every result into a single ZIP. Because sizing is proportional, the mark covers the same share of each photo even in a batch of mixed resolutions.

**What image formats can I watermark?**
JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, BMP and AVIF can be read, and you can export as PNG, JPG or WebP. An animated GIF is flattened - the watermark is applied to the first frame only.

**Should I export as PNG or JPG?**
Use PNG when the original was a PNG, when the image has transparency, or when it contains text and sharp edges — PNG is lossless, so the watermark edges stay crisp. Use JPG for photographs you are publishing online, where the smaller file matters more than a perfectly clean edge. WebP usually beats both on size at the same visual quality, and every current browser supports it.

**Why can I still see the watermark clearly on a bright photo?**
The Outline option draws a thin edge in the opposite tone — dark behind a light watermark, light behind a dark one. A plain white watermark disappears against a white sky or a sheet of paper, so the outline is on by default. Turn it off if you want a softer, flatter mark.

**What is the difference between tiled and diagonal placement?**
Tiled repeats the mark across the whole image on a staggered grid, which is the hardest to crop out and is what proof and preview images normally use. Diagonal draws a single line of marks from corner to corner — lighter, and easier to see the photo through. Use a single corner placement when the watermark is branding rather than protection.

**Does a watermark stop someone stealing my photo?**
It raises the effort, it does not make theft impossible. A corner mark can be cropped and a faint one can be painted out. A tiled, rotated, medium-opacity mark is far harder to remove cleanly. Treat it as a deterrent and an attribution.

**Can I use my own logo or signature?**
Yes. Switch to the Logo tab and upload a PNG, JPG or SVG. A PNG with a transparent background works best because the image behind it shows through; a JPG logo will carry its own white box. If you need to prepare a signature first, the Signature Resizer can crop and clean it up.

**Does the watermark reduce my image quality?**
The pixels under the mark are altered by design; the rest is redrawn at the original resolution with no resizing. PNG and lossless WebP add no compression loss at all. A JPG export re-encodes once, so keep quality at 90 or above.

**Is there a file size or image resolution limit?**
There is no imposed limit, but browsers cap how large a canvas can be — roughly 16 megapixels on the strictest browsers. Above that the tool scales the working canvas down to stay inside the cap. Very large batches are limited by your device's memory rather than by any rule here.

**Can I watermark a PDF instead of an image?**
Yes, but with a different tool. Add Watermark to PDF applies a text or image mark across the pages of a PDF while keeping it a real PDF. This page is for raster images — JPG, PNG and WebP.

#### Frequently asked questions (26)

**What is a grayscale image?**
A grayscale image uses only shades of gray from black to white, with no colour information. Each pixel stores a single brightness value instead of red, green and blue.

**How do I convert an image to grayscale?**
Upload your image, preview the black-and-white result with the slider, adjust the intensity if you like, then download the grayscale version.

**Is this tool free?**
Yes, it is completely free with no signup, no watermark and no limits.

**Will the image quality change?**
Only the colour is removed; resolution and detail are preserved. Exporting as PNG is lossless, while JPG and WebP let you pick a quality level.

**Can I convert PNG to grayscale?**
Yes. PNG, JPG, WebP, GIF and BMP images are all supported.

**Can I convert JPG images?**
Yes. JPG and JPEG images convert to grayscale instantly.

**Does grayscale reduce file size?**
Often yes, because colour data is removed — especially when you export as JPG or WebP. The exact saving depends on the image.

**Can I use it on mobile?**
Yes. The converter is mobile-first with touch support for the before/after slider.

**Is my image stored or uploaded?**
No. Conversion happens entirely in your browser; your images are never uploaded to a server.

**Do I need to install software?**
No installation needed — it works right in your browser on any device.

**Can I convert multiple images at once?**
Yes. Add several images and download them all as a single ZIP of grayscale versions.

**Is there a file size limit?**
There is no hard limit, but very large images are scaled to a sensible maximum on export for performance while keeping high quality.

**Can I convert WebP images?**
Yes. WebP images are supported for both input and output where your browser allows.

**How fast is the conversion?**
Instant. The preview updates in real time and the download is produced in a moment because everything runs locally.

**Can I control how strong the grayscale is?**
Yes. The intensity slider lets you go from a subtle partial desaturation to a full black-and-white conversion.

**Is the conversion secure?**
Yes. Because the image never leaves your device, it's safe for private photos, documents and screenshots.

**What is the difference between grayscale and desaturation?**
They usually produce the same result but are defined differently. Desaturation pulls the saturation of every colour to zero, while grayscale converts each pixel to a single luminance value weighted for how bright the human eye perceives red, green and blue. This tool uses the luminance method, which keeps relative brightness closer to what you saw in the original.

**Does converting to grayscale reduce image quality?**
No. Resolution, sharpness and detail are untouched — only the colour information is discarded. If you export as JPG or WebP the quality slider controls compression, exactly as it would for a colour image. Export as PNG if you want no compression loss at all.

**Can I convert a grayscale image back to colour?**
Not with this tool, and not faithfully with any tool. Converting to grayscale throws the colour information away permanently, so the original hues cannot be recovered. Always keep your colour original if you might need it later.

**What is the best format to save a grayscale image?**
Use JPG or WebP for photographs, where the smaller file matters and slight compression is invisible. Use PNG for logos, screenshots, line art or anything with transparency, because it is lossless and keeps edges crisp.

**Why does my grayscale image look flat or washed out?**
Colours that differ in hue but match in brightness collapse to the same grey. A red and a green of similar luminance become almost identical. Try the intensity slider at around 80–90% to keep a hint of colour separation, or adjust contrast in an image editor after converting.

**Does grayscale work on images with transparency?**
Yes. Transparency is preserved when you export as PNG or WebP. Exporting as JPG flattens transparent areas onto a white background, because the JPG format has no alpha channel.

**How does the intensity slider work?**
At 100% the image is fully grayscale. Lower values blend the grayscale result back toward the original colour, so 40% gives a muted, partly desaturated look. It is the same blend the CSS grayscale() filter performs, so the preview and the downloaded file match exactly.

**Can I convert HEIC or RAW files?**
Only if your browser can decode them, which most cannot for RAW and many cannot for HEIC. Convert those to JPG or PNG first — our HEIC converter handles iPhone photos — then bring the result here.

**Is grayscale the same as monochrome?**
Not quite. Monochrome means an image built from a single hue, which may be grey but could equally be sepia or blue-toned. Grayscale specifically means shades of grey between black and white.

**Does this converter work offline?**
Once the page has loaded, the conversion itself needs no network — everything runs on your device. If you reload without a connection the page may not load, but an already-open tab keeps working.

#### Frequently asked questions (28)

**What is an image color picker?**
An image color picker is a tool that lets you click any pixel in an uploaded image and instantly read its exact color value in formats like HEX, RGB, and HSL — useful for matching brand colors, building palettes, and design work.

**Is my image uploaded to a server?**
No - everything runs client-side using the Canvas API; your image is never transmitted anywhere.

**How accurate is the color picked from my image?**
Sampling reads the true full-resolution pixel data, not a downscaled preview, so values match the real source pixel.

**What's the difference between HEX, RGB, HSL, HSV, CMYK, and LAB?**
HEX/RGB describe screen light directly, HSL/HSV describe hue-saturation-lightness intuitively, CMYK approximates print ink, and LAB is a perceptually uniform color-science model.

**Why do RGB and CMYK give different-looking colors for print?**
RGB is an additive light model used by screens; CMYK is a subtractive ink model used by printers. The CMYK conversion shown is a standard approximation — always verify against your actual printer's color profile for critical print work.

**What is the magnifier and pixel inspector for?**
Hovering shows a zoomed circular magnifier with a pixel grid so you can see exactly which pixel your cursor is over before clicking, which matters for fine detail like anti-aliased edges.

**Can I pick a color from anywhere on my screen, not just the uploaded image?**
In supporting browsers (Chrome and Edge), a native screen EyeDropper button lets you sample any pixel on your entire screen, not only inside the uploaded image.

**How is the color palette generated?**
Dominant colors use median-cut quantization, which groups similar pixels for a cleaner result than simple frequency counting.

**What's the difference between dominant colors and average color?**
Dominant colors are the most visually distinct clusters; average color blends every pixel into one value, which can look muddy on high-contrast images.

**Can I generate a gradient from my image?**
Yes - the Palette tab turns your extracted colors into a ready-to-use CSS linear-gradient() string.

**What is a WCAG contrast ratio?**
A 1:1-21:1 measure of luminance difference between two colors, used to ensure text stays readable for users with low vision.

**What's the difference between AA and AAA contrast?**
AA requires at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text — the common legal/practical baseline. AAA requires 7:1 and 4.5:1 respectively — a stricter, enhanced standard.

**Can I export colors as CSS variables?**
Yes - the Export tab generates a ready-to-paste :root block for your current palette.

**Can I export a Tailwind config?**
Yes - a Tailwind colors object is generated, ready for tailwind.config.js.

**Can I export Bootstrap SCSS variables?**
Yes - Bootstrap-style $variable declarations are generated from your palette.

**What is a Material-style tonal palette?**
A 50-900 lightness scale from a base color, similar in spirit to Material Design tonal palettes - an approximation, not the exact Google algorithm.

**Can I save favorite colors?**
Yes - star any picked color to save it to Favorites, stored in your browser across visits.

**Are recent or favorite colors stored online?**
No - both lists live only in your browser's local storage on your own device.

**What image formats are supported?**
Any format your browser decodes natively - JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, BMP, and SVG in most browsers.

**Is there a file size limit?**
No artificial limit - large images are bound only by your device's available memory.

**Can I use this for brand color extraction?**
Yes - upload a logo and use dominant-color extraction or manual sampling to recover exact brand HEX values.

**Can I use this for accessibility audits?**
Yes - sample text and background colors from a screenshot and instantly check WCAG AA/AAA contrast.

**Does this work on mobile and touch devices?**
Yes — tap to sample a color on touch devices; the magnifier and precision tools work best on a larger screen.

**Do I need to sign up?**
No account, email, or signup is required for any feature.

**Is this tool free?**
