#### Frequently asked questions (27)

**What is a JPG to PNG converter?**
A JPG to PNG converter reads a JPG/JPEG photo's pixel data and re-encodes it as a PNG file — a lossless format that adds transparency support and eliminates further JPEG compression artifacts on every future re-save.

**Is this JPG to PNG converter free?**
Yes. It's completely free with no watermark, no sign-up, and no limit on how many images you convert.

**Are my images uploaded to a server?**
No. Every conversion runs locally in your browser using the Canvas API. Your photos are never uploaded, stored, or seen by ToolAdda.

**Does converting JPG to PNG improve image quality?**
No. Converting can't restore detail a JPG already lost to compression — it simply stops any further lossy compression from happening again. The benefit is that the PNG output and every subsequent edit stay pixel-perfect from that point forward.

**Can I make the background transparent when converting JPG to PNG?**
JPG files never contain a transparency channel, so there's no hidden transparency to "unlock." This tool adds real transparency using a chroma-key: pick a background color (like white) and a tolerance, and matching pixels become transparent in the PNG. For subject-based background removal, use ToolAdda's dedicated Background Remover instead.

**How does the transparent background (chroma-key) feature work?**
Enable Transparent Background, pick the color to remove (default white) and a tolerance percentage, and every pixel within that color distance becomes transparent (or is replaced with a different solid color in Replace mode). It works best on solid, evenly lit backgrounds like product photos, scanned logos, or white-background portraits.

**Why isn't my whole background transparent after using chroma-key?**
JPEG compression introduces small color variations even in "solid" backgrounds, and uneven lighting or shadows shift the color further. Increase the tolerance slider gradually until the background clears — but going too high risks also clearing similar colors inside your subject.

**Will PNG output always be lossless?**
Yes. PNG uses lossless DEFLATE compression, so every pixel from the source image (or from your rotate/flip/resize/transparency settings) is preserved exactly, with no additional generation loss like repeated JPEG saves would cause.

**Why is my converted PNG file larger than the original JPG?**
This is expected and not a bug. JPEG's lossy compression discards detail to shrink file size; PNG keeps every pixel, so photographic images typically produce a noticeably larger PNG than the source JPG - a fundamental format trade-off, not a flaw in the conversion.

**Can I convert multiple JPG images at once?**
Yes. Select or drag in multiple files, apply one set of settings, and convert them all in a single batch. Download each PNG individually or all together as a ZIP.

**Can I resize, rotate, or flip images while converting?**
Yes. Rotate in 90° steps, flip horizontally or vertically, and optionally resize to an exact width or height with aspect ratio locked — all applied before the PNG is generated, visible live in the before/after preview.

**Does this tool preserve image resolution and DPI?**
Pixel resolution is preserved exactly unless you enable resizing. For DPI, this tool reads the original JPEG's DPI (from its JFIF header, when present) and writes a genuine PNG pHYs metadata chunk into the output, or you can set a custom DPI value instead.

**Does this tool preserve EXIF metadata?**
No, and this is intentional. Canvas-based conversion re-encodes the image from raw pixels, which strips EXIF metadata like camera model, GPS location, and timestamps - a privacy benefit if you plan to share the PNG publicly. Orientation is the one exception: it's read and applied correctly before conversion.

**Why does my photo rotate correctly even though I didn't set a rotation?**
Phone cameras often save a photo's EXIF orientation tag rather than physically rotating the pixels. This tool decodes images with the browser's imageOrientation: "from-image" option, which automatically applies that tag, so portrait photos come out right-side-up without you touching the Rotate setting.

**Can I use my camera to capture and convert a photo directly?**
Yes, on mobile devices. Tap Use Camera to open your device's camera and capture a photo directly into the converter.

**Can I paste an image from my clipboard?**
Yes. Copy an image, then press Ctrl+V (Cmd+V on Mac) anywhere on the page to add it to the conversion queue.

**What image formats can I upload?**
This tool accepts JPG and JPEG files specifically. For other source formats, ToolAdda has dedicated converters — including a HEIC Converter and a PNG to WebP Converter.

**Is there a limit on file size or number of images?**
No artificial limit is imposed. Very large images or large batches simply take longer since everything processes on your device's hardware rather than a server.

**Can I rename the output files?**
Yes. Set an optional filename prefix in Advanced Settings, and it's applied to every converted file in the batch.

**How do I download all converted images at once?**
After converting more than one image, a Download All (ZIP) button appears, packaging every converted PNG into a single ZIP archive.

**Does this work on mobile devices?**
Yes. The interface is fully responsive and touch-friendly, with camera capture available on supported mobile browsers and a sticky Convert button for quick access.

**Is this JPG to PNG converter free forever, with no watermark?**
Yes. No watermark is ever added to your output, there's no account requirement, and there's no premium tier gating core features.

**What is the difference between JPG and PNG?**
JPG uses lossy compression optimized for photographs and small file sizes, with no transparency support. PNG uses lossless compression that preserves every pixel exactly and supports a transparency (alpha) channel, typically at the cost of a larger file size for photographic content.

**When should I use PNG instead of JPG?**
Use PNG for logos, icons, screenshots, graphics with text or sharp edges, and anything needing transparency — situations where exact pixel fidelity matters more than file size.

**When should I use JPG instead of PNG?**
Use JPG for photographs and photo-realistic images where smaller file size matters more than perfect pixel fidelity — most web photography, email attachments, and social media images.

**Can I convert PNG back to JPG?**
This page is dedicated to JPG-to-PNG conversion. For the reverse direction, use any of ToolAdda's other image tools that export JPG, such as the Image Resizer or Image Compressor, which both support JPG output.

**Does this tool work offline?**
Once the page is loaded, core conversion works without a network connection, since everything runs in your browser's JavaScript engine. Downloading the page itself and the optional ZIP library still require an initial connection.

#### Frequently asked questions (32)

**What is WebP?**
WebP is an image format developed by Google for the web. It supports both lossy and lossless compression as well as transparency and animation, and it is designed to produce smaller files than PNG or JPEG at comparable visual quality. Every current browser can display it.

**How do I convert PNG to WebP?**
Drop your PNG files onto the upload area or use Select images. Leave the output set to WebP, adjust the quality slider if you want, then press Convert. Each result shows its new size next to the original, with a Download button.

**How do I convert JPG to WebP?**
Exactly as for PNG — the tool accepts .jpg and .jpeg alongside PNG and WebP. Add the files, keep WebP as the output format, set a quality and convert. You can mix PNG and JPG files in the same batch.

**How do I convert JPEG to WebP?**
JPEG and JPG are the same format with two common extensions, so the process is identical. Files ending .jpeg are accepted and converted the same way, and the output is named with a .webp extension.

**Can I convert WebP to PNG?**
Yes. Add your WebP files and change the output format to PNG. PNG supports transparency, so any transparent areas in the source are preserved.

**Can I convert WebP to JPG?**
Yes. Change the output format to JPG. Because JPG has no alpha channel, if any of your images contain transparency the tool asks you to choose a background colour and fills the transparent areas with it rather than picking one silently.

**Does WebP reduce file size?**
Usually, but not always. WebP typically produces smaller files than PNG for photographs and than JPEG at similar quality, though the result depends on the image content and the quality setting. Re-encoding an already well-optimised file can make it larger — when that happens this tool says the output is larger rather than reporting a saving.

**Is WebP smaller than PNG?**
For photographic content, almost always and often dramatically, because PNG is lossless and stores every pixel exactly. For flat graphics, logos and screenshots with few colours the gap narrows and PNG can occasionally win. The tool shows the actual numbers for your file.

**Is WebP smaller than JPG?**
Generally yes at comparable visual quality, though the margin varies with the image and the encoder. The browser's built-in WebP encoder is not the most aggressive available, so results here may differ from a command-line tool such as cwebp.

**Is WebP better than PNG?**
For most web imagery, yes — smaller files with transparency support. PNG remains the better choice when you need guaranteed lossless output, when you are editing and re-saving repeatedly, or when a tool in your pipeline does not read WebP.

**Is WebP better than JPG?**
For the web, usually: smaller at similar quality, and it supports transparency, which JPG cannot. JPG is still the safer choice for maximum compatibility with older software, cameras and print workflows.

**Does WebP support transparency?**
Yes. WebP supports an alpha channel in both its lossy and lossless modes, which is one of its main advantages over JPG. Converting a transparent PNG to WebP keeps the transparency.

**Does JPG support transparency?**
No. The JPEG format has no alpha channel at all. Any transparent area has to be filled with a solid colour, which is why this tool asks you to choose one before converting a transparent image to JPG.

**Is WebP lossless?**
WebP supports both lossy and lossless encoding. However, the browser's canvas encoder used by this tool produces lossy WebP only — quality 100 is the highest lossy setting, not lossless. If you need true lossless WebP, use a command-line encoder such as cwebp with its lossless flag.

**What quality should I use for WebP?**
80 is a good default for photographs and is what this tool starts with. Drop to 60–70 for large background images where fine detail does not matter, and raise to 90 for images with text or sharp edges. Compare a few settings on your own image rather than trusting a single number.

**Does conversion reduce image quality?**
Converting to WebP or JPG is lossy, so some information is discarded — how much depends on the quality setting. Converting to PNG is lossless, but a lossy source cannot regain detail it never had, so a WebP converted to PNG will not look better than the WebP did.

**Can I convert multiple images at once?**
Yes. Select or drop as many files as you like and press Convert. They are processed a few at a time rather than all at once, which keeps memory use bounded, and the progress indicator reports genuine completion rather than an animation.

**Can I download all converted images at once?**
Yes. Download all packages every converted image into a single ZIP that is built in your browser. If ZIP creation is unavailable, the files are downloaded individually instead.

**Can I resize images while converting?**
Yes. Resize by a custom width or height, by percentage, or by capping the longest edge to a preset such as 1920px. Aspect ratio is locked by default, so nothing is stretched unless you deliberately unlock it.

**What do the resize presets mean?**
They cap the longest edge of the image. A 1920px preset applied to a 3000×2000 photo produces 1920×1280; applied to a portrait 2000×3000 it produces 1280×1920. Images already smaller than the cap are left alone rather than being enlarged.

**Are my images uploaded to a server?**
No. Decoding, resizing, encoding and downloading all happen in your browser using the Canvas API. No network request carries your image data, and nothing is stored once you close the tab.

**Can I use this tool offline?**
Once the page has loaded, conversion needs no network at all, so an already-open tab keeps working without a connection. Loading the page fresh does require the network.

**Does conversion keep EXIF metadata?**
No. Browser-based conversion through the Canvas API discards metadata such as EXIF, including camera settings and any GPS coordinates. That is often desirable for privacy, but if you need to keep the metadata you will need a tool that copies it across explicitly.

**Will my photos be rotated incorrectly?**
No. Images are decoded with the orientation flag applied, so a portrait photo from a phone converts the right way up. Because the rotation is baked into the pixels, the result stays correct even though the EXIF orientation tag itself is not carried over.

**How large an image can I convert?**
There is a 30 MB per-file limit and a warning for images beyond roughly 40 megapixels, because very large canvases can exhaust browser memory. This is a browser constraint rather than a policy — a desktop application will handle bigger files.

**What happens if two files have the same name?**
The second gets a numbered suffix — image.webp, then image-1.webp — so one download cannot overwrite another in your downloads folder.

**Which formats can I upload?**
PNG, JPG, JPEG and WebP are fully supported. GIF and BMP are accepted where your browser can decode them, and animated GIFs convert as a single frame. Anything the browser cannot decode fails with a clear message rather than producing a broken file.

**Why did my file get larger after conversion?**
Usually because the source was already well compressed, or because a flat graphic with few colours was re-encoded with a lossy codec. Try a lower quality, or keep PNG for logos and screenshots. The tool tells you plainly when the output is larger instead of showing a saving.

**Does WebP improve website speed?**
Smaller images reduce transfer size, which usually helps — but page speed depends on the whole page. If your slowest element is a render-blocking script or a large font, converting images will not fix it. Measure before and after rather than assuming.

**Does WebP improve Core Web Vitals?**
It can help Largest Contentful Paint when the LCP element is an image, because a smaller file arrives sooner. It does nothing for Cumulative Layout Shift unless you also set width and height attributes, and nothing at all for Interaction to Next Paint.

**How do I use WebP on my website?**
Use a picture element with a WebP source and a JPG or PNG fallback, and the browser picks whichever it supports. All current browsers take the WebP, and older ones fall back automatically without any JavaScript.

**Is this converter free?**
Yes. Free, no sign-up, no email address, no watermark and no per-file charge.

#### Frequently asked questions (18)

**What size is a passport photo?**
It depends on the country. India, the UK, the Schengen area, Australia and Japan all use 35 by 45 mm. The United States uses 2 by 2 inches. Canada and Brazil use a larger 50 by 70 mm. This tool has 24 presets so you do not have to look it up.

**What is 35x45 mm in pixels?**
413 by 531 pixels at 300 DPI, which is the resolution almost every authority expects for a printed photo. At 600 DPI it would be 827 by 1063 pixels. Pixels alone are meaningless without a DPI, which is why this tool always states both.

**Why does DPI matter for a passport photo?**
Because a passport photo is a physical size, not a pixel count. A file can be exactly 413 by 531 pixels and still print at the wrong size if the DPI stored inside it is wrong. This tool writes the correct resolution into the JPEG header so the print comes out at 35 by 45 mm.

**How big should the head be in a passport photo?**
Most authorities specify it as a fraction of the photo height — commonly between 62 and 80 percent from chin to crown, though Canada and Brazil use a smaller fraction on their larger photo. The guide overlay is drawn from the published figure for whichever preset you pick.

**Can I make a passport photo with a white background?**
Yes. Choose white from the background swatches and it fills any area your photo does not cover. Note that this fills behind and around the photo — it does not cut your subject out of a busy background, so start from a photo taken against a plain wall.

**Does this tool remove the background automatically?**
No, and it is worth being clear about that. It sets the background colour behind and around your photo, but it does not detect and cut out the person. For that, use the Image Background Remover first, then bring the result here to size it.

**How do I resize a photo to 20 KB or 50 KB?**
Enter the limit in the target file size box. The tool searches JPEG quality settings to find the highest quality that fits your budget, and tells you honestly if the target cannot be reached without making the photo unusable.

**What size photo does SSC or UPSC need?**
Most Indian exam portals ask for around 200 by 230 pixels with a file between 20 and 50 KB, and there are presets for that. Portals change their requirements most years, so always check the current information bulletin before you upload.

**What size is a PAN card photo?**
25 by 35 mm, which is 295 by 413 pixels at 300 DPI. It is smaller than a passport photo, so a passport-sized image will not be accepted in its place.

**What size is a US visa or passport photo?**
2 by 2 inches, which is 600 by 600 pixels at 300 DPI, and it is square rather than portrait. US rules also measure the head from chin to crown at between 1 and 1 3/8 inches.

**Can I print several photos on one sheet?**
Yes. Choose a sheet size — 4 by 6 inch, 5 by 7 inch, A4, US Letter or 3.5 by 5 inch — and the tool works out how many copies fit, arranges them with a gap and optional cut marks, and exports the sheet at print resolution.

**Why does it warn that my photo is being enlarged?**
Because enlarging cannot add detail. If your source photo has fewer pixels than the target size needs, the result is soft and blurry, which is a common rejection reason. The warning appears so you can find a higher-resolution original instead of discovering the problem at the counter.

**Is my photo uploaded to a server?**
No. The photo is read by your browser, cropped on a canvas and saved straight back to your device. It never leaves your computer, which matters because a passport photo is identity data.

**Is there a watermark on the download?**
No. There is no watermark, no sign-up and no limit on how many photos you make.

**Can I use a selfie for a passport photo?**
Usually not well. Phone front cameras are wide-angle and held close, which distorts facial proportions, and most authorities reject photos that look like selfies. Have someone else take the photo from about two metres away with the rear camera.

**What should I wear and how should I pose?**
Face the camera squarely with a neutral expression and both eyes open and visible. Avoid hats, sunglasses and heavy shadows, and wear something that contrasts with the background so your shoulders do not disappear into it. Religious head coverings are generally allowed provided the full face is visible.

**Will this photo definitely be accepted?**
The tool gets the size, resolution and background right, and its guides reflect published head-size rules, but acceptance also depends on lighting, expression, shadows and the quality of your original photo — none of which software can judge for you. Always check the current requirements of the authority you are applying to.

**Which file format should I choose?**
JPEG for almost everything — it is what portals and print shops expect, and it is the only format that can carry a target file size. Choose PNG only if you specifically need a lossless file, since PNG photos are much larger.

#### How to print a large poster on multiple A4 or Letter pages

Split one image across several sheets of ordinary printer paper and assemble them into a large poster.

1. **Upload your image** — Drag your image into the upload box, paste it from the clipboard, or press Browse image. Nothing is uploaded to a server — the file is read directly by your browser.
2. **Choose paper size and orientation** — Pick A4, A3, Letter, Legal, Tabloid or a custom size, then portrait or landscape. The tool preselects A4 or Letter based on your region, and you can change it at any time.
3. **Set the finished poster size** — Set the size by page grid, by real-world width and height, or by magnification percentage. The live preview and page count update instantly.
4. **Check the quality advisor** — Read the effective PPI shown for your chosen size. Above 150 PPI prints sharply at arm's length. If it says Poor, reduce the poster size or use a higher-resolution image.
5. **Choose how the pages will join** — Pick Overlap and glue for a forgiving join with a shaded glue band, or Trim and butt-join for a seamless edge-to-edge finish with printed cut marks.
6. **Generate and download the PDF** — Press Generate PDF. Each page is rendered one at a time at your chosen DPI and combined into a single multi-page PDF that downloads to your device.
7. **Print at 100 percent, not Fit to Page** — In your print dialog set Scale to 100% or Actual Size and turn off Fit to Page or Shrink oversized pages. Scaling the print is the single most common reason tiled pages fail to line up.
8. **Assemble the poster** — Lay the pages out using the numbered assembly guide, work left to right and top to bottom, trim the leading margins, then glue or tape each sheet to its neighbour.

#### Frequently asked questions (20)

**Is this poster printer free?**
Yes, completely and without limits. There is no trial, no page cap, no paid tier and no watermark on the output. You can generate as many posters of as many pages as your device can handle.

**Do I need to sign up or install anything?**
No. There is no account, no email capture and nothing to download. It is a web page — open it and use it. You can optionally add it to your home screen to run it like an app and use it without a connection.

**Is my image uploaded to a server?**
No. Your image is read directly by your browser and every step - decoding, tiling, rendering and PDF assembly - happens on your device. You can verify this yourself: open developer tools, go to the Network tab, and generate a poster. No request carries your file. This is why the tool is safe for paid sewing patterns, client work under NDA and confidential drawings.

**What image formats can I use?**
JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, GIF, BMP and SVG all work directly, as long as your browser can decode them. SVG is rasterised at your chosen output DPI so it stays crisp at any size. HEIC (the default iPhone format) cannot be decoded by most desktop browsers - convert it first with our HEIC converter . PDF source files are not yet supported directly; use the PDF to images converter in the meantime.

**Can I use a PDF as the source?**
Not yet directly. Convert the page you need to a PNG at high resolution with our PDF to images converter , then bring that image here. Direct PDF input, including picking a page from a multi-page file, is the next major feature planned.

**What paper sizes are supported?**
A0 through A6, the ISO B series, JIS B4 and B5, US Letter, Legal, Tabloid/Ledger and Executive, plus any custom size you type in millimetres, centimetres or inches. Each can be portrait or landscape, and there is an auto option that picks whichever orientation needs fewer pages.

**How many pages will my poster need?**
It depends on your paper size, your printer margins and how much area the join consumes. The tool shows the exact count live as you change settings. As a rough guide on A4 portrait with a 10 mm overlap: 4 pages gives about 38 × 55 cm, 12 pages about 57 × 110 cm, and 16 pages is close to A0.

**Why does my poster look blurry?**
Because the source image does not have enough pixels for the size you printed. Printing bigger spreads existing pixels further apart; it never adds detail. Check the effective PPI shown in the quality advisor - below 100 PPI will look soft at close range. Either reduce the poster size, find a higher-resolution original (messaging apps heavily recompress photos), enlarge it with the image resizer , or switch to halftone mode where low resolution becomes a deliberate style.

**What resolution image do I need for a large poster?**
Multiply the finished width in inches by your target PPI. For a 100 cm (39.4 in) wide poster at a comfortable 150 PPI you want about 5900 pixels of width. At 100 PPI - perfectly acceptable for a wall poster viewed from two metres - about 3900 pixels is enough. A modern phone photo at 4032 px prints well to roughly one metre wide.

**Why don't my printed pages line up?**
Almost always one of two things. Either your print dialog scaled the pages - set it to 100% or Actual size and turn off Fit to page - or your printer's unprintable border is larger than the margin you told the tool about. Print the calibration sheet: if its 100 mm reference line does not measure 100 mm, the problem is scaling; if the inner corner markers are clipped, the problem is margins.

**Should I choose overlap or trim marks?**
Overlap and glue if you want a forgiving job - the shared strip is printed on both pages so you slide the sheets until the picture matches, which hides small errors. Trim and butt-join if you want an invisible seam and are willing to cut accurately with a knife and steel rule. For a first attempt, or for anything involving children, use overlap.

**How do I print at actual size instead of fit-to-page?**
In Adobe Reader choose Page Sizing & Handling → Actual size. In Chrome or Edge open More settings and set Scale to Custom → 100. In Firefox set Scale to 100% and untick Fit to page width. In macOS Preview set Scale to 100% and untick Scale to fit. Also disable any poster, N-up or borderless option in the printer driver itself, since those apply a second transformation.

**Can I print a sewing pattern at exactly 1:1 scale?**
Yes. Use Magnify mode set to 100% with the source resolution matching the pattern's, choose trim and butt-join, print at Actual size, and then verify with the pattern's own test square before cutting fabric. If the printed square measures 10 cm you are at true scale. Never cut fabric without checking that square.

**Can I print on Letter or Legal paper?**
Yes. Letter, Legal, Tabloid/Ledger and Executive are all supported alongside the ISO sizes, and the tool preselects Letter for visitors whose device locale suggests North America. Units switch to inches at the same time, and every dimension, margin and overlap field follows the unit you choose.

**Does it work on mobile and iPad?**
Yes. The layout puts the preview on top and the controls beneath, with a sticky generate button. Pages are rendered one at a time and released immediately so memory stays low, which is what makes large posters survivable on a phone. Note that some mobile print paths auto-fit pages - for a large job, generate on your phone but print from a desktop, or verify with the calibration sheet first.

**Can I print in black and white to save ink?**
Yes - switch on greyscale in Output quality. For much bigger savings, try halftone mode with a large dot pitch: it replaces solid tone with dots and can cut ink use dramatically while looking like a deliberate design choice rather than a compromise.

**How do I assemble and mount the finished poster?**
Lay every sheet out in the grid first using the guide page, trim the leading margins, then build one complete row at a time before joining the rows to each other. Align by matching the printed image, not the paper edges. Glue sticks give you a few seconds to reposition; wet glue buckles paper. For mounting, spray adhesive onto 5 mm foam board gives the flattest, most durable result.

**Is there a limit on file size or number of pages?**
There is no artificial limit, only your device's memory. The tool warns you above about 40 pages and asks for confirmation above 100, because a very large poster at 300 DPI can produce a PDF of several hundred megabytes. If you hit trouble, drop the DPI to 150, lower the JPEG quality, or use the ZIP export which writes pages out individually instead of holding a whole PDF in memory.

**Can I use my own custom paper size?**
Yes. Choose Custom in the paper selector and type any width and height in millimetres, centimetres or inches. This covers A3+ / super A3, roll-fed widths, index cards, and the various regional sizes not in the standard list.

**Are my settings remembered?**
Yes, in your browser's local storage on your own device - paper size, units, margins, joining mode and output quality come back next time. Nothing is stored anywhere else, and clearing your browser data clears it.

### Image Steganography

Hides a message or **any file** inside a PNG's pixel data using LSB encoding, and it is unusually serious about the crypto: the payload is encrypted with **AES-256-GCM via Web Crypto, with the key derived by PBKDF2-SHA256 over 200,000 iterations**, on by default. Bits per channel 1–4 with a live worst-case artifact preview, selectable R/G/B channels, and three pixel-ordering strategies — sequential, password-scattered via a seeded PRNG, or texture-preferred, which hides data in high-variance regions where it is least visible. A live capacity bar shows how much the cover image can hold. The Analyze tab is a real forensics toolkit: bit-plane visualiser, PSNR, a diff map against the original and a **chi-square LSB likelihood test**. Two limits to state honestly: it uses its own container format with a magic header, so it **cannot extract messages made by other steganography tools** — only its own; and the page itself says it is not forensic-grade undetectability. Output is always PNG, and the page warns that re-saving as JPEG or sending through WhatsApp, Instagram or Facebook destroys the hidden message. Covers above roughly 12 megapixels are downscaled.

#### How to hide a secret message inside an image

Use ToolAdda's free LSB steganography tool to embed a hidden text or file inside a PNG photo entirely in your browser.

2. **Enter secret content** — Type your secret message or attach a file. Set a strong password and keep AES-256 encryption enabled (recommended).
3. **Configure embedding** — Optionally adjust bits per channel, colour channels, and pixel ordering (sequential, password-scattered, or texture-preferred) in Advanced settings.
4. **Hide and download PNG** — Click Hide Message, review the before/after comparison and PSNR quality, then download the stego-image.png. Share it as a file attachment — not as a re-compressed photo.

#### Frequently asked questions (25)

**What is image steganography?**
Steganography hides secret data inside a cover image so casual viewers don't know a message exists. This tool uses LSB embedding - modifying the tiniest colour bits where changes are visually imperceptible.

**Is image steganography safe and private?**
All processing runs 100% in your browser — your image, message, and password are never uploaded. However, steganography only hides the existence of data; always enable AES-256 password encryption so extracted data remains unreadable without your password.

**Why must the output be PNG?**
LSB data lives in the least-significant bits of pixels. PNG is lossless and preserves those bits exactly. JPEG compression destroys them. You can upload JPG as cover, but output is always PNG.

**Why doesn't it work after sending on WhatsApp, Instagram or Facebook?**
These apps re-compress photos as JPEG when sent normally, destroying hidden bits. Send the PNG as a document/file attachment, or use email or cloud storage instead.

**Can someone detect the hidden message?**
Yes, potentially. Statistical tools (like our chi-square analysis) can flag likely steganography, especially at higher bit depths. This is a learning tool, not forensic-grade undetectability.

**Do I need a password for steganography?**
Strongly recommended and enabled by default. Without a password, anyone who suspects hidden data can extract it with any generic tool. With AES-256 encryption, they only get encrypted noise without the correct password.

**What is LSB steganography?**
LSB replaces the lowest bits of RGB colour channels with secret data bits. These bits contribute minimally to perceived colour, so the image looks unchanged.

**Can I hide a file, not just text?**
Yes. Switch to File mode in the Hide tab. Any file type can be embedded with filename and MIME preserved, and downloaded again from the Reveal tab.

**Can I hide a password or other short secret?**
Yes — a password or short note is just text, and text is the simplest and lowest-capacity-demand thing to hide, so it works reliably even in small cover images.

**Is real encryption included, or is this just hiding?**
Both. When enabled, your payload is encrypted with AES-256-GCM (via a password stretched through 200,000 rounds of PBKDF2) before it's ever embedded, so extraction alone doesn't reveal readable content.

**Can I extract the hidden data later, or does it expire?**
There's no expiry. As long as the PNG file itself is never edited, resized, or re-compressed, you can reveal the hidden data at any time in the future using this same tool.

**Does this tool work offline?**
Yes, once the page has loaded. Hiding and revealing both run entirely in your browser's memory with no network requests involved.

**Is it free to use?**
Yes, completely free with no sign-up, no watermark, and no limit on how many times you use it.

**Can I use very large images?**
Yes. Images larger than roughly 12 megapixels are automatically downscaled before embedding so the page stays responsive - you'll see a notice if this happens.

**Can I hide a ZIP file or other binary file type?**
Yes. File mode accepts any file type — ZIP archives, documents, small config files — and preserves the original filename and MIME type for download after extraction.

**Can hidden data be removed or "cleaned" from an image?**
Any edit - resizing, cropping, filtering, or re-saving as JPEG - will destroy the embedded bits. This tool doesn't include a dedicated "strip hidden data" mode, but re-saving through almost any image editor achieves the same result.

**Is this secure enough for genuinely sensitive information?**
With encryption and password-scattered ordering enabled it's reasonably strong for casual and personal privacy, but treat it as a learning and hobby-grade tool, not a substitute for dedicated security software when the stakes are high - see the Digital Forensics section above.

**Can beginners use this without technical knowledge?**
Yes. The default settings (1-bit depth, all channels, sequential order, encryption on) work well out of the box - Advanced settings are entirely optional for more experienced users.

**What browsers are supported?**
Any modern browser with Canvas and Web Crypto API support — recent Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari all work, on both desktop and mobile.

**Does it work on mobile phones?**
Yes, the interface is fully responsive, including touch-friendly drag-and-drop alternatives (tap to browse) and a mobile-optimised control layout.

**Is there a limit on how much data I can hide?**
Capacity depends on your image size and embedding settings - the live capacity bar in the Hide tab shows exactly how many bytes you can fit before you start typing.

**Does hiding data change the visible image quality?**
At 1-2 bits per channel, no visible difference - the PSNR (peak signal-to-noise ratio) shown after hiding is typically well above 45 dB, meaning "visually identical." Higher bit-depths trade a little more risk of faint artifacts for extra capacity.

**Can I hide more than one message in the same image?**
Not in a single pass - each hide operation embeds one payload (text or one file) per image. To combine multiple secrets, bundle them into one file (for example a ZIP) and hide that as a single file payload.

**Are my images, messages or passwords stored anywhere?**
No. Nothing is uploaded, logged, or saved to any server — everything stays in your browser's memory for the current session only.

**Can I batch-process multiple images at once?**
Not currently — each image is hidden or revealed individually, one at a time, through the Hide and Reveal tabs.

#### Frequently asked questions (57)

**What is a QR code?**
A QR code is a two-dimensional barcode that stores data as a grid of black and white squares called modules. A camera reads the whole grid at once, which is why it holds far more than a traditional barcode and can be scanned from any angle.

**How do I create a QR code?**
Pick a type — URL, text, Wi-Fi, email, phone, SMS, contact, location or WhatsApp — fill in the fields, and the preview updates as you type. Adjust colours or error correction if you want, then download as PNG or SVG.

**Is this QR code generator free?**
Yes. It is free, needs no account or email address, adds no watermark, and there is no limit on how many codes you create.

**Do I need an account?**
No. There is no sign-up at any point. The generator runs entirely in your browser, so there is nothing for an account to store.

**How do I create a QR code for a website?**
Choose the URL type and paste your address. If you leave off the scheme, https:// is added; a URL that already names a scheme is encoded exactly as typed, including any query string.

**How do I create a Wi-Fi QR code?**
Choose Wi-Fi, enter the network name and password, and pick the security type. Scanning the result offers to join the network. Characters such as semicolons and colons in the name or password are escaped correctly, which is where naive generators produce the wrong credentials.

**Can I create a QR code for a Wi-Fi password?**
Yes, and it works on both iOS and Android. Be aware that anyone who scans or photographs the code gets your password — it encodes the credentials in plain text, so treat a printed Wi-Fi QR the way you would treat the password written on a card.

**Can I create a contact or vCard QR code?**
Yes. Fill in name, organisation, job title, phone, email, website and address, and the code encodes a standard vCard 3.0. Scanning it offers to save a new contact. Commas and semicolons in your details are escaped so the fields do not split in the wrong places.

**Can I create a QR code for email?**
Yes. Enter an address and optionally a subject and message body. The code encodes a mailto: link, so scanning it opens a pre-filled email. The subject and body are URL-encoded, so ampersands and spaces survive.

**Can I create a QR code for a phone number?**
Yes. The Phone type encodes a tel: link, and scanning it starts a call to that number. International formats with a leading plus and spaces or brackets are accepted.

**Can I create an SMS QR code?**
Yes. Enter a number and an optional message, and scanning opens the messaging app with both pre-filled. The recipient still has to press send.

**Can I create a location QR code?**
Yes. Enter latitude and longitude and the code encodes a geo: URI that opens in the phone's map app. Latitude is validated to between -90 and 90, longitude to between -180 and 180.

**Can I create a WhatsApp QR code?**
Yes. Enter a phone number with country code and an optional message; the code encodes a wa.me link that opens a chat with the message pre-filled.

**Can I add a logo to my QR code?**
Yes. Upload a PNG, JPG or WebP and it is placed in the centre. Error correction is raised to H automatically, because a logo covers modules that the error correction then has to reconstruct. Keep the logo small — above about 30% of the width the code stops scanning reliably.

**Can I change the QR code colours?**
Yes, foreground and background are both adjustable, and there are presets. The contrast ratio is calculated as you change them and you are warned when the combination is likely to fail — under 3:1 it is refused as unscannable.

**Can I change the QR code size?**
Yes. The export size is separate from the on-screen preview, so you can work with a comfortable preview and still download at 1024 or 2048 pixels for print.

**What is QR error correction?**
QR codes store redundant data so they still scan when part of the symbol is damaged, dirty or covered. There are four levels — L, M, Q and H — with H holding the most redundancy and therefore the least payload for a given symbol size.

**Which error correction level should I use?**
M is a good default for screens and clean printing. Use Q or H for codes that will be printed on packaging, displayed outdoors, or that carry a logo. Use L only when the payload is long and the code will be scanned from a screen in good conditions.

**Why is my QR code not scanning?**
The usual causes are too little contrast between foreground and background, a code printed too small for its data density, a missing quiet zone — the light margin around the symbol — or a logo covering too much of the pattern. Try black on white at a larger size to isolate which one it is.

**What is the quiet zone and why does it matter?**
The quiet zone is the blank margin of at least four modules that must surround a QR code. Without it a scanner cannot tell where the symbol ends, and codes placed flush against coloured backgrounds often fail. Every code this tool produces includes the margin.

**How can I make a QR code easier to scan?**
Use dark on light, keep the quiet zone, print it larger than you think you need, shorten the data so the grid is less dense, and raise the error correction level. Then test it with more than one phone before printing a batch.

**Can I download my QR code as PNG?**
Yes, and PNG is the recommended format for screens, documents and most printing. It is lossless, so the module edges stay sharp.

**Can I download my QR code as SVG?**
Yes. The SVG is a genuine vector — one path built from the module grid, not a PNG wrapped in markup — so it scales to any size without losing sharpness. Note that a centre logo is not included in the SVG export.

**Is SVG better for printing?**
Usually yes. A vector prints crisply at any physical size, which matters for posters, signage and packaging where a raster would show soft edges. For a business card at a fixed size, a high-resolution PNG is equally fine.

**Can I print my QR code?**
Yes. The Print button produces a clean page containing only the QR code and a short label — no navigation, controls or page furniture.

**Do QR codes expire?**
No. A QR code is just an encoding of data; it has no expiry and needs no service to keep working. What can stop working is what it points at — if the URL inside it goes away, the code still scans but leads nowhere.

**Are QR codes permanent?**
The codes produced here are static: the data is baked into the pattern and cannot be changed afterwards. Editing the destination later requires a dynamic QR service that redirects through its own URL, which is a different product with its own tracking and dependency.

**Does a QR code require internet?**
Scanning does not — the data is in the image itself. Acting on it might: a URL code needs a connection to load the page, while a Wi-Fi, contact or SMS code works entirely offline.

**Are QR codes secure?**
A QR code is neither secure nor insecure by itself — it is just encoded data that anyone can decode. The risk is what it points to, since a scanner cannot tell a genuine code from a sticker placed over it. Check the URL your phone shows before opening it.

**Is my QR data stored or uploaded?**
No. The code is generated in your browser by a local library. Nothing you type — including Wi-Fi passwords and contact details — is sent anywhere, logged, or saved to local storage.

**Does the generator support Hindi, Chinese or emoji?**
Yes. Text is encoded as UTF-8, so Devanagari, Chinese, Japanese, Arabic, accented Latin and emoji all survive scanning intact. This is worth checking in any generator — a common library default encodes Latin-1 and silently turns non-ASCII text into mojibake.

**How much data can a QR code hold?**
Up to roughly 2,953 bytes at the lowest error correction level and about 1,273 at the highest. In practice much less is advisable: more data means a denser grid, which needs a larger print size to stay scannable. This tool refuses payloads that will not fit and warns when one is getting dense.

**How large should a printed QR code be?**
A common rule of thumb is that the code should be about a tenth of the scanning distance — roughly 3 cm for arm's length, and much larger for a poster read from across a room. Denser codes need to be bigger, so shortening the data is often the cheapest way to shrink the print size.

**Can I use these QR codes for business?**
Yes. There is no licence, watermark or attribution requirement on the codes you generate, and the QR standard itself is free to use. Menus, packaging, business cards and signage are all fine.

**Can I use a transparent background?**
Yes, for PNG and SVG. It is worth testing though — with a transparent background the code takes on whatever is behind it, and a busy or mid-tone surface can destroy the contrast a scanner needs.

**What is the full form of QR code?**
QR stands for Quick Response. The name reflects the design goal: a camera reads the whole two-dimensional grid in a single capture instead of sweeping across a set of lines, so decoding is near-instant. In Hindi it is commonly written as क्विक रिस्पॉन्स कोड.

**Who invented the QR code?**
A team led by Masahiro Hara at Denso Wave, part of the Toyota group, developed it in 1994 to track automotive parts faster than barcodes allowed. Denso Wave chose not to charge for use of the standard, which is why QR codes became universal. QR Code remains its registered trademark, while the specification is published as ISO/IEC 18004.

**What is the difference between a barcode and a QR code?**
A barcode is one-dimensional and stores roughly 20 to 48 characters in the widths of vertical bars, read along a single line. A QR code is two-dimensional, holds up to about 4,296 alphanumeric characters, scans at any angle, and carries error correction so a damaged symbol still resolves. Code 128 is a barcode symbology, not a type of QR code.

**How do I make a QR code for a Google Form?**
Open the form, press Send or Share, and copy the link — the short forms.gle address is better than the long one because fewer characters mean a less dense code. Paste it into the URL type here and download the result.

**How do I create a QR code for a location?**
Two ways. The Location type takes latitude and longitude and encodes a geo: URI that opens the phone's default map app, which works for places with no listing. Alternatively copy a Google Maps share link and encode it with the URL type, which opens the full listing with directions and reviews.

**Can I create a QR code for my Google review link?**
Yes. Copy the "Ask for reviews" short link from your Google Business Profile — usually of the form g.page/r/…/review — and encode it with the URL type. Printed on a table card or receipt it takes customers straight to the review box.

**How do I convert a link into a QR code?**
Choose the URL type, paste the link, and the preview updates as you type; then download PNG or SVG. Shorter links produce less dense codes that stay readable at smaller print sizes, so trim tracking parameters where you can.

**Can I turn a PDF, image or video into a QR code?**
Not directly — a QR code holds a few hundred characters of text, not a file of any kind. Host the PDF, image or video somewhere with a public link, set the sharing permission to anyone with the link, then encode that link with the URL type. Every "file to QR code" service does exactly this behind a friendlier label.

**Can I create a UPI, Google Pay or PhonePe payment QR code?**
No, and deliberately so. A collection or merchant QR carries a verified payee identifier — and for merchant codes a signature only the issuer can produce — so it must come from your bank, your payment app or your gateway dashboard. You can, however, encode a link to your own payment or donation page with the URL type.

**Can I generate QR codes in bulk?**
No. This tool makes one code at a time and has no CSV or spreadsheet upload for batch output. For a small number, change the input and download again — the settings and fields keep their values between codes.

**Can I edit a QR code after I have created it?**
No. A static QR code is not an editable document; the data is baked into the module pattern, so changing it means generating a new code. Editing a destination after printing requires a dynamic QR service that redirects through a URL it owns, or your own redirect on a domain you control.

**Can this tool scan or decode a QR code?**
No — this page only creates codes. To read one from your camera, a screenshot or an image file, use the ToolAdda QR code scanner, which also runs entirely in your browser.

**How do I scan a QR code on an iPhone?**
Open the Camera app, point it at the code, and tap the banner that appears; no app is needed on iOS 11 or later. You can also add the Code Scanner to Control Centre, or read a code inside a saved photo by opening it in Photos and tapping the Live Text button.

**How do I scan a QR code on Android?**
Most Android cameras detect codes automatically; otherwise use Google Lens or the QR scanner tile in the Quick Settings panel. Google Lens can also decode a code from a picture already in your gallery via Google Photos.

**How do I scan a QR code on a laptop or PC?**
Use a browser-based scanner: either grant webcam access and hold the code up, or upload the image file, which is usually easier and needs no camera at all. That is what the ToolAdda QR code scanner is for, and it requires no installation.

**How do I scan a QR code from a photo in my gallery?**
Upload the image to a scanner that accepts files, or use Google Lens from within Google Photos on Android. This is also the reliable way to handle a code displayed on the same screen you are reading — a camera cannot photograph its own display.

**Why does my phone say the QR code is invalid or the format is unrecognised?**
Usually the image is cropped, blurry, stretched or missing its quiet zone, or the code decoded correctly but the app expected its own payload format — a payment app shown a plain URL will call it invalid. Login and ticket codes are also short-lived session tokens that are meaningless outside their own app. Decode the image in a general-purpose scanner: if the raw text comes out cleanly, the pattern is fine.

**Can I make a WhatsApp group QR code?**
Yes, indirectly. Open the group, choose Invite via link, copy the invite link, and encode it with the URL type — scanning then opens the join screen. The WhatsApp type itself builds a wa.me chat link to a single number.

**Can I create the WhatsApp Web or Telegram login QR code?**
No. Those are rotating session tokens generated by WhatsApp and Telegram themselves and cannot be produced by any third-party generator. Never scan a login QR code that somebody else has sent you — doing so hands them access to your account.

**Can I make a heart-shaped or artistic QR code?**
Not here. This generator keeps clean square modules because they scan most reliably. For rounded modules, custom corner shapes and heavier styling, use the ToolAdda custom QR code maker, and test any decorative code on several phones before printing it.

**Do I need an app to scan a QR code?**
No. The built-in camera on any current iPhone or Android phone reads QR codes without an extra app, and on a desktop a browser-based scanner works from your webcam or from an uploaded image. Dedicated scanner apps are rarely necessary.

**What is a static QR code generator?**
One that writes your data directly into the pattern, with no service in the middle — which is what this page is. Static codes never expire, need no account, are not tracked, and work offline for Wi-Fi, contact and location types. The trade-off is that the destination cannot be changed after the code is printed.

#### Frequently asked questions (14)

**Do these QR codes expire?**
No. The code is generated in your browser and encodes your text or link directly, with no redirect service in between. Nothing can stop working later, which is a real risk with free QR services that route through their own shortener.

**Is my data sent to a server?**
No. The code is drawn on your device, so whatever you encode never leaves the browser. No tracking is inserted either — what you type is exactly what is encoded.

**What does error correction actually do?**
It adds redundant data so the code still scans when part of it is dirty, creased or covered. Low recovers from about 7% damage, Medium 15%, Quartile 25% and High about 30%.

**Which error correction level should I choose?**
Medium is a sensible default for printing. Use Quartile for small print or packaging that gets handled. Use High whenever you place a logo in the middle, because covering the centre is deliberate damage that only the redundancy can absorb.

**Can I put my logo in the middle?**
Yes, and it usually looks better. Raise the error correction to High when you do — a logo at Medium may scan on your screen and then fail on a printed poster, which is an expensive way to find out.

**Why does my QR code not scan?**
Usually one of three things: the colours are inverted, so a light code sits on a dark background; the contrast is too low; or the quiet zone around the code has been cropped away. Scanners expect dark modules on a light background with clear margin.

**Can I invert the colours?**
You can, but many scanners will fail on it. If your design needs to be dark, place a light panel behind the code rather than inverting the code itself.

**How big should I print a QR code?**
Roughly one tenth of the distance it will be scanned from. Read at arm's length, about 30 cm, the code wants to be around 3 cm across. On a poster read from three metres, around 30 cm.

**Why is my QR code so dense?**
Because the data is long. Every extra character means more, smaller modules. A URL with tracking parameters produces a much busier code than a short link, so shortening the link before encoding is often the simplest fix.

**What can I encode besides a website?**
Anything that is text. Common uses are Wi-Fi credentials so guests can join without being told the password, contact links for business cards, payment links on invoices, and plain text on product packaging.

**What size and format can I download?**
You can set the pixel size before downloading, and the code exports as an image ready to place into a document, a design file or a print layout.

**Should I test the code before printing?**
Always, and with two different phones. Scanners vary, and the difference between working and not working is often contrast or margin rather than the data. A minute of testing saves a reprint.

**Is there a limit on how much text I can encode?**
The QR standard itself has a limit of a few thousand characters, but long before that the code becomes too dense to scan reliably at normal print sizes. Keep it short — a link is almost always better than the content itself.

**Is this QR generator free?**
Yes. No sign-up, no watermark, no scan limit, and no expiry on any code you make.

#### Frequently asked questions (25)

**What is a barcode generator?**
A barcode generator converts a piece of data into the pattern of bars and spaces defined by a barcode symbology, then renders that pattern as an image. It does not assign or register the number itself — it encodes whatever value you give it into a machine-readable form.

**How do I create a barcode?**
Select the symbology your scanner or standard requires, type the value you want to encode, adjust the size if you have a specific label to fit, then download the result as SVG for print or PNG for screens and documents. The whole process takes under twenty seconds.

**Is this barcode generator free?**
Yes. No sign-up, no watermark, no usage cap and no paid tier. The barcodes you generate are yours to use commercially.

**Which barcode type should I use?**
CODE 128 if you are labelling things for your own systems - it takes letters and digits and is the most compact general-purpose option. EAN-13 or UPC-A only if you are selling through retail and hold a real GTIN. ITF-14 for shipping cartons, and CODE 39 when older or industrial hardware requires it.

**What is CODE 128?**
A high-density linear symbology that encodes any of the 128 ASCII characters. It switches automatically between three character subsets so runs of digits pack two per symbol character, making it the shortest general-purpose barcode for mixed data. It always carries a hidden mod 103 check character.

**What is EAN-13?**
The 13-digit retail product barcode used worldwide. Twelve digits carry the GS1 company prefix and item reference, and the thirteenth is a mod 10 check digit. The first digit is not drawn as bars at all - it is encoded in the parity pattern of the left-hand six digits.

**What is UPC-A?**
The 12-digit retail barcode used in the United States and Canada. Structurally it is an EAN-13 with a leading zero, which is why modern scanners read both interchangeably.

**Can I create a barcode for inventory?**
Yes, and CODE 128 is the right choice. Internal inventory codes need no registration, so you can use any scheme you like - a location prefix, a SKU, a serial number - as long as each value is unique within your system.

**Can I create printable barcodes?**
Yes. Download SVG for print: it is vector, so it stays sharp at any physical size and your label software can scale it without softening the bar edges. For raster, use the high-resolution print preset, which renders at four times the on-screen size for roughly 300 DPI.

**Can I download barcodes as PNG?**
Yes. PNG is lossless and keeps bar edges hard, which makes it the right raster format for barcodes. Choose a print resolution preset first so the file is rendered at the size you need rather than scaled up afterwards.

**Can I download barcodes as SVG?**
Yes, and it is recommended for print and label design. The SVG contains one rectangle per bar plus a text element, so it opens cleanly in Illustrator, Inkscape, Figma and label software, and can be recoloured or resized with no quality loss.

**Can I generate barcodes in bulk?**
Yes. The Batch tab accepts one value per line or a CSV file, validates every row, shows which rows failed and why, and downloads all successful barcodes as a ZIP containing both PNG and SVG for each value. The ZIP is built in your browser.

**What is a barcode checksum?**
An extra character calculated from the others so a scanner can detect a misread. EAN, UPC and ITF-14 use a mod 10 weighted sum; CODE 39 offers an optional mod 43 character; CODE 93 carries two mod 47 characters; CODE 128 always carries a mod 103 check character that is never printed.

**Why is my barcode showing as invalid?**
Almost always one of three things: the value contains characters the symbology cannot encode, the length is wrong for a fixed-length format, or the check digit does not match. The error message names which, and gives the corrected value where one exists.

**Why will my barcode not scan?**
Usually a missing or truncated quiet zone, bars printed too narrow for the printer's resolution, insufficient contrast, or a raster image scaled up after export. Print at actual size from a vector file and keep the quiet zone clear.

**How much white space should be around a barcode?**
At least ten times the narrow bar width on each side for most symbologies, and eleven modules on the left of an EAN-13. It must be genuinely empty - no text, borders or graphics - because the scanner uses it to locate where the symbol starts and ends.

**Can barcodes contain letters?**
Some can. CODE 128 encodes the full ASCII set including lowercase and punctuation; CODE 39 and CODE 93 encode uppercase letters, digits and a handful of symbols. EAN, UPC, ITF and MSI are numeric only.

**Can I customize barcode colours?**
Yes, but carefully. Scanners read contrast, not colour, and most red laser scanners are effectively blind to red bars. Keep bars dark and the background light, aim for 7:1 contrast or better, and never invert. The tool warns you when a colour choice puts scanning at risk.

**Do I need to sign up to create a barcode?**
No. There is no account, no email capture and no limit on how many barcodes you generate or download.

**Is my barcode data uploaded to a server?**
No. The encoder, the renderer and the file export all run in your browser as JavaScript, with no network request involved. Serial numbers, internal SKUs and customer references never leave your device.

**Does this tool give me a real product barcode number?**
No, and no free tool can. A retail EAN-13 or UPC-A number must be allocated from a GS1 company prefix licensed to your business. This tool renders a number you already hold into a correctly encoded image - it cannot issue or register the number itself.

**What is the difference between a barcode and a QR code?**
A traditional barcode is one-dimensional, encoding a short identifier in the widths of vertical bars that a database then resolves. A QR code is a two-dimensional matrix holding far more data - URLs, contact details, Wi-Fi credentials - readable by a phone camera at any rotation.

**Can I validate a barcode number I already have?**
Yes. The Validate tab checks a value against the character set, length rules and check digit of any supported symbology and tells you precisely what is wrong, including the corrected check digit when that is the problem.

**What size should a barcode be printed at?**
Keep the narrow bar at 0.25 mm or wider - about 3 pixels at 300 DPI - and make the bars tall enough that a scanner sweeping at a slight angle still crosses every bar, roughly 15% of the symbol width. A full-size EAN-13 is about 37 mm by 26 mm.

**Does this barcode generator work offline?**
Once the page has loaded, yes. Everything runs from JavaScript already in your browser with no further network calls, so generating and downloading keeps working if you go offline.

#### Frequently asked questions (34)

**What is a JSON formatter?**
A JSON formatter takes JSON text, parses it into a data structure and writes it back out with consistent indentation and line breaks. The data is unchanged — only the whitespace differs — which is why the result is safe to paste back into whatever produced it.

**What is JSON beautification?**
Beautifying and formatting are the same operation under two names: turning compact JSON into an indented, readable layout. A minified API response on one long line becomes a document you can actually scan for the field you need.

**What is a JSON validator?**
A validator answers one question: is this text syntactically valid JSON? If it is not, a good validator says where the problem is. This one reports the line, the column, the reason and — where the cause is unambiguous — a hint such as "standard JSON does not allow a trailing comma".

**What is a JSON minifier?**
A minifier removes every space, tab and newline that sits between JSON tokens, producing the smallest text that still parses to the same data. Whitespace inside string values is part of the data and is never touched.

**How do I format JSON?**
Paste your JSON into the input editor. It is parsed and formatted as you type, and the result appears on the right with syntax highlighting. Choose 2 spaces, 4 spaces or tabs from the indentation control, then use Copy or Download.

**How do I validate JSON?**
Validation runs automatically on every change, and the Validate button reports on demand without touching the output. A valid document shows a green Valid JSON status; an invalid one shows the line, column, reason and the offending line with a caret under the exact position.

**How do I minify JSON?**
Press Minify, or use Ctrl+Shift+M. The document is parsed first, so minification can only succeed on valid JSON — you can never produce a compact string that does not parse. The statistics panel shows how many bytes the whitespace was costing.

**What is pretty print JSON?**
Pretty printing is another name for formatting: adding indentation and line breaks so the structure is visible. In JavaScript it is JSON.stringify(value, null, 2), which is exactly what this tool runs after parsing your input.

**Why is my JSON invalid?**
The usual causes are a trailing comma before a closing brace or bracket, single quotes instead of double quotes, unquoted object keys, a missing comma between members, an unclosed brace or bracket, or a JavaScript-style comment. All six are legal JavaScript and none are legal JSON.

**How do I fix a JSON syntax error?**
Start at the reported line and column. Note that an unclosed brace is usually reported at the end of the document rather than where it opened, so if the position looks wrong, count your brackets from the top. Formatting a partially fixed document often makes the remaining problem obvious.

**What does "unexpected token" mean in JSON?**
It means the parser found a character that cannot legally appear at that point. A stray } usually means a comma or a value is missing before it; a letter usually means an unquoted key or a bare word where a value was expected.

**Why does JSON require double quotes?**
Because the specification defines a string as a sequence of characters wrapped in double quotes, with no alternative. Single quotes are a JavaScript convenience that JSON deliberately left out to keep the grammar unambiguous for every language, not just JavaScript.

**Are trailing commas allowed in JSON?**
No. A comma after the last member of an object or array makes the document invalid, even though JavaScript accepts it. This tool detects the case specifically and tells you so rather than reporting a generic unexpected token.

**Can JSON contain comments?**
No. There is no comment syntax in JSON at all — neither // nor /* */. Formats that allow them, such as JSON5 and JSONC, are separate specifications. If you need comments in configuration, YAML is usually the better choice.

**What is the difference between JSON and JSON5?**
JSON5 is a superset that adds comments, trailing commas, single-quoted strings, unquoted keys and a few number forms. It is a different format with its own parsers. This tool processes standard JSON only, so a JSON5 document is reported as invalid rather than silently accepted.

**Can this tool format large JSON files?**
Yes. Formatting and analysis are linear in document size and a file with tens of thousands of records completes in well under a second. For very large input the live pass is debounced longer, syntax highlighting is skipped and the tree starts collapsed so the first paint stays fast.

**Can I format API responses?**
Yes, and it is the most common use. Paste a minified response straight from your network tab or a curl command. Because everything runs locally, a response containing a token or personal data never leaves your machine.

**Can I download formatted JSON?**
Yes. Download saves exactly what is in the output pane as formatted.json, or minified.json if you last minified. It is generated in the browser with a Blob and there is no upload step.

**Can I copy minified JSON?**
Yes. Copy minified produces the compact form from the same parsed data without changing what is displayed, so you can keep reading the formatted version while pasting the compact one.

**Does formatting change JSON data?**
No. Formatting only adds whitespace between tokens. Every key, value, type and array order is identical, and parsing the formatted output gives a structure equal to parsing the original.

**Does minification change JSON data?**
No. Minification removes whitespace between tokens only. Spaces, tabs and newlines inside string values are part of the data and are preserved exactly.

**What is the difference between formatting and validating JSON?**
Validating asks whether the text is legal JSON and answers yes or no. Formatting rewrites valid JSON into a readable layout. Formatting implies validation — a document has to parse before it can be reformatted — but validating on its own leaves the text untouched.

**Can JSON contain arrays?**
Yes. An array is an ordered list in square brackets and may hold any mix of values, including other arrays and objects. Order is significant and is always preserved by this tool, including when key sorting is switched on.

**Can JSON contain nested objects?**
Yes, to any depth. The statistics panel reports the maximum depth of your document, and the tree view lets you collapse branches you are not interested in.

**How are null values handled?**
null is preserved as the JSON literal null. It is never turned into the string "null", into undefined, or into an empty string, and it is never silently dropped from an object or an array.

**How are booleans handled?**
true and false are preserved as literals. A string containing the text "true" is different data and stays a quoted string, so the two can never be confused.

**Can JSON contain Unicode?**
Yes. Devanagari, Chinese, Japanese, Arabic, accented Latin and emoji all pass through unchanged. There is an optional Escape Unicode setting that rewrites them as \uXXXX sequences — a change of representation, not of the underlying text — and it is off by default.

**How are large numbers handled?**
JavaScript reads every JSON number as a 64-bit float, so an integer beyond 9,007,199,254,740,991 loses precision during parsing — in this tool and in every other browser-based one. If your data contains large identifiers, keep them as strings in the JSON.

**What happens to duplicate keys?**
They are detected and reported with the key name and line number, and nothing is removed for you. JSON parsers keep the last occurrence and discard earlier ones, so a duplicate usually means data is being lost silently somewhere upstream — which is worth knowing about rather than having quietly cleaned up.

**What is JSON tree view?**
A collapsible outline of the parsed document. Each branch shows its type and how many members it has, each leaf shows its value and type in words as well as colour, and clicking a leaf reveals its path such as $.user.profile.name.

**Does sorting keys change my data?**
It changes the order properties appear in, which some systems care about, so it is off by default. The values themselves are untouched and array order is never altered.

**Is JSON formatting safe?**
Yes, when the tool treats JSON as data rather than code. This one parses with JSON.parse, never eval, and every character it displays — including the syntax highlighter and the tree — is escaped or inserted as text, so a document containing HTML or a script tag is shown, not run.

**Is my JSON uploaded to a server?**
No. Parsing, formatting, minifying and downloading all happen in your browser and no network request carries your data. This matters because JSON pasted into a formatter routinely contains API keys, tokens and personal data.

**Is this JSON formatter free?**
Yes. Free, no sign-up, no email address and no limit on document size beyond what your browser can hold.

#### Frequently asked questions (25)

**What is a JSON to TypeScript generator?**
A JSON to TypeScript generator analyzes a JSON object or array and produces matching TypeScript type declarations — interfaces, type aliases, classes, or enums — so you get compile-time type safety and editor autocompletion for that data shape instead of typing it out by hand.

**How does the JSON to TypeScript generator work?**
It parses your JSON, walks the resulting value recursively, and infers a structural shape for every object and array. When an array contains multiple objects, their shapes are merged so fields missing from some items become optional and fields with different value types become unions — then TypeScript code is generated from that merged shape.

**Is my JSON data uploaded to a server?**
No. Parsing, type inference, and code generation all run locally in your browser using JavaScript. Nothing you paste, upload, or drag and drop is ever sent to ToolAdda's servers.

**Does it support nested JSON objects and arrays?**
Yes. Nested objects become their own named interfaces or types, nested arrays become typed arrays of the inferred element type, and this works to any depth, including arrays of arrays and objects nested inside arrays inside objects.

**Can it generate TypeScript interfaces?**
Yes, interface is the default output. Choose Interface in the Declaration Type setting to generate a named interface for every distinct object shape found in your JSON.

**Can it generate type aliases instead of interfaces?**
Yes. Switch Declaration Type to Type to generate type X = { ... } aliases instead of interfaces — useful when you need to compose the result with union or intersection types elsewhere in your code.

**Can it generate TypeScript classes?**
Yes. Switch Declaration Type to Class to generate typed class field declarations, which is handy for frameworks like NestJS that use classes as DTOs and validation targets.

**Does it support enums?**
Yes, optionally. When a string field repeats across array items with a small, consistent set of values (like "active" | "inactive" | "pending"), set Enum Detection to String Literal Union for an inline union type, or Named Enum to generate a proper TypeScript enum instead.

**What happens with null values in my JSON?**
By default a field that is ever null becomes a union with null (for example city: string | null ). Change Null Handling to Optional Field to mark it with a ? instead, or Both to apply both the union and the optional marker.

**Does it support optional properties?**
Yes. When Optional Field Detection is set to Auto (the default), a property is marked optional ( ? ) automatically whenever it's missing from at least one object in a merged array of objects. You can also force every field to optional, or force every field to required.

**Can I download the generated code?**
Yes. Click Download .ts to save the generated TypeScript as a file, or Copy to copy it straight to your clipboard.

**Is this JSON to TypeScript converter free?**
Yes. It's completely free, has no usage limits, and requires no account or sign-up.

**Does it work offline?**
Once the page is loaded, all conversion logic runs in your browser's JavaScript engine with no network calls, so it keeps working even if your connection drops.

**Does it support React projects?**
Yes. Choose the React preset to generate readonly interfaces suited to typing props and API responses in React and Next.js components.

**Can I use it with Angular?**
Yes. The Angular preset generates interfaces with JSDoc hints, a good match for typing HttpClient responses and Angular services and models.

**Does it support Vue?**
Yes. The Vue preset generates plain interfaces that work directly with Vue 3's Composition API, defineProps, and TypeScript-based stores.

**Can I customize interface and type names (prefix, suffix, root name)?**
Yes. Set a custom Root Name for the top-level type, and an optional Prefix or Suffix (for example prefix "I" or suffix "Dto") applied to every generated interface, type, or class name.

**Does it detect dates, UUIDs, emails, and URLs?**
Yes, optionally. Enable JSDoc Format Hints and string fields matching an ISO date, date-time, UUID, email, or URL pattern get a /** @format ... */ comment above the field - the property type itself stays string , since TypeScript has no native date/UUID primitive.

**Does it support generics like Record<string, T>?**
Yes. Enable Detect Dynamic Keys and an object whose keys look machine-generated (all-numeric or all-UUID) is generated as Record<string, ValueType> - an index signature - instead of one interface per key.

**Can I convert large JSON files?**
Yes. Smaller and mid-sized files convert live as you type; very large inputs (roughly 400KB+) pause live conversion and wait for you to click Convert, so the browser tab stays responsive.

**How are duplicate or repeated object shapes handled?**
With Deduplicate Identical Shapes enabled (the default), two structurally identical objects anywhere in your JSON — even at different paths — generate a single shared interface instead of two separate, redundant ones.

**What is the difference between interface and type in the generated code?**
For the object shapes this generator produces, interface and type behave almost identically: both describe an object's properties. interface can later be extended or declaration-merged; type can be combined with unions and intersections and works for primitive/array aliases too. Pick whichever matches your codebase's existing convention.

**Can JSON contain circular references?**
No. JSON.parse cannot produce circular references — only JavaScript objects constructed at runtime can reference themselves — so circular-reference handling isn't applicable to a JSON to TypeScript conversion.

**Does it support readonly properties?**
Yes. Enable the Readonly Properties toggle to prefix every generated field with readonly , which is useful for immutable state, Redux/Zustand stores, and React props.

**Can I generate NestJS DTOs?**
Yes. The NestJS preset switches Declaration Type to Class and applies a Dto suffix, giving you a starting point for request/response DTO classes.
