#### Frequently asked questions (31)

**Is my password sent anywhere when I use this checker?**
No. Every calculation happens in your browser using JavaScript that runs locally. Your password is never transmitted, and it is never written to localStorage or cookies. You do not have to take our word for it: disconnect from the internet and the checker keeps working exactly as before, because there is nothing for it to call.

**What is zxcvbn and why does it matter?**
zxcvbn is a realistic password strength estimator originally built by Dropbox. Instead of just counting uppercase letters, digits, and symbols, it models how real attackers actually guess — dictionary words, names, keyboard walks like 'qwerty', dates, repeats, sequences, and common leetspeak substitutions like '@' for 'a' — giving a far more honest strength estimate than character-counting checkers.

**How does password strength actually work?**
It's about how many guesses an attacker realistically needs, not how complex a password looks. A dictionary word plus substitutions can crack instantly despite looking complex; random unrelated words can take centuries despite looking simple.

**What is password entropy, exactly?**
Entropy measures unpredictability in bits; each extra bit doubles the guesses needed. This tool shows two entropy numbers: 'real entropy' derived from zxcvbn's pattern-aware guess count (what actually matters), and 'naive pool-based entropy' — what a simplistic character-counting checker would report, which is usually a big overestimate since it assumes every character is equally random.

**How is crack time actually estimated?**
Crack time = estimated guesses required ÷ guesses per second an attacker can make. Guesses per second varies enormously by scenario — a rate-limited login form might allow under 100 guesses per hour, while an attacker running stolen, poorly-hashed data on GPUs can try tens of billions of guesses per second — so this tool shows crack time across 5 realistic scenarios rather than one misleading number.

**What is a brute-force attack?**
A brute-force attack tries every possible character combination systematically until one works. It's the slowest, most exhaustive method and is why length matters so much — every additional character multiplies the total combinations an attacker must exhaust.

**What is a dictionary attack?**
A dictionary attack tries real words, names, and known-leaked passwords first — including predictable tweaks like a capital first letter or '123' appended — before resorting to brute force. This is why 'Password123!' is weak despite mixing character types: it's a dictionary word plus tweaks the attacker's wordlist already anticipates.

**What are rainbow tables, and does a strong password protect against them?**
A rainbow table is a precomputed lookup of hash values mapped back to the plaintext that produced them, letting an attacker reverse a stolen hash instantly instead of computing it fresh. Properly implemented sites defeat rainbow tables with 'salting' (adding a unique random value to each password before hashing), which is a server-side defense — but a longer, more random password still helps, since it wouldn't appear in a precomputed table even without salting.

**What is credential stuffing?**
Credential stuffing takes username/password pairs leaked from one breached site and automatically tries them on many other sites, exploiting password reuse. A strong, unique password per account fully defeats it, since a breach elsewhere becomes irrelevant to accounts using a different password.

**Does this tool check my password against real data breaches like Have I Been Pwned?**
Not via a live query — this tool checks your password against a curated local list of the most common passwords found in public breach research (like NordPass's and SplashData's annual "worst passwords" reports), entirely offline. It intentionally does not call any external API like Have I Been Pwned, because doing so would require sending at least part of your password's hash over the network, which this page deliberately never does. For a live breach check, use a dedicated service directly.

**Why does this tool detect India-specific weak passwords?**
Generic checkers miss passwords built from common Indian names, cities, cricket terms, Bollywood names, Hindi words, or mobile number patterns - exactly what a regionally-tuned attack would try first.

**Does this checker support Unicode passwords, like emoji or non-Latin scripts?**
Yes. The character-count stat uses Unicode-aware counting (so an emoji correctly counts as one character, not two), and the tool flags whether your password contains any non-ASCII characters at all, which is useful context since some login forms silently reject or mangle non-ASCII input.

**Should I be worried about clipboard security when copying a generated password?**
Yes, mildly — clipboard contents can be read by other applications on some operating systems and by some malicious browser extensions. This tool shows a reminder after every copy to clear your clipboard once you've pasted the password where it's needed, and a password manager's autofill avoids the clipboard entirely for routine logins.

**How long should a password be?**
Length matters more than complexity. A random 16+ character password, or a 6-word random passphrase, is far stronger than an 8-character password stuffed with symbols, because every extra character multiplies the number of guesses an attacker needs — this is also the core recommendation in NIST's current digital identity guidelines (SP 800-63B).

**Are symbols necessary for a strong password?**
Not as much as people think. Adding one symbol to a short, dictionary-based password barely slows an attacker who already tries common substitutions like '@' for 'a' or '0' for 'o'. A longer password or passphrase without any symbols is usually stronger than a short one with symbols crammed in.

**Is a passphrase better than a traditional password?**
Often yes, and it's easier to remember and type correctly. Several random, unrelated words strung together create a long password with strong guess-resistance, without needing to memorize symbol substitutions — the words just need to be chosen by a random process, not by you.

**What is multi-factor authentication (MFA) and do I still need it with a strong password?**
MFA (or 2FA) requires a second proof of identity beyond your password — a code from an authenticator app, a hardware key, or a biometric check. Yes, you still need it: MFA protects you even if a strong password is somehow phished or leaked from a breach, since a password alone stops being enough to log in.

**Should I use a password manager?**
Yes. A password manager generates and remembers a unique, random password for every account, so you only need to remember one strong master password or passphrase — it's the practical way to actually use unique, high-entropy passwords across dozens of accounts without writing them down insecurely.

**What should a business password policy look like?**
Modern guidance favors a generous minimum length over forced complexity rules, screening new passwords against known-breached lists, dropping mandatory periodic rotation for passwords that haven't been compromised (which tends to produce weaker, more predictable passwords over time), and mandating MFA plus a company-approved password manager wherever feasible.

**What's the difference between 'real entropy' and 'naive entropy' shown on this page?**
Naive entropy assumes every character in your password is equally random given the character types present — length × log2(pool size) — which overestimates strength for anything containing patterns. Real entropy is derived from zxcvbn's actual guess-count estimate, which accounts for dictionary words, patterns, and known substitutions, and is the number that reflects real-world crack resistance.

**Why do the same password's crack times vary so much between scenarios?**
Guess rate varies by many orders of magnitude depending on the attack: a throttled login form might allow only ~100 guesses per hour, while an attacker who has stolen a poorly-hashed database and runs it offline on GPUs can try tens of billions of guesses per second — the same password can be effectively uncrackable in one scenario and instant in another.

**What are keyboard patterns, and why are they weak?**
Keyboard patterns are sequences typed by moving along the keyboard layout rather than choosing random characters — like 'qwerty', '1qaz2wsx', or 'asdfgh'. They look random at a glance but are among the very first patterns any real password-cracking tool checks, since they're extremely common.

**Can I check multiple passwords at once?**
Yes - the Bulk Check tab analyzes a list locally, shows a weakest/strongest comparison, and exports results as CSV.

**What does the 'What if...' section show?**
It re-runs the analysis on small variations of your password — adding two random characters, adding a trailing symbol, or removing a detected dictionary word — so you can see concretely how much (or little) each change actually improves your real crack-time estimate.

**Is the password and passphrase generator on this page cryptographically secure?**
Yes. Both generators use the Web Crypto API's crypto.getRandomValues() with unbiased rejection sampling (never Math.random(), which is not designed for security), so every character or word is drawn with a mathematically equal probability.

**Why does the pattern highlighting matter more than a plain strength score?**
A single score or color doesn't tell you what to fix. Seeing exactly which segment of your password was matched as a dictionary word, a date, or a repeated pattern — and which parts were genuinely unpredictable — tells you precisely what's dragging your password down, so you can target that specific weakness instead of guessing.

**Does a good score guarantee my account is safe?**
No - reused passwords, phishing, malware, and breaches at the service itself can compromise an account regardless of password strength. MFA and not reusing passwords matter just as much.

**Is this checker really free with no limits?**
Yes - no sign-up and no limit on checks, generations, or bulk audits.

**Does this tool work offline?**
Yes. Once the page has loaded (including the zxcvbn library), every feature — checking, generating, bulk auditing — works with no internet connection at all, which you can verify by disconnecting and continuing to use the page.

**Why type a variation of my real password instead of the actual one?**
Even though nothing leaves your browser here, it's a good general habit never to type your actual live password into any third-party tool. Type a close variation (swap a few characters) to get an equally meaningful strength read without ever exposing your real credential anywhere outside your password manager.

**What common password mistakes does this tool help catch?**
Dictionary words and names, keyboard walks, repeated or sequential characters, dates and years, common leetspeak substitutions, membership in the common-breached-password list, and India-specific predictable patterns — covering the vast majority of real-world weak password patterns in one pass.

#### Frequently asked questions (26)

**What is an SSH key?**
An SSH key is a pair of cryptographic keys — a private key you keep secret and a public key you share — used to log in to servers and services like GitHub without typing a password, and more securely than a password.

**Is this SSH key generator secure?**
Yes. It uses your browser's native Web Crypto API to generate the key pair — the same cryptographic engine built into every modern browser — rather than a custom or unverified implementation. Key generation and formatting happen entirely on your device.

**Does my private key ever leave my browser?**
No. The private key is generated, formatted, and displayed entirely in your browser's memory. Nothing is sent to ToolAdda's servers or any third party at any point.

**Which algorithm should I choose?**
Ed25519 is recommended for most modern uses — it's fast, produces short keys, and is supported by GitHub, GitLab, and virtually all current servers. Choose RSA only if you need to support very old systems that predate Ed25519 support.

**Is Ed25519 better than RSA?**
For most purposes, yes — Ed25519 offers equivalent or stronger security than RSA-2048/3072 with much shorter keys and faster signing, and it has no configurable key-size footgun (unlike RSA, where 1024-bit keys are insecure). RSA remains useful only for compatibility with legacy systems.

**What key size is recommended?**
For RSA, use at least 3072 bits (4096 for long-term keys); 2048 is the practical legacy minimum. Ed25519 has a single fixed, modern security level and needs no size decision.

**Can I use these keys with GitHub?**
Yes. Copy the generated public key into GitHub under Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key, and keep the private key on your device for git to use when connecting over SSH.

**Can I use them with AWS, GCP, or Azure?**
Yes. Add the public key to your cloud provider's instance metadata, key pair settings, or an authorized_keys file on the server, then connect using the matching private key with ssh -i.

**Can I regenerate keys?**
Yes. Click Regenerate to create a brand-new key pair at any time — every generation uses fresh cryptographic randomness, so no two key pairs are ever the same.

**Can I protect my key with a passphrase?**
This tool doesn't add passphrase encryption to the private key in-browser, to avoid shipping an unverified, home-grown implementation of OpenSSH's passphrase key-derivation function. After downloading your private key, run ssh-keygen -p -f your_key locally to add a passphrase using OpenSSH's own trusted tooling.

**Is this tool free?**
Yes. It's completely free, has no usage limits, and requires no account or sign-up.

**Does it work offline?**
Once the page is loaded, key generation runs entirely through your browser's built-in Web Crypto API with no network calls, so it keeps working even if your connection drops.

**Can I download a PKCS8 PEM version?**
Yes. Alongside the OpenSSH private key format, this tool also exports a standard PKCS8 PEM private key, which many non-SSH tools and libraries (TLS, code-signing, some cloud APIs) expect instead.

**What is a fingerprint?**
A fingerprint is a short cryptographic hash of the public key, used to visually or programmatically confirm you're connecting to the right server or that a public key wasn't tampered with, without comparing the entire key text.

**How do I install my public key on a server?**
Append the public key line to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the target server (or use ssh-copy-id user@host , which does this for you), ensuring the file has 600 permissions and the .ssh directory has 700.

**Where should I store my private key?**
Keep it only on your local device, typically in ~/.ssh/ , with file permissions restricted to your user ( chmod 600 ). Never email it, commit it to a repository, or paste it into a chat tool.

**Can I rotate SSH keys?**
Yes — generate a new key pair, add the new public key everywhere the old one was authorized, confirm the new key works, then remove the old public key from every server and service.

**Why shouldn't I share my private key?**
Anyone with your private key can authenticate as you on every server and service where your matching public key is trusted — it is the equivalent of your password, not something safe to share, back up in plain chat, or store in shared drives.

**Does it support Windows?**
Yes. The generated OpenSSH-format keys work directly with Windows 10/11's built-in OpenSSH client, PowerShell, and WSL.

**Does it support Linux and macOS?**
Yes. The generated keys are in the same OpenSSH format produced by ssh-keygen on Linux and macOS, and work identically with both operating systems' built-in SSH clients.

**Can I use it in CI/CD pipelines?**
Yes. Generate a dedicated deploy key, add its public half to the target service (GitHub deploy keys, a server's authorized_keys, etc.), and store the private key as an encrypted secret in your CI/CD platform (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins credentials).

**Does it support Kubernetes?**
SSH keys generated here work anywhere OpenSSH keys are used, including SSH access to Kubernetes nodes or git-based deploy keys referenced by Kubernetes Secrets for private repository access.

**How is randomness generated?**
Key material is generated using the Web Crypto API's cryptographically secure random number generator (backed by your operating system's CSPRNG), the same source browsers use for TLS and other security-critical operations.

**Is browser cryptography safe for this?**
Yes — the Web Crypto API is a W3C standard implemented natively by the browser vendor (not by this website), and is the same engine used for WebAuthn, TLS-adjacent operations, and other browser security features.

**Why isn't DSA offered?**
DSA has been disabled by default in OpenSSH since version 7.0 (2015) due to its weak fixed 1024-bit key size, and the Web Crypto API has never supported it — so it isn't offered here rather than shipping an unverified, insecure legacy algorithm.

**Can I inspect an existing key's fingerprint here?**
This tool focuses on generating new key pairs. For newly generated keys, the fingerprint and randomart are shown automatically alongside the key material.

#### Frequently asked questions (25)

**What is a PEM file?**
PEM (Privacy-Enhanced Mail) is a base64 text container used by OpenSSH, cloud providers, and almost all Linux/macOS tooling to store a private key, wrapped in "-----BEGIN ... PRIVATE KEY-----" lines.

**What is a PPK file?**
A .ppk file is PuTTY's own private key format, used by PuTTY, WinSCP, FileZilla, and other Windows SSH tools. It stores the algorithm, an optional encrypted private section, a comment, and an integrity MAC as plain text.

**What's the difference between PEM and PPK?**
They hold the same underlying key material in different containers. PEM is the cross-platform standard; PPK is PuTTY-specific. Converting between them changes only the container, never the actual cryptographic key.

**Is my private key uploaded anywhere?**
No. Parsing and re-encoding run locally in your browser. Your key is never sent to ToolAdda's servers or any third party.

**Is this PEM to PPK converter free?**
Yes — completely free, with no watermark, no signup, and no limit on conversions.

**Which PEM key formats are supported?**
Unencrypted RSA private keys in either PKCS#1 ("-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----") or PKCS#8 ("-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----") form.

**Does this tool support ECDSA and Ed25519 keys, or just RSA?**
This converter currently focuses on RSA, the most common case for legacy PEM keys. For ECDSA and Ed25519 support (in the other direction), see ToolAdda's PPK to PEM Converter .

**Can I convert an OpenSSH-format PEM key?**
Not directly - modern "-----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----" files aren't parsed by this tool. Convert it to classic PEM first with ssh-keygen -p -m PEM -f yourkey , then paste the result here.

**Can I convert a passphrase-encrypted PEM key?**
Not yet - encrypted PEM keys aren't supported. Remove the passphrase first (for example with ssh-keygen -p ) and convert the resulting unencrypted key.

**What PPK version does this tool produce?**
PPK format v2, the widely-supported version accepted by every current release of PuTTY, WinSCP, and plink.

**Will the generated PPK file work directly in PuTTY?**
Yes. The output includes correctly formatted public and private key blobs and a genuine HMAC-SHA1 Private-MAC computed the same way PuTTYgen computes it, so PuTTY accepts the file without any "corrupt key file" warning.

**Does this tool set a passphrase on the output PPK?**
No — the generated PPK is unencrypted. Open it in PuTTYgen afterward if you want to add a passphrase before saving it long-term.

**What is the PPK Private-MAC, and does this tool generate a valid one?**
The Private-MAC is an HMAC-SHA1 checksum PuTTY uses to detect a corrupted file or wrong passphrase before ever using the key. This tool computes a real, correct MAC over the exact key data it writes, matching what PuTTYgen itself would produce.

**Can I paste my key instead of uploading a file?**
Yes — paste the PEM text directly into the editor, or drag & drop a .pem/.key file onto it, or use the Browse button.

**Why do I need PPK instead of PEM?**
PuTTY, WinSCP, and FileZilla on Windows are built around the PPK format and don't read raw PEM files directly — converting once lets your existing key work with that whole toolchain.

**Which tools require a PPK file?**
PuTTY, PuTTYgen, Pageant (PuTTY's SSH agent), WinSCP, and FileZilla's SFTP client all use PPK natively on Windows.

**Can I use the converted PPK with WinSCP or FileZilla?**
Yes. Both accept standard PPK v2 files for SFTP/SCP key-based authentication, exactly what this tool produces.

**Does converting a key change its fingerprint?**
No. The fingerprint is derived from the public key material, which is identical before and after conversion — only the private key's container format changes.

Outputs PEM in the right shape per key type (PKCS#1 for RSA, SEC1 for EC, PKCS#8 for Ed25519) or an OpenSSH `openssh-key-v1` file, and can optionally **write a passphrase-encrypted PEM**. Also gives SHA-256 and MD5 fingerprints and keeps an in-session history. No key data is transmitted; note that its crypto libraries load from a CDN, so PPK v3 conversion in particular needs connectivity. #### Frequently asked questions (30)

**What is a PPK file?**
A .ppk file is PuTTY's own private key format, used by PuTTY, WinSCP, FileZilla, and other Windows SSH tools. It stores the key's algorithm, an optional encrypted private section, a comment, and an integrity MAC in a simple text format.

**What is a PEM file?**
PEM (Privacy-Enhanced Mail) is a base64 text container format used across almost every non-Windows SSH client and cloud provider. An SSH private key in PEM form is Base64-encoded DER wrapped in "-----BEGIN ... PRIVATE KEY-----" lines - the format ssh-keygen, OpenSSH, AWS EC2, and most Linux tooling expect.

**What's the difference between PPK and PEM?**
They store the same underlying key material in different containers. PPK is PuTTY-specific (Windows-focused); PEM is the cross-platform standard used by OpenSSH, cloud providers, and nearly all Linux/macOS tooling. Converting between them changes only the container, never the actual cryptographic key.

**Is my private key uploaded anywhere?**
No. Every parsing, decryption, and re-encoding step runs locally in your browser. Your key is never sent to ToolAdda's servers or any third party.

**Is this PPK to PEM converter free?**
Yes — completely free, with no watermark, no signup, and no limit on conversions.

**What PPK versions are supported?**
Both PPK format v2 and v3 are supported, including encrypted keys of both versions — v2 uses AES-256-CBC with a SHA-1-derived key, and v3 uses Argon2id/Argon2i/Argon2d, both handled entirely client-side.

**Does this tool support ECDSA and Ed25519 keys, or just RSA?**
All three: RSA, ECDSA (nistp256, nistp384, nistp521), and Ed25519. Each is re-encoded into its correct native PEM form - PKCS#1 for RSA, SEC1 for ECDSA, and PKCS#8 for Ed25519.

**My PPK file is passphrase-protected — can I still convert it?**
Yes. Enter the passphrase in the Unlock step; it's used only in-memory to decrypt the key locally and is never transmitted or stored.

**What happens to the passphrase when I convert?**
It's held in a JavaScript variable for the duration of the decryption and eligible for garbage collection immediately afterward - never written to disk, localStorage, or any network request.

**Can I add a new passphrase to the PEM output?**
Yes. Enable "Encrypt output with a passphrase" and enter a new one - the PEM output is encrypted as a standard PKCS#8 EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo (AES-256, PBKDF2/SHA-256). OpenSSH-format output is always exported unencrypted in this tool.

**What's the difference between PEM and OpenSSH output format?**
PEM (PKCS#1/SEC1/PKCS#8) is the older, universally-compatible container. OpenSSH format ("-----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----") is the modern container OpenSSH generates by default today, with cleaner Ed25519 support. Both are provided; use whichever your target tool expects.

**Which output format should I use for AWS EC2?**
AWS EC2 SSH access expects a traditional PEM file (PKCS#1 for RSA) — use the PEM output and save it with a .pem extension.

**Which output format should I use for GitHub/GitLab SSH?**
Either works - GitHub and GitLab authenticate using your public key regardless of which private key container you keep locally. Modern OpenSSH clients handle both transparently.

**Can I use the converted PEM with Terraform or Ansible?**
Yes. Terraform's connection blocks and Ansible's ansible_ssh_private_key_file both expect a standard PEM (or OpenSSH-format) private key file — exactly what this tool produces.

**Does this tool verify the integrity of my PPK file?**
For PPK v2 files, yes - the file's Private-MAC is recomputed and checked, showing a verified/mismatch badge. For PPK v3, integrity verification isn't implemented (the key material still converts correctly; only the extra MAC badge is unavailable), shown honestly rather than faked.

**What is an SSH key fingerprint?**
A fingerprint is a short hash of a public key, used to visually verify you're connecting to the right key without comparing the entire (much longer) key blob. This tool computes both the SHA256 and legacy MD5 fingerprint formats.

**What's the difference between the MD5 and SHA256 fingerprint?**
They're two different hash algorithms applied to the same public key blob. SHA256 (shown as "SHA256:base64…") is the modern default since OpenSSH 6.8; MD5 (colon-separated hex) is the legacy format some older tools and cloud console screens still show.

**Why does my fingerprint not match what my cloud provider shows?**
Double-check whether your provider displays an MD5 or SHA256 fingerprint (this tool shows both), and whether it's fingerprinting the public or private key file.

**Does this tool support PPK v3's Argon2 encryption?**
Yes. The Argon2id/Argon2i/Argon2d WebAssembly module is loaded only when you open an encrypted PPK v3 file, keeping the page lightweight for the common case while still fully supporting v3.

**Is Argon2 decryption slow?**
It can take a few seconds, and that's intentional - Argon2 is deliberately memory- and time-hard to resist brute-force passphrase guessing, using the exact parameters stored in your PPK v3 file.

**What happens if I enter the wrong passphrase?**
The tool detects the resulting garbage data structurally (invalid field lengths) and shows a clear "could not unlock" error rather than producing a corrupted or nonsensical key file.

**Does converting a key change its fingerprint?**
No. The fingerprint is derived purely from the public key material, which is identical before and after conversion — only the private key's container format changes.

**Can I convert multiple keys in one session?**
Yes. Convert a key, then use "Convert another" to load a new file — each conversion is added to your session history.

**What is a session conversion history, and is it saved anywhere?**
It's a simple in-memory list of this session's conversions (filename, algorithm, fingerprint) so you can quickly reopen a recent result. It's never written to localStorage, cookies, or disk, and disappears when you close or refresh the tab.

**Does this tool work offline?**
Core RSA/ECDSA conversion works offline once the page and its cryptography library are loaded. PPK v3 encrypted-key support loads a small Argon2 module on first use, which requires a connection at that moment.

**Can I use this on my phone?**
Yes. The interface is fully responsive and touch-friendly, including file upload from your device's file picker.

**Is this tool open source?**
The page uses the open-source node-forge and hash-wasm libraries for cryptographic primitives; the PPK parsing and key re-encoding logic is original code written for ToolAdda.

**How is this different from PuTTYgen?**
PuTTYgen is a desktop application you must download and install on Windows. This tool does the same PPK↔PEM conversion instantly in any modern browser, on any OS, with no install - plus fingerprints, integrity checking, and a conversion history.

**How is this different from other online PPK to PEM converters?**
Most online converters either upload your key to a server (a serious concern for a private key) or only support unencrypted RSA. This tool processes everything client-side and supports encrypted PPK v2 and v3, plus ECDSA and Ed25519.

**Can I convert PEM back to PPK?**
Yes — use ToolAdda's dedicated PEM to PPK Converter for the reverse direction.

### Sitemap Generator

#### Frequently asked questions (18)

**What is an XML sitemap?**
An XML sitemap is a file that lists important pages on your website so search engines like Google and Bing can discover and crawl them more efficiently, especially pages that aren't well linked internally.

**Is this sitemap generator completely free?**
Yes. ToolAdda's Sitemap Generator is free, requires no account, and processes everything locally in your browser.

**Can I use relative URLs in the sitemap generator?**
Yes. Paths like /about.html are automatically converted into full URLs using the base website URL you provide.

**Is my URL data uploaded to a server?**
No. All sitemap generation happens locally in your browser using JavaScript, so your URL list never leaves your device.

**How do I submit my sitemap to Google Search Console?**
Upload sitemap.xml to your website root (e.g. https://yoursite.com/sitemap.xml), then add that URL in Google Search Console under Sitemaps.

**How many URLs can one sitemap.xml file contain?**
The sitemaps.org protocol caps a single sitemap at 50,000 URLs and 50MB uncompressed. This tool enforces that limit and tells you to split into multiple files under a sitemap index if you exceed it.

**What should I do if my site has more than 50,000 URLs?**
Split your URLs into multiple sitemap files, each under the limit, then create a sitemap index file listing all of them and submit only the index URL to search engines.

**Does Google actually use the priority and changefreq values?**
Largely no - Google has said it mostly ignores these and relies on its own crawl signals. They're still valid per the protocol and other engines may weight them lightly, but don't expect them to meaningfully change Google's crawl behavior.

**What is the difference between a sitemap and robots.txt?**
robots.txt restricts what crawlers may access; a sitemap proactively lists what you want discovered. Most sites use both, often with robots.txt pointing to the sitemap's URL.

**Do I need a sitemap if my site is already well linked internally?**
It still helps - a sitemap gives search engines a direct, authoritative list of canonical URLs and lastmod hints, speeding up discovery beyond what crawling links alone would achieve.

**Can I include images or videos in a sitemap?**
Yes, using the separate image/video sitemap extensions with <image:image> or <video:video> tags. This tool generates the standard page-URL sitemap without those extension tags.

**What's the ideal lastmod date format?**
W3C Datetime format, most simply YYYY-MM-DD - what this tool's date picker produces. Only set it to when content actually changed; inflating it on every page reduces the signal's usefulness.

**Should every page on my site be in the sitemap?**
No — include only canonical, indexable pages you want search engines to rank. Leave out duplicate/parameterized URLs, pages blocked by robots.txt or noindex, redirects, and error pages, since listing non-canonical or non-indexable URLs can create sitemap warnings in Search Console.

**Does a sitemap guarantee my pages will be indexed?**
No - it aids discovery, but indexing still depends on content quality, crawl budget, and technical accessibility. It's a discovery aid, not an indexing guarantee.

**How often should I regenerate and resubmit my sitemap?**
Whenever you add, remove, or significantly update pages - for actively changing sites, monthly or as part of your deploy process keeps search engines working from current data.

**Can I use this tool for very large websites?**
Yes, up to the 50,000 URL protocol limit per file — paste your full URL list and the tool deduplicates and validates them locally. For sites beyond that limit, generate multiple sitemap files in batches and combine them under a sitemap index.

**Why did I get an "Invalid URL" error?**
A pasted line couldn't be parsed as a valid URL even combined with your base URL - check for stray spaces or non-URL text; the error names the exact line to fix.

**Is this sitemap generator accurate for SEO purposes?**
Yes — it produces standard-compliant sitemap.xml markup per the sitemaps.org protocol that Google Search Console, Bing Webmaster Tools, and virtually all crawlers accept without modification.

#### Frequently asked questions (25)

**What is DNS lookup?**
DNS lookup is the process of querying the Domain Name System to retrieve the records associated with a domain — such as its IP address (A/AAAA), mail servers (MX), or text records (TXT) — translating human-readable names into the machine-readable data that powers the internet.

**How does DNS work?**
When you look up a domain, a recursive resolver asks a root name server which server handles the domain's TLD, then asks that TLD server which name server is authoritative for the exact domain, and finally asks that authoritative server for the actual record — a process called recursive resolution.

**What is an A record?**
An A record maps a domain name to an IPv4 address, such as example.com pointing to 93.184.216.34. It's the most fundamental DNS record type, used by browsers to know where to connect.

**What is an AAAA record?**
An AAAA record maps a domain name to an IPv6 address, the 128-bit successor to IPv4 designed to accommodate the internet's growth beyond IPv4's address space.

**What is an MX record?**
An MX (Mail Exchange) record specifies which mail servers accept email for a domain, along with a priority number — lower numbers are tried first — so a domain can list backup mail servers.

**What is a TXT record?**
A TXT record stores arbitrary text data attached to a domain, commonly used for SPF, DKIM, DMARC, domain ownership verification, and other machine-readable metadata.

**What is an SPF record?**
SPF (Sender Policy Framework) is a TXT record listing which mail servers are authorized to send email on behalf of a domain, helping receiving servers reject forged 'from' addresses.

**What is a DMARC record?**
DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting & Conformance) is a TXT record at _dmarc.yourdomain.com that tells receiving mail servers what to do with messages that fail SPF or DKIM checks, and where to send reports.

**What is a DKIM record?**
DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) publishes a public key at a selector subdomain (like selector._domainkey.yourdomain.com) so receiving servers can verify a cryptographic signature added to outgoing mail, proving it wasn't altered in transit.

**How do I check DNS records for a domain?**
Enter the domain into this tool, choose a record type or 'All Records', and click Lookup — results come back in seconds directly from public DNS-over-HTTPS resolvers.

**How often do DNS records update?**
Updates depend on the record's TTL (time to live). A record with a 3600-second TTL can take up to an hour to be reflected everywhere, since resolvers cache the old value until it expires.

**Why are my DNS changes not visible yet?**
DNS propagation isn't instant — different resolvers around the world cache records for different durations based on TTL, so changes can take anywhere from minutes to 48 hours to be visible everywhere.

**What is TTL in DNS?**
TTL (Time To Live) is the number of seconds a resolver is allowed to cache a DNS record before re-querying the authoritative server, balancing update speed against query load.

**What is DNSSEC?**
DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) cryptographically signs DNS records so resolvers can verify they weren't tampered with in transit, protecting against cache poisoning and spoofing attacks.

**Can I look up subdomains?**
Yes — enter any subdomain or hostname, such as api.example.com or mail.example.com, exactly as you would a root domain.

**Can I check email authentication records?**
Yes — this tool automatically checks SPF and DMARC, and includes a one-click check against common DKIM selectors to find published DKIM keys.

**Can I export the results?**
Yes — export any lookup as JSON, CSV, or plain TXT, copy a formatted summary to your clipboard, print the page, or copy a shareable link that reruns the same lookup.

**Is this DNS lookup tool free?**
Yes — completely free, with no signup, no rate limits, and no watermarked results.

**Does it work on mobile?**
Yes — the interface is fully responsive with a sticky mobile search button, and every feature works identically on phones, tablets, and desktops.

**Is DNS lookup secure and private?**
Lookups are sent directly from your browser to public DNS-over-HTTPS resolvers (Google and Cloudflare) over encrypted HTTPS — ToolAdda's own servers never see or log the domains you search.

**What is a CNAME record?**
A CNAME (Canonical Name) record aliases one domain name to another, so all DNS queries for the alias are redirected to the target domain's records instead.

**What is an NS record?**
An NS (Name Server) record identifies which servers are authoritative for a domain, i.e., which servers hold the master copy of its DNS records.

**What is a SOA record?**
An SOA (Start of Authority) record holds administrative information about a DNS zone: the primary name server, admin contact, serial number, and timing values like refresh, retry, and expire.

**What is a PTR record?**
A PTR (Pointer) record maps an IP address back to a domain name — the reverse of an A record — used for reverse DNS lookups, mail server verification, and network diagnostics.

**What is a CAA record?**
A CAA (Certification Authority Authorization) record specifies which certificate authorities are permitted to issue TLS/SSL certificates for a domain, reducing the risk of mis-issued certificates.

#### Frequently asked questions (25)

**What is DNS propagation?**
The process by which a DNS change becomes visible across resolvers worldwide, governed by TTL and each resolver's independent cache.

**How long does DNS propagation take?**
It depends on the record's TTL — a record with a 300-second TTL can be fully visible within 5 minutes of expiry, while one left at a default 86400-second (24-hour) TTL can take up to a full day on any given resolver.

**Why are my DNS changes not visible yet?**
Resolvers that already cached the old record won't re-check the authoritative server until that cached entry's TTL expires — so it isn't broken, it's just waiting out the cache window.

**What is TTL?**
TTL (Time To Live) is the number of seconds a resolver is allowed to cache a DNS answer before it must re-query the authoritative server for a fresh value.

**Why do different resolvers show different results?**
Each resolver caches independently based on when it first saw the record and that record's TTL, so during the propagation window it's normal and expected for some resolvers to still return the old value while others already show the new one.

**What is DNS cache?**
A DNS cache is a temporary local store of previously resolved DNS answers, kept by resolvers (and browsers and operating systems) to avoid repeating the same lookup, discarded automatically once the record's TTL expires.

**Can I force DNS propagation?**
Not directly — you can't force other resolvers to drop their cache, but lowering the record's TTL well before a planned change shortens the natural propagation window for the next update.

**Does Cloudflare speed up propagation?**
Cloudflare's own authoritative DNS is very fast to publish changes, but it can't force third-party resolvers elsewhere to expire their cache early — propagation to the wider internet still follows each resolver's cached TTL.

**How often should I refresh a propagation check?**
Every few minutes is reasonable for a short-TTL record; this tool's auto-refresh option can re-check every 30 seconds automatically while you wait.

**Can I check MX propagation?**
Yes - select MX to see mail server and priority changes across resolvers.

**Can I verify TXT record propagation?**
Yes — TXT is fully supported, useful for confirming SPF, DKIM, DMARC, or domain-verification TXT records have gone live.

**Does this tool check DNS propagation worldwide?**
It queries four independently operated public DNS resolver networks (Google, Cloudflare, DNS.SB, and RethinkDNS) that are used by a large share of internet traffic globally — a strong practical signal, though it is not a literal probe from every country, since this tool runs entirely in your browser with no backend server network.

**Is this DNS propagation checker free?**
Yes — completely free, with no signup, no rate limits, and no watermarked results.

**Can I export propagation reports?**
Yes — export as JSON, CSV, or TXT, copy a formatted summary, print the page, or copy a shareable link that reruns the same check.

**Does it support mobile devices?**
Yes — the interface is fully responsive with a sticky mobile search button, and every feature works identically on phones, tablets, and desktops.

**Is my lookup secure and private?**
Yes — every query is sent directly from your browser to each resolver over encrypted HTTPS; ToolAdda's own servers never see or log the domains you check.

**What happens if propagation shows as failed?**
A 'failed' resolver means that specific resolver didn't respond to the query (often a transient network issue) — the tool lets you retry just the failed resolvers without re-running the whole check.

**How accurate are the results?**
Results are the real, live answers returned by each resolver at the moment you run the check — nothing is cached, simulated, or estimated by this tool itself.

**Can I monitor propagation continuously?**
Yes — enable auto-refresh to automatically re-check every 30 seconds while you keep the page open, useful while waiting out a TTL window.

**Why do different ISPs update at different times?**
Each ISP typically runs (or contracts) its own resolver infrastructure with its own cache state, so the exact moment an ISP's users see a DNS change depends on when that ISP's resolver last cached the old value.

**Why isn't there a literal world map with country markers?**
A real per-country map requires probe servers physically deployed in each location. This tool runs entirely in your browser with no backend, so every query genuinely originates from wherever you are — labeling that as 'Germany' or 'Japan' would be fabricated. Instead, it shows real, honestly-labeled results from four independent resolver operators.

**What is a DNS resolver?**
A DNS resolver is a server that looks up DNS records on behalf of a client, following the chain from root servers to TLD servers to the authoritative server, then caching the answer for future requests.

**What does 'consensus' mean in this tool?**
Consensus is the answer returned by the largest group of checked resolvers; a resolver 'matches consensus' when its returned value agrees with that majority answer.

**Can I check an expected value specifically?**
Yes — enter the exact value you expect (like a new server IP) in the optional 'expected value' field, and each resolver row will show whether it matches that specific value rather than just general consensus.

**Does DNSSEC affect propagation?**
DNSSEC doesn't change propagation timing, but a broken DNSSEC signature chain after a change can cause validating resolvers to reject the new record entirely (SERVFAIL) rather than simply serving a cached old value — this tool surfaces that distinction.

### Internet Speed Test

Measures download and upload throughput, ping over ten samples and jitter, testing primarily against **Cloudflare's speed endpoints** with jsDelivr, httpbin and postman-echo as fallbacks. Three methodology details worth citing: it uses **eight parallel download streams** because a single connection often cannot saturate a fast link; it **discards the first second** so TCP slow-start does not understate the result; and it deliberately transfers **incompressible data** (already-compressed JPEGs) because counting the decompressed bytes of a gzipped asset would overstate speed several-fold. Jitter is the **mean change between consecutive latency samples**, not the standard deviation, and ping is a trimmed mean. Beyond the raw numbers it answers the question people actually ask — **what the connection can handle** — grading the result against the published requirements for twelve activities from web browsing to 4K video, 1080p group calls, online gaming and cloud gaming, marking each supported, marginal or not, and naming the specific shortfall. It also estimates download times for familiar file sizes and compares the run against previous runs on the same device. Live gauge, PNG result card export, print-to-PDF and local history; ping and upload failures degrade gracefully rather than killing the run. Be accurate about limits: it does **no IP, ISP or geolocation lookup**, it measures against third-party endpoints rather than a nearby server, it cannot see past your Wi-Fi or your device, and a full run **consumes real data** — so treat the numbers as indicative of this device right now rather than authoritative for the line.

#### Frequently asked questions (18)

**How accurate is this internet speed test?**
It measures real transfers over your actual connection using eight parallel streams to a Cloudflare endpoint, discards the first second while TCP ramps up, and falls back to other providers if Cloudflare is blocked. That makes it comparable to any other browser-based test. What no browser test can do is bypass your Wi-Fi, your device or the browser itself, so treat the number as the speed available to this device right now rather than the speed on your line.

**Why is my speed lower than the plan I pay for?**
Almost always Wi-Fi rather than the line. A plan is sold as the speed to your router; what a laptop in another room sees after walls, interference and an older Wi-Fi standard can be a fraction of it. Test again with an Ethernet cable, or standing next to the router, and compare the two numbers before contacting your provider.

**What is a good internet speed?**
For one person browsing and streaming HD, 25 Mbps is comfortable. A household with 4K televisions and several people working wants 100 Mbps or more. Beyond about 200 Mbps most people stop noticing improvements, because the bottleneck moves to the servers you are talking to rather than your connection.

**What do download and upload speed actually mean?**
Download is how fast data reaches you, which decides streaming, browsing and downloads. Upload is how fast data leaves you, which decides video calls, cloud backups and sending large files. Most home connections are deliberately asymmetric, with upload a small fraction of download.

**What is ping and why does it matter?**
Ping is the round trip time for a small packet, in milliseconds. It has nothing to do with bandwidth: a very fast connection can still have terrible ping. It is what decides whether a video call feels natural and whether an online game is playable, so it matters more than raw speed for anything interactive.

**What is jitter?**
Jitter is how much the ping varies from one packet to the next. Steady 60 ms is fine; a ping that swings between 20 ms and 200 ms has high jitter and will break up calls and live video even though the average looks acceptable. Under 20 ms is comfortable for calls.

**Why is my upload speed so much lower than download?**
Because that is how most home broadband is designed. Cable and DSL reserve far more capacity for download because that is what households mostly do. Fibre connections are often symmetric, with upload matching download. A very low upload only becomes a problem when you make video calls or back up large files.

**Does Wi-Fi slow down my internet speed?**
Yes, often substantially. Distance, walls, interference from neighbouring networks and older hardware all reduce what reaches your device. The most useful diagnostic is to run this test once over Wi-Fi and once over Ethernet: if the wired result matches your plan, the problem is your Wi-Fi rather than your provider.

**How can I make my internet faster?**
Move closer to the router or use Ethernet, switch to the 5 GHz band if your router offers one, restart the router, and check nothing else on the network is downloading in the background. If the wired speed is still well below your plan, the issue is with the line or the provider and is worth reporting.

**Why does my speed change every time I test?**
Real connections vary with network congestion, what else is using your connection, and which server you reach. Run the test a few times at different moments and use the pattern rather than any single number. The tool keeps your recent results so you can see that pattern.

**Does this speed test use my data allowance?**
Yes. A full test transfers real data — typically tens to a few hundred megabytes depending on how fast your connection is, because a faster line moves more data in the same fixed time. On a metered or mobile connection, run it sparingly.

**Is my speed test result sent anywhere?**
No. The test runs in your browser and the results are stored only in your own browser's local storage so you can compare runs. Nothing is uploaded to ToolAdda and there is no account. The measurement traffic itself necessarily goes to a public test endpoint, which is how any speed test works.

**Which servers does the test use?**
It measures against Cloudflare's public speed endpoint by default. If that is unreachable — some corporate and school networks block it — it automatically falls back to large incompressible files on a public CDN, and then to other public endpoints. The result panel names the provider that was actually used.

**Why does the test need incompressible files?**
Because a compressed text file would be sent over the network in a small compressed form and then expanded by the browser. Counting the expanded bytes would report a speed several times higher than the real transfer. This test deliberately uses already-compressed data, such as JPEG images, so the bytes counted are the bytes that actually crossed the network.

**Do I need to close other apps before testing?**
It helps. Anything else downloading, syncing or streaming is competing for the same connection and will lower your result. For a clean measurement, pause large downloads and cloud backups first.

**Can I test the speed on my phone?**
Yes, the test works the same on a phone or tablet. Bear in mind it will measure your Wi-Fi or mobile connection as your phone sees it, and that a mobile test consumes data from your plan.

**What is Mbps, and how is it different from MB/s?**
Mbps is megabits per second and is how internet plans are sold. MB/s is megabytes per second and is what a download manager shows. There are eight bits in a byte, so a 100 Mbps connection downloads at about 12.5 MB/s at best — which is why a fast plan can look slow in a download window.

**Do I need to install anything to run this test?**
No. It runs entirely in your browser with no app, plugin, sign-up or Flash. Open the page and press start.

#### Frequently asked questions (16)

**What is a LinkedIn post previewer?**
It is a tool that renders your draft as it will appear in the LinkedIn feed, before you publish. The main thing it shows is where the feed collapses your post behind see more, so you can tell how much of your opening is actually visible to someone scrolling.

**How many characters before LinkedIn cuts a post?**
Roughly 210 characters on desktop and about 140 on mobile, after which the post collapses behind see more. Those figures are approximations: LinkedIn has changed them more than once and the real cut also depends on line breaks and screen width, so the tool lets you adjust the threshold.

**What is the LinkedIn character limit for a post?**
3,000 characters for the post body. That is a hard platform limit, and the counter in this tool turns red once you pass it. Comments and article bodies have different limits.

**Why does my post get cut off with see more?**
The feed shows only the first few lines of every post so more posts fit on screen. Anything past that point requires a tap. This is why the opening line matters far more than the rest, and why the previewer marks the cut point.

**Do line breaks count towards the fold?**
Yes. The collapsed view shows a limited number of lines as well as a limited number of characters, so blank lines are expensive. A post with a blank line after a short opening can be cut much earlier than its character count suggests.

**How do I write bold text on LinkedIn?**
LinkedIn strips markdown, so there is no real bold. What people use instead is a set of Unicode characters that look bold. Select text in the composer and apply the Bold style and the tool substitutes those characters for you.

**Is Unicode bold text bad for accessibility?**
Yes, and it is worth knowing before you use it. Screen readers announce these characters oddly or skip them entirely, so a heading in Unicode bold can be unreadable to someone using assistive technology. They are also not indexed properly by search. Use them for a word or two, never for a whole post.

**How many hashtags should a LinkedIn post have?**
Around three to five is the range most commonly recommended, and the tool flags a post with more than ten. Hashtags help the post reach beyond your immediate network, but a wall of them reads as spam to human readers.

**Does the previewer show my post exactly as LinkedIn will?**
It is a close approximation, not a pixel-exact copy. Fonts, spacing and the fold position all vary with device, browser and LinkedIn's own changes. Treat it as a reliable guide to length and structure rather than a guarantee of exact rendering.

**Can I preview an image, carousel or poll post?**
Yes. Switch the post type between text, single image, carousel, video, poll and link share. Each changes the card layout, and an attachment pushes the text further up, which is worth seeing before you publish.

**Is my post uploaded anywhere?**
No. Everything runs in your browser. The draft autosave writes to your own browser storage only, and nothing is sent to a server or to LinkedIn.

**Does this tool post to LinkedIn for me?**
No. It has no connection to your account and cannot publish, schedule or read anything. Copy the finished post and paste it into LinkedIn yourself.

**Will my line breaks survive when I paste the post?**
Single and double line breaks paste through fine. Runs of three or more blank lines get collapsed when the post is published, so the spacing may tighten slightly compared with what you typed.

**What makes a good LinkedIn hook?**
Something that is complete enough to make sense on its own and incomplete enough to be worth expanding. A concrete claim, a surprising number or a short story opening all work. Vague throat-clearing like Excited to share does not, because it says nothing before the fold.

**Can I save a draft?**
Yes. The tool autosaves to your browser's local storage as you type, and offers to restore it next time rather than overwriting whatever you are working on.

**Is this LinkedIn post previewer free?**
Yes. It is free, needs no account and has no limits. This tool is not affiliated with, endorsed by or connected to LinkedIn.

#### Frequently asked questions (26)

**What is a character counter?**
A character counter is a tool that measures the length of a piece of text — usually as raw character count, word count, and related statistics — so writers can meet length requirements for platforms like Twitter, SEO meta tags, SMS, or academic assignments.

**How are characters counted?**
Every visible symbol counts as a character, including letters, numbers, punctuation, spaces, and emoji. This tool counts by Unicode code point (using proper grapheme-aware iteration for multi-part emoji), which matches how most social platforms and CMS systems count length.

**Does whitespace count as a character?**
It depends on which number you look at. "Characters (with spaces)" includes every space, tab, and line break. "Characters (without spaces)" strips all whitespace so you see just the visible text content.

**What's the difference between words and characters?**
A character is a single letter, digit, symbol, or space. A word is a sequence of characters separated by whitespace or punctuation. "Cat" is one word made of three characters; "The quick fox" is three words and thirteen characters.

**Is this tool free?**
Yes. It's completely free, has no usage limits, and requires no account or sign-up.

#### Frequently asked questions (14)

**How do I convert text to uppercase or lowercase?**
Paste your text and choose the case you want. The result appears immediately and can be copied straight back out. There is nothing to install and no button sequence to learn.

**What is the difference between Title Case and Capitalized Case?**
Strict title case leaves short words such as a, the, of and in lowercase unless they start the title. Capitalized case capitalises every word without exception. Both are widely used — the important thing is being consistent within a document.

**What is sentence case?**
Only the first letter of the sentence is capitalised, along with anything that would normally be capitalised anyway, such as names. It is the right default for body text, descriptions and most interface copy.

**How do I fix text I typed with caps lock on?**
Paste it in and choose sentence case. That fixes an accidentally shouted paragraph in one step rather than retyping it, which is the most common reason people reach for this tool.

**Why is text in all capitals harder to read?**
Because readers recognise the overall shape of a word rather than reading it letter by letter, and the ascenders and descenders that give words their shape disappear in capitals. Every word becomes the same rectangle, so reading measurably slows.

**Is uppercase text an accessibility problem?**
For anything longer than a short label, yes. Accessibility guidance discourages long runs of capitals, and some screen readers spell out extended capitals letter by letter because they mistake them for acronyms. Use bold for emphasis instead.

**Why would I lowercase everything?**
Usually to normalise data before comparing or storing it. Lowercasing both sides is the standard way to compare text case-insensitively, and it makes messy imported data consistent before you work with it.

**Does it handle accented and non-English characters?**
Yes. The conversion uses your browser's own Unicode-aware case rules, so accented Latin characters and other scripts are handled correctly rather than being stripped or mangled.

**Is my text sent to a server?**
No. Everything happens in your browser as you type, so the text never leaves your device. That matters because what people paste into a case converter is often a real document — a customer list, a draft email, an internal announcement.

**Is there a limit on how much text I can convert?**
The practical limit is your device's memory, since the work is done locally. Ordinary documents of any realistic length convert instantly.

**Does it preserve my line breaks and paragraphs?**
Yes. Only letter casing changes — spacing, line breaks and punctuation are left exactly as they were, so pasted formatting survives the conversion.

**Can I undo a conversion?**
Your original text stays in the input box, so you can switch between cases freely or copy the original back out. Nothing is destroyed by choosing a case.

**Does it work offline?**
Yes, once the page has loaded. Disconnecting from the network and watching it keep working is the simplest way to confirm nothing is being uploaded.

**Is it free?**
Completely. No sign-up, no download and no limit on how many times you use it.

#### Frequently asked questions (28)

**What is Base64 encoding?**
Base64 represents binary data - images, files, or raw bytes - using only 64 printable ASCII characters (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, +, /). It exists because many text-based systems (email, JSON, XML, URLs) can't safely carry arbitrary binary bytes, so Base64 re-packages that data as plain text any system can transport without corruption.

**Is Base64 a form of encryption?**
No. Base64 is encoding, not encryption - it uses no secret key and provides zero confidentiality. Anyone can decode a Base64 string instantly, including this tool. Use real encryption (AES, TLS) to protect sensitive data, and Base64 only to make the resulting bytes transportable as text.

**Is my data uploaded to a server?**
No. Every encode/decode runs locally in your browser using native JavaScript APIs. Nothing you type or upload is transmitted anywhere - the one exception is the optional Import from URL feature, which fetches directly from the URL you provide.

**Does this tool support Unicode, emoji, and non-Latin scripts?**
Yes. Text is encoded as UTF-8 bytes using the browser's native TextEncoder/TextDecoder before Base64 encoding, so emoji, accented letters, Hindi, Chinese, Arabic, and any other Unicode text round-trip correctly - unlike tools built on the deprecated escape()/unescape() trick.

**What is URL-safe Base64 and when do I need it?**
Standard Base64 uses + and /, which have special meaning inside URLs. URL-safe Base64 replaces + with -, / with _, and typically omits = padding. Use it for URLs, filenames, cookies, and JWT segments; use standard Base64 for Data URIs and MIME email.

**Why does Base64 make my output about 33% larger?**
Base64 packs every 3 bytes of input into 4 output characters (6 bits per character instead of 8). That fixed 4:3 ratio is where the ~33% overhead comes from - it's mathematically unavoidable, the trade-off for safe, universal text transport.

**Can I convert an image to Base64?**
Yes. Switch to File / Image, then drag & drop, browse, paste from your clipboard, or import from a URL. The tool encodes the raw bytes and shows a live preview so you can confirm it before copying the string.

**Can I convert Base64 back into a downloadable image or file?**
Yes. Paste a Base64 string and the tool decodes the bytes, detects the file type from its binary signature, shows an image preview when applicable, and lets you download the result in one click.

**What file types are supported?**
Any file type, since Base64 works on raw bytes. This tool adds smart handling for JSON, XML, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and SVG, plus binary signature detection for PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, ICO, WebP, PDF, ZIP, and GZIP.

**Is there a file size limit?**
No artificial limit is imposed by the tool. Because everything runs on your own device, the practical ceiling is your browser tab's available memory — a few hundred megabytes typically processes without issue, though very large files will simply take longer and use more RAM than small ones.

**Does this tool work offline?**
Once the page has loaded, all encoding/decoding logic runs locally and needs no network connection - only Import from URL inherently requires connectivity.

**Can I encode or decode JSON, XML, HTML, CSS, or SVG specifically?**
Yes. Paste any of these as text and encode normally. On decode, the tool recognizes JSON, XML, HTML, and SVG automatically and offers Pretty/Minify, with SVG output also rendering as a live image preview.

**What's the difference between standard Base64 and Base64 URL-safe?**
They encode the same underlying bytes but use a different character set: standard Base64 uses + and / with = padding; URL-safe Base64 substitutes - and _ and usually drops padding so the string is safe to place directly in a URL, filename, or cookie without extra escaping. This tool's URL-safe toggle switches the output character set; decoding accepts either flavor automatically.

**Why did decoding fail with an "Invalid Base64" error?**
Common causes: characters outside A-Z, a-z, 0-9, +, /, -, _ (often stray line breaks or quotes); a length that isn't a multiple of 4 after removing whitespace; or missing/incorrect padding. Click Validate for a specific diagnosis.

**Can I batch-convert multiple files at once?**
Yes. Drop or select multiple files and each is encoded independently into a queue - click any item to load it, copy its Base64, or download every result together as a ZIP.

**Does this tool keep a history of my conversions?**
Yes, a short local history of recent text conversions is kept in your browser's localStorage for convenience - it never leaves your device, caps at 15 entries, and can be cleared anytime.

**Can I copy a decoded image directly to my clipboard?**
Yes, in browsers supporting the Clipboard API's ClipboardItem (current Chrome, Edge, Safari). Use Copy Image next to the preview; Download works everywhere as a fallback.

**What keyboard shortcuts are available?**
Ctrl/Cmd+Enter runs the current mode, Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+C copies output, Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+X clears everything, Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+S swaps input/output, and Ctrl/Cmd+Z / Shift+Z undo and redo.

**Can I paste an image directly from my clipboard?**
Yes. Copy an image anywhere, click into the page, and press Ctrl+V (Cmd+V on Mac) - it's detected as a file and encoded automatically.

**Can I import a file directly from a URL?**
Yes, via the Import from URL field. This depends on the target server allowing cross-origin requests (CORS); if it blocks them, download the file yourself and drag it in instead - a browser security restriction, not a tool limitation.

**Does Base64 work the same in every programming language?**
The core RFC 4648 algorithm is universal - a string encoded in JavaScript decodes identically in Python, Java, Go, or PHP. What differs is API defaults: some languages default to URL-safe encoding, strip padding, or require explicit UTF-8 handling.

**Why do email attachments use Base64?**
SMTP was designed for 7-bit ASCII text and can corrupt raw binary in transit. MIME email wraps attachments in Base64 so every mail server can relay them safely as text, and the receiving client decodes them back to the original file.

**What's the difference between Base64 and hashing (MD5/SHA-256)?**
Base64 is fully reversible - you can always recover the original bytes. Hashing is one-way and produces a fixed-size fingerprint that cannot be reversed. Base64 is for safe transport; hashing is for integrity checks and password storage.

**Can I use this for Basic Auth headers or JWT segments?**
Yes, for understanding and debugging - Basic Auth sends "username:password" Base64-encoded (not encrypted), and JWTs are three Base64URL segments joined by dots. To build or verify a signed JWT, use ToolAdda's dedicated JWT Encoder and JWT Debugger.

**Does encoding or decoding change my original file?**
No. Base64 is lossless in both directions — decoding a correctly encoded string reconstructs the exact original bytes, with no quality loss for images or corruption for any other file type. This tool never modifies your source file; it only reads it to produce a new encoded or decoded output.

**Is this tool free, and is there a usage limit?**
Yes, completely free with no sign-up, watermark, or usage cap. Since processing happens on your own device, there's no server quota to run into.

**Does this work on mobile devices?**
Yes. The interface is fully responsive and touch-friendly, with a tap-to-browse upload flow and a sticky action bar for quick access on small screens.

**Why do some Base64 strings end with = or == and others don't?**
Base64 processes input in 3-byte groups. When the final group has only 1 or 2 bytes instead of 3, padding characters (= for one missing byte, == for two) are added so the output length stays a multiple of 4. URL-safe Base64 commonly omits this padding entirely since the decoder can infer it from the string length.

**Is my typed text stored or sent anywhere?**
No. Every conversion happens locally in your browser with JavaScript. Nothing you type is uploaded to a server.

Yes, use the "Wrap with symbols" control to add decorative borders to every result.

**Will fancy text hurt my SEO or accessibility?**
If used in body content meant for everyone, yes - it can be unreadable to screen readers and won't match plain-text search. It's fine for bios and nicknames.

#### Frequently asked questions (18)

**How do I copy an emoji from this page?**
Click or tap any emoji, kaomoji, or symbol tile. It is copied to your clipboard the moment you click it — there is no separate 'copy' button to press and no page reload.

**What is a kaomoji?**
A kaomoji (顔文字, literally 'face character') is a Japanese-style emoticon built from Unicode letters, punctuation, and symbols that you read face-on, like (＾▽＾) or ¯\_(ツ)_/¯, instead of sideways like a classic Western emoticon such as :).

**Is this emoji picker free?**
Yes. Every emoji, kaomoji, symbol, and feature on this page is free with no account, no signup, and no hidden paywall.

**Do I need to install an app or extension?**
No. Everything runs directly in your browser. There is nothing to install, and it works on desktop and mobile browsers alike.

**Why does an emoji look different on my phone than on my friend's phone?**
Emoji are Unicode characters, not pictures. Apple, Google, Samsung, and Microsoft each draw their own artwork for the same character, so the meaning stays identical but the exact look changes by device and app.

**Why does an emoji show as a box or question mark?**
Your device's font hasn't been updated to include that newer emoji yet. Updating your OS usually resolves it.

**How do I use these emojis on Instagram or WhatsApp?**
Copy the emoji or kaomoji here, open Instagram or WhatsApp, tap into the bio, caption, or chat field, and paste using your device's normal paste action (long-press → Paste on mobile, Ctrl+V or Cmd+V on desktop).

**Can I use kaomoji in usernames and bios?**
Usually yes - they're plain Unicode text, so they work anywhere text is accepted, unless the platform restricts special characters.

**Does this work on mobile?**
Yes, the picker is fully responsive and touch-friendly, with tap-to-copy, long-press for details, and a layout that avoids horizontal scrolling on any screen size.

**Can I copy multiple emojis at once?**
Yes. Turn on 'Build a string' mode, tap each emoji or kaomoji you want in order, and then use 'Copy all' to copy the entire combined string in one go.

**How do I change emoji skin tone?**
Use the skin tone dropdown above the grid; it applies to supported hand and people emoji and is remembered on this device.

**Are my copied emojis stored anywhere?**
Recents and favourites are saved only in your browser's local storage on your device - nothing is uploaded.

**What is the shrug emoji and how do I type it?**
The shrug emoticon ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ is a kaomoji, not a standard emoji — it isn't on your phone's default keyboard. Search 'shrug' on this page to copy it instantly.

**What is a Lenny face?**
A Lenny face, ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°), is a specific viral kaomoji used to convey a smug or suggestive tone. It's built from Unicode combining characters, which is why it's hard to type by hand — search 'lenny' here to copy it directly.

**Do these emojis work in Word, Excel, and Gmail?**
Yes. Because emoji and kaomoji are standard Unicode text, they paste correctly into Word, Excel, Google Docs, Gmail, and virtually any modern app that accepts text.

**What is the Windows emoji keyboard shortcut?**
Win + . (period) or Win + ; (semicolon) opens the native panel from any text field.

**Why do some kaomoji break or show as boxes when pasted?**
Kaomoji often use rare Unicode combining marks and symbol blocks. Some apps strip unsupported characters, some fonts don't include the glyph, and some input fields sanitize text — pasting into a plain-text field usually works best.

**Can I search by feeling instead of exact name?**
Yes. The search understands everyday words like 'crying', 'shrug', 'happy', or 'flip table' in addition to exact emoji names and shortcodes, and it tolerates small typos.
