#### Frequently asked questions (30)

**What is an OMR sheet?**
An OMR sheet is a printed answer form where each question has a row of bubbles and the candidate fills exactly one of them. Because every bubble sits at a known position, the completed sheet can be marked quickly by eye against a key, or read by optical mark recognition software that detects which positions are dark.

**What does OMR stand for?**
Optical Mark Recognition. It is the technique of detecting marks — filled bubbles, ticked boxes — at fixed positions on a page, rather than reading handwriting. It is what makes large multiple-choice exams practical to grade.

**How do I create an OMR sheet online?**
Set the number of questions, choose how many options each question has, pick your paper size, and switch on whatever header fields you need. The preview updates as you type, so you can see the finished sheet before committing. When it looks right, print it or download a PDF.

**Can I create a 50-question OMR sheet?**
Yes, and it is the default. Fifty questions with four options fits comfortably on a single A4 page in two columns alongside a roll number grid and an instructions block.

**Can I create a 100-question OMR sheet?**
Yes. The tool supports 1 to 300 questions and works out how many pages are needed from the real millimetre dimensions of your chosen paper. A hundred questions typically fits one A4 page in three or four columns, or two pages with larger bubbles.

**Can I choose 4 or 5 answer options?**
You can choose anything from 2 to 6 options per question. Two is useful for true/false papers, four and five are the common MCQ formats, and six covers matching-style questions. You can also override the bubble labels entirely — for example T and F instead of A and B.

**Can I create an A4 OMR sheet?**
Yes. A4 is the default. Letter, Legal and A5 are also available, and each can be set to portrait or landscape. The preview and the printed output both use the exact dimensions of the size you pick.

**Can I print the generated OMR sheet?**
Yes. The Print button sends only the sheet pages to the printer — the settings panel, site header and everything else are excluded. The page size and orientation you chose are written into the print rules, so the browser does not have to guess.

**Can I download the OMR sheet as PDF?**
Yes. The PDF is drawn as true vector graphics rather than a screenshot, so the bubbles stay perfectly circular at any zoom and the file remains small. You can also generate several blank copies inside a single PDF.

**Can I download the sheet as an image?**
Yes. PNG export renders the current page at roughly 300 dpi, which is enough for printing or pasting into a document. SVG export gives you the sheet as a scalable vector file you can edit in a drawing program.

**Can I add candidate information?**
Yes. Name and class lines, a date line, a signature line and a photo box can each be switched on or off. There is also a roll number grid where each digit gets its own column of bubbles from 0 to 9, which is the standard encoding used in board and entrance exams.

**Can I add an exam name and school name?**
Yes. The exam title, institution name, exam date, subject code and an optional form ID all appear in the sheet header. Leave any of them blank and the header closes up around the gap rather than leaving an empty line.

**Can I add a school logo?**
Yes. Choose an image and it appears in the header. The file is read in your browser using the FileReader API and is never uploaded anywhere. The aspect ratio is preserved so the logo is not stretched, and you can remove it at any time.

**Can I create multiple pages?**
Yes, and it happens automatically. The tool measures how much vertical room is left after the header, footer and signature line, works out how many rows fit per column, and starts a new page when it runs out. Pages after the first carry a slim continuation header, so they gain more room for questions.

**Can I change the number of columns?**
Yes, from one to five. Auto layout is on by default and picks a sensible number for your question count and paper width. If you set the columns yourself and ask for more than physically fit, the tool uses as many as fit and tells you why.

**Can I change the bubble size and spacing?**
Bubbles come in small, medium and large, and row spacing can be compact, normal or spacious. Larger bubbles are easier to fill accurately but use more space, so they may push the sheet onto an extra page — the tool warns you when that is likely.

**What bubble shapes are available?**
Circle, oval, square and rounded square. Circles are the default because they are the most familiar and the easiest to fill cleanly. Scanner-friendly mode forces circles regardless of what is selected.

**Can I create an answer key?**
Yes. Switch on the answer key, then tap the correct option for each question in the grid. The key is generated as a separate page at the end of the PDF with the correct bubbles filled in — it is never part of the student sheet, so there is no risk of handing it out by accident.

**Is the generated OMR sheet scanner compatible?**
It is designed to be readable: bubbles are evenly spaced, consistently sized and printed in solid black on white. Scanner-friendly mode goes further by removing decoration and adding corner registration marks. That said, commercial OMR scanners are usually calibrated to their own vendor templates, so test a sample sheet with your specific scanner before running a real exam.

**What is scanner-friendly mode?**
It strips the sheet back for machine reading: decorative elements and the photo box are removed, bubbles are forced to plain circles at a consistent size, and four solid registration squares are printed in the corners so alignment software has fixed reference points.

**What is the best paper size for an OMR sheet?**
A4 for most of the world and Letter in the United States. Both give enough room for a roll number grid plus 50 to 100 questions on one page. Legal helps when you need many questions on a single sheet, and A5 suits short class quizzes.

**How should I print an OMR sheet?**
Print at 100% or Actual Size, never Fit to Page. Scaling changes the physical size of every bubble, which matters if the sheets will be read by software calibrated to specific dimensions. Use plain white paper and check that a printed bubble is a clean outline rather than a filled or broken circle.

**Why does print scale matter so much?**
Because an OMR reader looks for marks at expected coordinates. If the browser shrinks the page to fit the printer margins, every bubble moves and shrinks by the same few percent, and a reader calibrated to the original layout can start missing them. Printing at actual size keeps the geometry exactly as designed.

**Does the OMR generator work on mobile?**
Yes. On a phone the settings appear first and the preview below them, and the sheet keeps the true proportions of the paper rather than stretching to the screen. Use the zoom buttons to inspect small bubbles.

**Are my exam details uploaded anywhere?**
No. Everything — the layout, the preview, the PDF and the saved settings — happens inside your browser. No exam title, candidate field or logo is sent to any server. Settings are stored on your own device so the tool remembers them next time.

**Can I save and reuse my settings?**
Yes. Settings are saved automatically on your device, and you can export them as a JSON file to share with a colleague or move to another computer. Importing that file restores the whole configuration, including the answer key.

**What is the form ID for?**
It is an optional identifier printed in the header and repeated on later pages — useful when an institution runs several papers on the same day and needs to tell the sets apart. It is plain text, so you can use any coding scheme your exam office already uses.

**How many copies can I generate at once?**
Up to 100 blank copies in a single PDF. Each copy is labelled so an invigilator can tell them apart while distributing. Large copy counts make a bigger file, so give the browser a moment to finish.

**What if my settings do not fit on the page?**
The tool does not silently produce a broken sheet. If you ask for more columns than fit, it uses the number that does fit and shows a note explaining why, with the specific things to change — enable auto layout, reduce the bubble size, or switch to landscape.

**Is this OMR sheet generator free?**
Yes. It is free with no sign-up, no watermark on the output and no limit on how many sheets you generate or download.

### Exam Seating Arrangement Planner

Takes a list of classes as **label plus roll-number range** (`CSE 101-160`, `MECH 2021ME01-2021ME40`, or a bare count like `PHYSICS 45`) and a list of rooms as **rows x columns** seat grids, and produces a seating chart in which **no two students from the same class, branch or paper occupy neighbouring seats**. Four mixing modes: strict (guards left, right, front and back), row-only, column-only, and block (no mixing, for a single class). Three fill orders (row, column, snake) and a choice between spreading every class proportionally across all rooms or filling one room at a time. Produces four printable outputs from one plan - the **seating chart** (one room per page, board at the top), a **room-wise attendance list** with a signature column, a **roll-number index** sorted numerically for the notice board, and a **large-type door notice** per hall - plus CSV export. Roll prefixes and zero padding are preserved, and sorting is numeric so roll 2 precedes roll 10.

#### How to make an exam seating arrangement

Turn a list of roll numbers and a list of rooms into a printable seating chart in which same-class students are not adjacent.

1. **Enter the classes** — Type one class per line as a label and a roll number range, for example 'CSE 101-160'. A bare count such as 'PHYSICS 45' is read as roll numbers 1 to 45, and prefixes like '2021ME01-2021ME40' are preserved.
2. **Enter the rooms** — Type one room per line with its seat grid, for example 'Room 101 6x5' for six rows of five seats. If you only know the capacity, write 'Room 101 30' and the planner picks a sensible grid.
3. **Choose the mixing rule** — Strict keeps students of the same class off all four neighbouring seats. Row only guards left and right, column only guards front and back, and block seats each class together when mixing is not wanted.
4. **Read the warnings** — The planner checks feasibility before it allocates. If one class holds more than half the seats, it says so, because in that case some of its students must end up adjacent whatever the arrangement.
5. **Print or export** — Print the seating charts one room per page, print the room-wise attendance lists and door notices from their tabs, or download the whole plan as a CSV to open in Excel.

#### Frequently asked questions (18)

**Can I stop students of the same class sitting next to each other?**
That is the default and the reason the tool exists. Strict mode treats the seats to the left, right, front and back as neighbours and will not place two students from the same class in any of them. If only side-by-side copying concerns you, row-only mixing drops the front-to-back rule and leaves the planner more freedom.

**How many students of one class can I mix before it becomes impossible?**
Half the seats, rounded up. If you are seating sixty students, no single class can exceed thirty without two of its members ending up adjacent — you can see this by imagining a chessboard, where the most seats you can occupy without touching is every other square. The planner does this arithmetic before it allocates and warns you by name if a class is over the line, so you find out before printing rather than afterwards.

**Why does the chart mark some seats with an exclamation mark?**
Because the planner could not keep that seat apart from its neighbour, and would rather show you than hand over a chart that silently fails its own rule. Add a room, split the oversized class into two papers, or move those few students by hand.

**What happens if I have more students than seats?**
Nobody is dropped. Every available seat is filled, the shortfall is stated in numbers at the top, and the leftover roll numbers are listed under "Not allotted a seat" in the Room lists tab.

**How do I seat two different question papers in one room?**
Enter each paper as its own group, even when the students share a class - Paper A 1-30 and Paper B 31-60 . The planner alternates them, so a candidate looking sideways sees answers to a different paper.

**How do I enter roll numbers like 2021CS101?**
Write the range exactly as your institution writes it: 'MECH 2021ME01-2021ME40'. The letter prefix is kept on every roll number, and the zero padding of the first number sets the width, so 2021ME01 through 2021ME09 keep their leading zero. A plain range like '1-45' gets no padding.

**Can I split one class across several rooms?**
Yes, and by default that is what happens. In spread mode every room receives the same proportional mix of every class, which keeps any single invigilator from facing one entire class and makes the mixing rule easier to satisfy. Choose fill mode instead if you want the first room filled completely before the next one is used.

**Does the seat order change how students are numbered?**
It changes which physical seat each roll number lands on. Row order fills left to right along the front row first, column order fills down the first column before moving across, and snake order runs left to right then right to left on alternate rows so consecutive roll numbers are never diagonal neighbours. Seat labels themselves are always row letter plus column number — A1, A2, B1 — regardless of fill order.

**Can I print a separate notice for each room door?**
Yes. The Door notices tab produces one large-type sheet per room listing the roll numbers allotted to it, with the exam name and date if you entered them. Printing from that tab puts each notice on its own page, ready to tape to the hall door.

**Can students look up their own room and seat?**
The Roll index tab is exactly that list: every roll number sorted in order with its room and seat, which is the sheet normally pinned on the notice board outside. It sorts numerically rather than alphabetically, so roll 2 comes before roll 10 instead of after it.

**Can I get an attendance sheet for the invigilator?**
The Room lists tab gives one table per room - serial number, roll number, class, seat and a blank signature column - sorted by roll number and printed one room per page.

**Can I export the seating plan to Excel?**
Download CSV gives you one row per student with roll number, class, room, seat label, row and column. Excel, LibreOffice and Google Sheets all open it directly, and commas or quotation marks inside a class name are escaped properly rather than splitting the row.

**What if I only know a room's capacity, not its rows and columns?**
Write the capacity on its own, like 'Room 101 30', and the planner works out a near-square grid that is slightly wider than it is deep. Wider rows give the mixing rule more room to work, so if you do know the real shape it is worth typing it as rows by columns instead.

**Does this work for a single class with no mixing?**
Yes — choose block mode, which seats each group together in sequence and makes no adjacency promise. This is what you want for a single class writing one paper, where you only need roll numbers laid out in order with a room list and door notice.

**Are my students' roll numbers uploaded anywhere?**
No. The whole plan is computed in your browser in JavaScript. No roll number, class name or exam title is sent to any server, and there is no account to create. Your last settings are kept on your own device so the tool reopens where you left it, and clearing your browser storage removes them.

**Will I get the same chart if I run it again?**
Yes. The allocation is deterministic — the same classes, rooms and options always produce the same seating chart. That matters because an exam office often prints the charts, then reprints one page after a correction, and the two must agree.

**How does it decide which class to seat next?**
At every seat it looks at which classes are already sitting in the neighbouring seats, rules those out, and from the classes that remain picks the one with the most students still to be seated. Taking the largest remaining class first is what stops the planner painting itself into a corner and being unable to fill the last few seats legally.

**Is this free, and is there a limit on students or rooms?**
Free, with no sign-up and no watermark. There is no limit on the number of rooms, and each room can be up to 60 rows by 60 columns. A single class range is capped at 20,000 roll numbers, which is well past what any hall arrangement needs and exists only so a mistyped range cannot freeze the page.

- No third-party libraries, no sign-up and no watermark
- Runs entirely offline in the browser

#### How to make printable bingo cards

1. **Choose a game type** — Pick 75-ball, 90-ball UK, or custom words and pictures for a themed game.
2. **Add your content** — For a word game, load one of the themed lists and edit it, or paste your own list with one item per line.
3. **Set how many cards you need** — Enter anything from 1 to 500. The tool checks that many genuinely different cards are possible before it generates.
4. **Style the cards** — Set the title, colours, font and whether to show the free square, then generate and page through the preview.
5. **Export** — Download a multi-page PDF, a ZIP of PNG files, or print directly with cut lines.
6. **Run the game** — Use the digital caller to draw calls without repeats, and paste the calls into the win checker to confirm a claimed win.

#### Frequently asked questions (18)

**Are the generated bingo cards really unique?**
Yes. Every card is compared against the ones already produced and is discarded if it matches, so a batch of 30 contains 30 genuinely different cards. If your settings cannot produce that many distinct layouts, the tool tells you how many it managed rather than padding the batch with duplicates.

**How many bingo cards can I make at once?**
Up to 500 in one batch. They are laid out at 1, 2 or 4 cards per sheet, so 500 cards is 125 sheets at four per page.

**What is the difference between 75-ball and 90-ball bingo?**
75-ball is the American game: a 5 by 5 grid with a free centre square and columns headed B, I, N, G and O drawing from 1-15, 16-30, 31-45, 46-60 and 61-75. 90-ball is the British game: a 3 by 9 grid holding exactly 15 numbers, five per row, with no free square.

**Can I make bingo cards with my own words?**
Yes. Switch to Words mode and paste your list with one item per line. A 5 by 5 card with a free square needs at least 24 items, and the more items you supply beyond that, the more different cards become possible.

**How many words do I need for bingo cards?**
At least as many as there are squares — 24 for a 5 by 5 card with a free centre, or 25 without. For a class of 30 children you want noticeably more than the minimum, otherwise the cards will share most of their squares. The tool shows how many distinct cards your list can produce.

**What does the seed do?**
The seed drives the shuffling, so the same seed always produces exactly the same batch of cards. That means you can reprint a lost card, or verify a card someone brings back weeks later, without keeping the file.

**Can I verify a winning card?**
Yes. Enter the card ID or the seed printed on the card, paste the calls that have been made, and pick the pattern. The checker matches each call exactly against each square, and if it is not a win it tells you how close the card is and which squares are still missing.

**Why does the win checker reject a card that looks like a winner?**
Most often because a call was mistyped or missed from the list. The checker deliberately requires an exact match, so B7 does not satisfy a square holding B75 — loose matching would confirm wins that never happened.

**Which win patterns are supported?**
Any line, any row, any column, any diagonal, four corners, an X, the outer frame, and a full blackout. Diagonals and the X are only offered on square grids, because a 3 by 9 card has no diagonal.

**Does the digital caller repeat numbers?**
No. It draws from the remaining calls only, so nothing comes up twice, and it stops when every call has been drawn. You can undo the last call or reset the whole game.

**Can the caller read the numbers out loud?**
Yes, using your browser's built-in speech. Turn on spoken calls and each draw is announced. The available voices come from your operating system, so quality varies between devices.

**How do I print bingo cards at home?**
Choose your paper size and how many cards go on each sheet, then use Print or download the PDF. Turn on cut lines to see where to cut, and make sure your print dialog is set to actual size rather than fit to page.

**What is ink-saver mode?**
It drops the coloured fills and prints black outlines on white, which uses far less ink on a large batch and stays readable on a monochrome laser printer.

**Can I download the cards as images instead of a PDF?**
Yes. The ZIP download gives you one PNG per card, named by card ID, which suits sending cards to players individually or dropping them into a slide deck.

**Does this work offline?**
Yes, once the page has loaded. It uses no third-party libraries at all — the PDF and ZIP files are assembled by the page itself — so nothing breaks if you are on a school network that blocks external scripts.

**Are my word lists uploaded anywhere?**
No. Cards are generated and files are assembled entirely in your browser, and your settings are saved only in your own browser storage. Nothing is sent to a server.

**Is there a watermark or a limit?**
No watermark, no sign-up and no limit on how many batches you make. The only cap is 500 cards in a single batch, which keeps the browser responsive.

**Can I use these bingo cards in my classroom or business?**
Yes. The cards you generate are yours to use, print and share, including for teaching and commercial events. The themed word lists are ordinary vocabulary and carry no restriction.

#### Frequently asked questions (11)

**Is the random name picker actually fair?**
Yes. Every name has an equal chance unless you intentionally weight the odds by entering a name more than once. The wheel uses the browser's random number generator, and the live odds table shows the exact percentage chance for every name before you spin.

**Can I pick more than one winner at a time?**

**How do I stop the same person from winning twice?**
Turn on "Remove winners after each draw" (raffle mode). Every name that wins is taken out of the wheel, so future spins can only land on names that have not won yet. Use Reset wheel to bring everyone back for a new round.

**What happens if I type the same name twice?**
By default, repeated entries increase that name's chance of being picked - similar to putting more than one raffle ticket in a hat. If you want every unique name to have exactly the same odds instead, turn off duplicate weighting or use the Remove duplicates button.

**Can someone with several entries win twice in raffle mode?**
No. When raffle mode is on, all of a winner's entries are removed, so each person wins at most once per round even if they had several tickets. In a single spin with several winners, a person can only be picked once either way.

### Coin Flip

Animated 3D coin toss with synthesised sound, a running heads/tails tally and percentage kept in local storage, and a mute toggle. One flip at a time.

- URL: https://tooladda.online/coin-flip.html
- Page title: Coin Flip Online | Free Heads or Tails Game | ToolAdda

#### How to flip a coin online

1. **Open the game** — Visit the Coin Flip page and wait for the coin to load.
2. **Flip the coin** — Click Flip Coin or press the Space bar to toss the virtual coin.
3. **See the result** — Watch the 3D animation and view whether it landed on Heads or Tails.
4. **Track your stats** — Review total flips, heads percentage, and recent flip history saved locally.

#### Frequently asked questions (14)

**Is this coin flip fair?**
Yes. Where the browser provides one — which every current browser does — each flip uses the cryptographic random number generator, the same source used to create encryption keys. Older browsers fall back to the ordinary generator. Each flip is independent and both sides have an equal chance.

**Is a digital flip fairer than a real coin?**
In one respect, yes. Physical coins are not perfectly balanced, and research on coin tossing has found a small bias toward the side that started facing up, because a tossed coin wobbles rather than rotating cleanly. A digital flip has no physics to bias it.

**Why do I keep getting the same result several times in a row?**
Because that is what randomness looks like. In twenty flips, a run of four or five identical results is expected rather than suspicious. People tend to read streaks as evidence of rigging, but genuinely random sequences contain more clustering than most of us intuitively expect.

**If I get five heads, is tails more likely next?**
No. A coin has no memory, so the chance of tails is still one half. The belief that a result is somehow due is called the gambler's fallacy, and it is one of the most persistent errors in reasoning about chance.

**Then why do results even out over time?**
They even out in proportion, not in count. Ten flips can easily land 8 to 2. A thousand flips will sit close to half and half — not because the coin corrects itself, but because an early run gets diluted by everything that comes after it.

**Can I flip more than once?**
Yes, as many times as you like. The running tally shows how the results are splitting, which is the clearest way to watch a proportion settle down as the number of flips grows.

**Are my flips saved?**
The recent history and counts are kept in your browser while you use the page. Nothing is uploaded to us and nothing is tied to an account.

**Can I use this to settle a bet?**
For something friendly, yes — that is what it is for. For anything with real money or legal weight, use a method both parties can see and verify in person; nobody should have to trust a web page for that.

**Is heads or tails better to call?**
Neither. With a fair flip the two are exactly equal, so calling one over the other makes no difference. If you are calling a real coin, there is a very slight edge in calling whichever side is facing up before the toss.

**Can I flip a coin more than two ways?**
Not with a coin — it has two sides. For three or more options, or for picking a winner from a list where every entry must have an equal chance, use the Random Name Picker instead.

**Does it work on a phone?**
Yes. The coin scales to the screen and you can tap anywhere on it to flip. The history and counts work the same as on a desktop.

**Does it work offline?**
Yes, once the page has loaded. The flip is generated on your device with no server involved, so it keeps working if your connection drops.

**Is it free?**
Completely. No sign-up, no download and no limit on how many times you flip.

**How should I actually use a coin flip to decide something?**
The most useful trick is not the result itself. Flip the coin, and pay attention to how you feel when you see the outcome. If you are disappointed, you already knew which option you wanted — the coin just made you admit it.

#### Frequently asked questions (10)

**What is the 2048 game?**
2048 is a sliding tile puzzle on a 4×4 grid. Merge matching numbers to double their value - 2 becomes 4, 4 becomes 8, and so on - until you reach 2048 or run out of moves.

**How do I control 2048 on mobile?**
Swipe up, down, left, or right on the game board. You can also use the on-screen direction pad below the board for tap-based control.

**Is this 2048 game free and unblocked?**

**What is the best strategy to win 2048?**
Keep your highest tile locked in one corner, build descending values along one edge, use primarily two directions, and maintain empty cells for flexibility.

**How does scoring work in 2048?**
Every merge adds the new tile's value to your score. Merging two 256 tiles into 512 adds 512 points. Bigger merges = bigger score jumps.

**Who invented 2048?**
Gabriele Cirulli, an Italian web developer, created 2048 in March 2014. It became a viral sensation within days of release.

No. Everything runs locally in your browser. Scores and game state are stored only on your device using localStorage.

### Minesweeper

Beginner 9×9 with 10 mines, intermediate 16×16 with 40, expert 16×30 with 99, **plus fully custom rows, columns and mine count**, with a guaranteed-safe first click and best times per difficulty. Installable as a PWA and playable offline.

- URL: https://tooladda.online/minesweeper.html
- Page title: Play Minesweeper Online — Free, No Download | ToolAdda
- Meta description: Play Minesweeper online free — beginner to expert boards, custom sizes, mobile and keyboard controls. No download, no signup, best times saved on your device.

#### How to play Minesweeper

Clear every square that does not hide a mine, using the numbers to work out where the mines are.

1. **Click any square to start** — Your first click is always safe — mines are placed after it, never underneath it or its eight neighbours. The timer starts on this click.
2. **Read the numbers** — A number tells you how many of the eight squares touching it contain mines. A blank square has none, so its neighbours open automatically.
3. **Flag the mines you have worked out** — Right-click on desktop, or long-press on a phone, to place a flag. Flags stop you clicking a square by accident and let you use chording.
4. **Use chording to move faster** — Click a revealed number that already has the right count of flags around it and every remaining neighbour opens at once.
5. **Clear every safe square to win** — You win when every square without a mine is open. You do not need to flag all the mines.

#### Frequently asked questions (21)

**What is Minesweeper?**
A logic puzzle on a grid. Some squares hide mines. Each safe square you open shows how many of its eight neighbours are mined, and you use those numbers to work out where the rest of the mines are. You win by opening every square that is not a mine.

**How do I play Minesweeper?**
Click any square to start - the first click is always safe. Read the numbers to deduce where mines are, right-click (or long-press on a phone) to flag them, and keep opening squares you can prove are safe. Clear every non-mine square to win.

**Is this Minesweeper game free?**
Yes, completely. No account, no trial, no paid tier, and no limit on games.

**Does it work on mobile?**
Yes, and it is built for it rather than merely tolerating it. Tap to open, long-press to flag, tap a finished number to chord. Large boards keep a usable cell size and scroll, with zoom and fit-to-screen controls, instead of shrinking to unhittable specks.

**Do I need to download anything?**
No. It is a web page — nothing to install, no extension, no app store. You can add it to your home screen if you want it to open like an app.

**What do the numbers mean?**
A number counts the mines in the eight squares touching it, diagonals included. A 3 means exactly three of its neighbours are mined. A blank square touches no mines at all, which is why the board automatically opens the whole empty region around it.

**How do I flag a mine?**
Right-click on a computer, long-press for about a third of a second on a phone or tablet, or press F on the keyboard. There is also a Flag mode button that switches tapping to flagging. Flag again for a question mark, and once more to clear.

**Can I play Minesweeper with a keyboard?**
Yes, completely. Arrow keys move between squares, Enter or Space opens (or chords on a revealed number), F flags, R starts a new game, and 1 / 2 / 3 switch difficulty. Only the focused square is in the tab order, so Tab skips past the board rather than stepping through every cell.

**What happens if I click a mine?**
The game ends. The board reveals every mine, highlights the one you hit in red, and crosses out any flags you placed on safe squares - so you can see exactly where your reasoning went wrong. The timer stops and a Play again button appears immediately.

**Is the first click safe?**
Always. Mines are placed after your first click, never underneath it, and the eight squares around it are kept clear too wherever the board has room to spare them. That means your opening click almost always reveals a useful blank region rather than a lone number.

**How do I win Minesweeper?**
Open every square that does not contain a mine. You do not need to flag the mines — the game ends the moment the last safe square is revealed, however many flags you have placed.

**What is chording?**
Clicking a revealed number that already has the right count of flags around it, which opens all its remaining neighbours at once. It is the biggest speed gain in the game. On touch, simply tap a revealed number. If the flags do not match the number nothing happens, so a mistimed chord is harmless - but if your flags are wrong and the count happens to match, it will open a mine.

**What is the best Minesweeper strategy?**
Open a corner first - corners have three neighbours instead of eight, so their numbers are far easier to solve. Then alternate two rules: if a number equals its unopened neighbour count, those are all mines; if a number equals its flag count, the rest are safe and you can chord. When those stop yielding, use subset subtraction, then the global mine count. Guess only when nothing is forced, and guess early rather than late.

**What is beginner mode?**
A 9×9 board with 10 mines - about 12% density. It is the right place to learn the numbers and the 1-1 and 1-2-1 patterns. A good game takes 10 to 40 seconds.

**What is expert mode?**
A 16×30 board with 99 mines, the standard competitive size. Density jumps to about 21%, which is what really makes it hard - roughly one square in five is mined instead of one in eight. Finishing under 100 seconds is a strong result.

**Can I create a custom board?**
Yes. Open the Custom panel and set rows (5-40), columns (5-60) and mines. The tool validates your numbers as you type, shows the resulting mine density with a plain-language difficulty estimate, and refuses configurations that cannot work - such as more mines than there are squares to put them in.

**Are my statistics saved?**
Yes, in your browser's local storage on this device, separately for each difficulty. Games played, wins, win rate, best time, current streak and best streak. There is a Clear statistics button with a confirmation if you want to reset them.

**Is my gameplay uploaded anywhere?**
No. There is no server component to send it to. Board generation, your moves, your times and your statistics all happen and stay in your browser. Open developer tools, go to the Network tab and play a full game - you will see the page's own files load once and nothing afterwards.

**Can I play offline?**
Yes, after your first visit. A service worker caches the page, so it keeps working with no connection - on a plane, on the underground, or on a patchy mobile signal.

**Does Minesweeper require an account?**
No. There is no signup, no email, and no login. Open the page and play.

**Is every board solvable without guessing?**
No, and any site claiming otherwise without running a solver during generation is guessing too. Mines are placed randomly after your first click, so some boards contain positions where two squares are genuinely indistinguishable and you must pick one. Guaranteed no-guess generation requires solving each candidate board before serving it; it is on our roadmap and we would rather tell you than pretend.

### Snake Game

The classic arcade Snake on a **20 × 20 board with solid walls** — no wrap-around, so the edges genuinely end the run. Each apple is **10 points** and one segment of length; the snake accelerates every 30 points down to a floor of 60 ms, so it gets demanding without outrunning human reaction time. Three starting speeds (Easy, Medium, Hard) all follow that same acceleration curve. Controls are arrow keys or WASD, swipe, or an on-screen D-pad, with spacebar to pause; a 180° reversal is deliberately ignored once the snake is longer than one segment. The high score and mute preference live in **local storage**, tied to that browser rather than an account, and there is no reset button by design. The theoretical maximum is **3,970 points** (397 apples on 400 squares). The page also carries genuine strategy guidance and the game’s history — the 1976 arcade game Blockade, then Taneli Armanto’s 1997 version for the Nokia 6110. Free, no sign-up, no download, nothing uploaded.

#### How to play the Snake game

1. **Start the game** — Press the start button or the spacebar. The snake begins three segments long in the middle of the board, already moving right.
2. **Steer with the arrow keys** — Use the arrow keys or WASD on a keyboard, or swipe the board or tap the D-pad on a touchscreen.
3. **Eat the apples** — Guide the head onto each apple. Every apple adds 10 points and one segment of length.
4. **Avoid the walls and your tail** — The board does not wrap around, so touching an edge ends the game, as does running into any part of your own body.
5. **Manage the growing tail** — As the snake lengthens, work in loops around the outside of the board rather than cutting through the middle, so you never seal yourself into a pocket.

#### Frequently asked questions (18)

**How do I control the snake?**
Use the arrow keys or WASD on a keyboard. On a phone or tablet, swipe anywhere on the board or use the on-screen D-pad below it. Press the spacebar to pause and resume.

**How do I score points?**
Every apple you eat is worth 10 points and makes the snake one segment longer. There is no bonus fruit and no multiplier, so your score is simply ten times the number of apples you have eaten.

**Does the game get faster as I play?**
Yes. The snake speeds up slightly every 30 points, which is every three apples, and keeps accelerating until it reaches its fastest step of 60 milliseconds. That ceiling means the game becomes demanding but never impossible to react to.

**What do the Easy, Medium and Hard speeds change?**
They set how fast the snake moves before any acceleration: Easy starts slowest, Medium is the default, and Hard starts noticeably quicker. All three then speed up on the same schedule as your score rises.

**What happens if I hit the wall?**
The game ends. This version has solid walls rather than a wrap-around board, so the edges are a real boundary and cornering safely is part of the challenge.

**Can I pass through my own tail?**
No. Running into any part of your own body ends the game, which is what makes a long snake so much harder to steer than a short one.

**Why can't I turn back on myself?**
A 180-degree reversal would drive the head straight into the neck, so the game ignores it once the snake is longer than one segment. To double back you have to turn twice, which is a deliberate part of Snake's design rather than an unresponsive control.

**Can I pause the game?**
Yes. Press the Pause button or tap the spacebar to pause, then the same key or button to resume. The timer stops while you are paused.

**Is my high score saved?**
Yes. Your best score is stored in your own browser using local storage, so it is still there when you come back. It is never uploaded, and it is tied to that browser on that device rather than to an account.

**How do I reset my high score?**
Clear the site data for tooladda.online in your browser settings, which removes the saved best score along with your other preferences for the site. There is no reset button, because accidentally wiping a hard-won score would be worse than the inconvenience.

**What is a good score in Snake?**
On the default Medium speed, 200 points is a solid warm-up, 500 shows real control, and anything past 1,000 means you are managing your tail deliberately rather than reacting. Where you land also depends on which speed you started on.

**What is the highest score possible?**
The board is 20 by 20, so 400 squares. The snake starts three segments long, which leaves 397 apples to eat and a theoretical maximum of 3,970 points. Filling the board completely is close to impossible in practice, because the last apples appear in gaps only a perfectly coiled snake can reach.

**What is the best strategy for a high score?**
Follow the edges rather than cutting through the middle, and keep your tail in a predictable shape you can steer around. Most players die because they trapped themselves in a pocket, not because they misjudged a single turn. Plan the move after the one you are making.

**Why do I keep dying just as the snake gets long?**
Because a long snake turns the board into a maze of your own making. The fix is to stop chasing apples in a straight line and start deciding where your tail will be in a few seconds, working in loops around the outside instead of zig-zagging.

**Can I play Snake on my phone?**
Yes. The board scales to your screen and you can swipe in any direction on it or tap the D-pad underneath. Everything works the same as on a desktop, including the saved high score.

**Is this Snake game free?**
Yes, completely. There is no sign-up, no download and no paid tier. Open the page and press start.

**Do I need to install anything to play?**
No. It runs in the browser you already have, on desktop or mobile, with no plugin, app store or download involved.

**Where did the Snake game come from?**
The idea goes back to the 1976 arcade game Blockade, but Snake became a household name in 1997 when Taneli Armanto adapted it for the Nokia 6110. Because it shipped preinstalled on tens of millions of phones, it became one of the most played video games ever made.

### Tic Tac Toe

Two-player pass-and-play on one device, or against the computer at easy, medium or **unbeatable**. The hard opponent runs a **depth-aware minimax**: it searches every continuation to the end of the game, and because wins are scored as (10 − depth) and losses as (depth − 10) it takes the **fastest** win available and **prolongs** a lost position rather than conceding — a plain minimax scores every win alike and so declines immediate wins. Unbeatability is not asserted but **proved by exhaustion in the test suite**, which plays all 569 reachable games with the human moving first and all 73 with the computer first: the human wins none. Two perfect players always draw. Medium is deliberately beatable (take-win, block-loss, then centre and corners), and easy is genuinely random. The page also carries a real strategy guide — the win/block/centre/fork priority order, why the centre is strongest (it sits on 4 of the 8 winning lines, versus 3 for a corner and 2 for an edge), and how forks decide almost every real game — plus the game-theory context that tic tac toe has exactly **255,168 playable games**, which is why it is a solved draw. Scoreboard persists in local storage; the board is fully keyboard playable and screen-reader friendly. Nothing is uploaded.

- URL: https://tooladda.online/tic-tac-toe.html
- Page title: Tic Tac Toe — Play Online Free vs Unbeatable AI | ToolAdda
- Meta description: Play tic tac toe online free against an unbeatable computer or a friend. Three difficulty levels, saved scoreboard, and a guide to never losing.

#### How to play tic tac toe

1. **Pick an opponent** — Choose two players on one device, or the computer at Easy, Medium or Unbeatable.
2. **X moves first** — Take turns placing your mark on any empty square. X always starts.
3. **Make three in a row** — Win by completing any row, column or diagonal. The winning line is highlighted.
4. **Win, then block** — Each turn, take a winning square if you have one; otherwise block your opponent's.
5. **Look for a fork** — Play a square that creates two threats at once, because only one of them can be blocked.

#### Frequently asked questions (18)

**Can I play tic tac toe against the computer?**
Yes. Choose Easy, Medium or Unbeatable. Easy plays at random and can be beaten by anyone, Medium takes obvious wins and blocks obvious threats, and Unbeatable searches the whole game to the end.

**Can the hard mode be beaten?**
No, and that is not a boast — it is a property of the game. Tic tac toe is small enough to be solved completely, so the computer can see every possible continuation before it moves. Perfect play cannot lose. The best result available to you is a draw.

**How does the unbeatable computer work?**
It uses minimax: for every legal move it plays out every possible continuation to the end of the game, assumes you will always reply with your best move, and picks the branch with the best guaranteed outcome. With only 255,168 possible games it can examine all of them instantly.

**Why does the computer sometimes take longer to win than it could?**
It should not. The search is depth-aware, meaning a win in one move scores higher than the same win three moves later, and a loss delayed scores better than a loss now. So it takes the quickest win available and, when it is losing, makes you finish the job properly.

**Is it possible to win at tic tac toe if both players play well?**
No. Tic tac toe is what game theorists call a solved draw: if neither player makes a mistake, every game ends level. Wins only happen when someone errs, which is why the game is usually outgrown at around eight years old.

**What is the best first move in tic tac toe?**
The centre. It sits on four of the eight winning lines, more than any other square. Corners are next best at three lines each, and edges are weakest at two. Taking the centre does not guarantee a win, but it gives your opponent the most ways to go wrong.

**How do I never lose at tic tac toe?**
Follow a simple priority order every turn: win if you can, block if your opponent can win next, take the centre, take a square that creates two threats at once, block a fork, then take a corner and finally an edge. Applied consistently, that will never lose.

**What is a fork in tic tac toe?**
A move that creates two separate winning threats at the same time. Your opponent can only block one of them, so the other wins. Forks are how nearly all real wins happen, and spotting them a move early is the whole skill of the game.

**Does the player who goes first always win?**
No, but going first is a real advantage. The first player has more chances to create a fork, so against an imperfect opponent X wins far more often than O. Against perfect play the advantage is not enough, and the game is drawn.

**How many possible tic tac toe games are there?**
255,168 games can actually be played out, from 26,830 distinct board positions. That is small by the standards of board games — chess has more possible games than there are atoms in the observable universe — which is exactly why tic tac toe can be solved outright.

**Can I play two players on the same device?**
Yes. Choose Two players and take turns on the same screen. X always moves first, and the board shows whose turn it is.

**Is the scoreboard saved?**
Yes. Wins, losses and draws are kept in your own browser, so they survive closing the tab. They are tied to that browser on that device and are never uploaded.

**How do I reset the score?**
Use the Reset score button. It clears the wins and draws while leaving the board ready for a new game.

**Does this game work on a phone?**
Yes. The board scales to the screen and the squares stay large enough to tap comfortably. Everything works the same as on a desktop, including the saved scoreboard.

**Can I play tic tac toe with the keyboard?**
Yes. The squares are real buttons, so you can move between them with Tab and play with Enter or Space. That also means screen readers announce the board properly.

**Is this tic tac toe game free?**
Completely. There is no sign-up, no download and no paid mode. Open the page and start.

**Does the game work offline?**
Once the page has loaded, yes. Everything runs in your browser with no server involved, so the game keeps working if your connection drops.

**Where did tic tac toe come from?**
Versions of three-in-a-row go back to ancient Rome, where a game called terni lapilli used three pieces each that players moved around rather than placed. The modern pencil-and-paper name noughts and crosses appears in Britain in the nineteenth century, and the game became an early landmark in computing when OXO ran on the EDSAC in 1952.

### Connect Four

The four-in-a-row board game on a standard 7x6 grid, in the browser. Two modes: against the computer, or two players on one device. The opponent is a real alpha-beta search rather than a table of tricks — Easy looks one move ahead and blunders on purpose, Medium three, Hard five, Expert seven, and every level above Easy always takes a win it can see and blocks one it cannot afford. The search is time-capped, so a slow phone gets a shallower move instead of a frozen page. #### How to play Connect Four

The rules of Connect Four and how to play it in the browser.

1. **Pick your opponent** — Choose the computer with a difficulty level, or two players sharing one device.
2. **Drop a disc** — Click any column, or press its number key from 1 to 7. The disc falls to the lowest free square in that column.
3. **Build a line of four** — Connect four of your discs in a row, a column or a diagonal, while blocking your opponent from doing the same.
4. **Win, or take it back** — The winning four are highlighted on the board. Undo steps back through the game, and New game deals a fresh board.

#### Frequently asked questions (15)

**How do you play Connect Four?**
Two players take turns dropping discs into a grid seven columns wide and six rows tall. A disc always falls to the lowest free square in the column you choose. The first player to line up four of their own discs horizontally, vertically or diagonally wins. If all 42 squares fill with no line of four, the game is a draw.

**Is Connect Four free to play here?**
Yes. There is no sign-up, no download and no limit on how many games you play. It runs entirely in your browser.

**Can I play Connect Four against a friend on one device?**
Yes. Switch to 2 players and the board simply passes back and forth — red plays, then yellow, on the same phone or laptop. Undo works the same way in two-player mode.

**How strong is the computer opponent?**
It depends on the level. Easy looks one move ahead and makes deliberate mistakes, Medium looks three moves ahead, Hard five, and Expert seven — a full alpha-beta search that will punish any threat you leave open. Every level above Easy always takes a win it can see and blocks one it cannot afford.

**Who wins Connect Four with perfect play?**
The first player, provided they start in the centre column. The game was solved independently by James Allen and Victor Allis in 1988: with perfect play from both sides, the first player wins on move 41. Starting anywhere other than the centre gives the win away — the second player can at least draw, and against the two outer columns can win.

**What is the best first move in Connect Four?**
The centre column. It is part of more winning lines than any other column — three of the four directions run through it — so a disc there does more work than the same disc anywhere else. The computer opens there for exactly that reason.

**Can I undo a move?**
Yes, as often as you like, right back to the empty board. Against the computer one press steps back over both your move and its reply, so you resume from your own decision rather than from its answer.

**Does it work on a phone?**
Yes. The board scales to the screen, each column is a full-height tap target, and the settings stack under the board on a narrow screen.

**Can I play with the keyboard?**
Yes. Press 1 to 7 to drop a disc into that column, use the left and right arrows to move between columns, N for a new game and U to undo. Every column is a real focusable button, so screen readers announce which column it is and how many spaces are left.

**Is my score saved?**
Wins, losses, draws and your best winning streak are kept in your own browser's local storage. Nothing is uploaded, and clearing your browser data resets the scoreboard.

**How many possible Connect Four positions are there?**
There are 4,531,985,219,092 legal positions on the standard 7 by 6 board — about four and a half trillion. That is why the opponent searches rather than looks anything up: even the Expert level examines only a few hundred thousand positions per move.

**What is a double threat, or fork?**
A position where you threaten to complete four in two different squares at once. Your opponent can only block one of them, so the other wins. Building a fork rather than a single threat is the core winning idea in Connect Four.

**Why should I avoid playing under my opponent's winning square?**
Because a disc in a column raises the landing square by one. If the square directly above yours completes four for your opponent, you have handed them the win. Before dropping, check what your move puts within reach.

**What board size is standard?**
Seven columns by six rows, 42 squares in total — the size of the original 1974 game. Other sizes exist and change the game completely: on a 6 by 5 board the first player still wins, while some larger boards are drawn with perfect play.

**Does the game work offline?**
Once the page has loaded, everything runs locally, so a dropped connection does not interrupt a game. There is no service worker yet, so the page itself still needs to load once.

### Checkers

Checkers in the browser with three rule sets: **American checkers / English draughts** (8x8, men capture forwards only, kings step one square, a crowning capture ends the move), **international draughts** (10x10, 20 men each, men capture backwards, flying kings, the compulsory maximum capture, no crown for a man that only passes the back row mid-capture) and **Russian draughts** (8x8, flying kings, free choice of capture, a man crowned mid-capture carries on as a king). Captures are compulsory and a multiple jump is entered one landing at a time, with the pieces that must capture highlighted; captured pieces are lifted only when the sequence ends (the Turkish strike rule). Play the computer — Easy, Medium, Hard or Expert, one alpha-beta search stopped at 2, 4 or 6 plies or deepened for as long as its time cap allows, always extending through pending captures — or two players on one device. Draws by threefold repetition, or after 40, 25 or 15 moves each with only kings moving and nothing captured. #### How to play checkers

The rules of checkers and how to play it in the browser.

1. **Choose rules and an opponent** — Pick American checkers, international draughts or Russian draughts, then the computer at one of four levels or two players on one device.
2. **Move a piece** — Tap one of your pieces, then a marked square. A man moves one square diagonally forwards onto an empty dark square.
3. **Capture** — Jump diagonally over an opposing piece to the empty square beyond it. Captures are compulsory, and a piece that can jump again must keep jumping.
4. **Crown a king and win** — A man that reaches the far row becomes a king. You win when your opponent has no pieces left or no legal move.

#### Frequently asked questions (15)

**How do you play checkers?**
Each player starts with 12 pieces on the dark squares of an 8 by 8 board. Pieces move one square diagonally forwards and capture by jumping over an opposing piece to the empty square beyond. Captures are compulsory, and a piece must keep jumping while it can. A piece that reaches the far row is crowned a king and can then move and capture backwards too. You win when your opponent has no pieces or no legal move left.

**Is this checkers game free?**
Yes. There is no sign-up, no download and no limit on how many games you play. It runs entirely in your browser.

**Can two people play checkers on one device?**
Yes. Switch the opponent to 2 players and pass the phone, tablet or laptop back and forth. The side that moves first sits at the bottom of the board, and undo works in two-player mode too.

**Is capturing compulsory in checkers?**
Yes, in every official rule set. If any of your pieces can capture, you must capture, and a piece that can carry on jumping after its first jump has to continue. When a capture is available, the pieces that can take pulse on the board, so you are never left guessing.

**Who moves first in checkers?**
In American checkers the dark pieces, usually called Black, move first. In international and Russian draughts White moves first. The game follows whichever rules you choose, and against the computer you decide whether you take the first move.

**What is the difference between checkers and draughts?**
They are one family of games. English draughts is the same game Americans call checkers: an 8 by 8 board, 12 pieces each and kings that move one square at a time. International draughts uses a 10 by 10 board with 20 pieces each, men that capture backwards, flying kings and a rule that you must take the most pieces you can. Russian draughts keeps the 8 by 8 board but adds flying kings and backward captures.

**What is a flying king?**
A king that moves any number of empty squares along a diagonal, like a bishop in chess, and captures a piece from a distance, landing on any empty square beyond it. International and Russian draughts have flying kings; in American checkers a king moves one square at a time.

**How strong is the computer opponent?**
Easy looks two moves ahead and plays a random move about three times in ten. Medium looks four moves ahead and occasionally slips, Hard looks up to six moves ahead, and Expert searches as deep as it can in under a second. Every level plays each capture sequence out to the end before it judges a position.

**Is checkers a solved game?**
Yes. In 2007 Jonathan Schaeffer's team at the University of Alberta proved that American checkers is a draw when both sides play perfectly, after a computation that had run on and off since 1989. Their program, Chinook, had become the first computer program to win a world championship title against human players in 1994.

**How many positions are there in checkers?**
About 500 billion billion, or 5 × 10²⁰, on the 8 by 8 board. That is why the computer searches ahead from the position in front of it instead of looking moves up in a table.

**Can I undo a move?**
Yes, all the way back to the start of the game. Against the computer one press takes back the computer's reply as well as your move, so you return to your own decision.

**Does the game save my progress?**
Yes. The game in progress is saved in your browser after every move and restored when you come back, even after closing the tab. Your score against the computer is kept as well. Nothing is uploaded.

**Can I play checkers with the keyboard?**
Yes. The arrow keys move between the dark squares, Enter or Space picks a piece up and puts it down, Esc cancels, U undoes, H shows a hint and N starts a new game. Every square is a labelled button, so a screen reader announces the square, its piece and whether that piece can move.

**What do the numbers on the squares mean?**
They are the standard square numbers used to write moves down: 1 to 32 in American checkers and 1 to 50 in international draughts, so 11-15 is a move from square 11 to square 15 and 15x24 is a capture. Russian draughts uses chess-style names such as c3-d4. Turn on Show square numbers to see them on the board.

**When is a game of checkers drawn?**
Here a game is drawn when the same position comes up three times with the same player to move, or when a long run of moves passes with only kings moving and nothing captured: 40 moves each in American checkers, 25 in international draughts and 15 in Russian draughts.

### Reversi

The disc-flipping board game on the standard **8x8** board or a quick **6x6**, from the fixed four-disc start with black moving first. Legal moves are marked on the board (and read out to screen readers with how many discs each flips), passes are applied and announced automatically, and the game ends when neither side can move. The computer has four levels — Easy (one ply, often random), Medium (three plies), Hard (up to five) and Expert (time-capped iterative deepening) — judging corners, X- and C-squares, mobility and frontier discs, and counting the finish out **exactly** from the last 6, 10 or 14 empty squares; the exact endgame is checked against an independent brute-force minimax in the test suite. #### How to play Reversi

The rules of Reversi and how to play it in the browser.

1. **Choose an opponent and a board** — Play the computer at one of four levels or two players on one device, on the standard 8 by 8 board or a quick 6 by 6 one.
2. **Place a disc** — Black moves first. Tap a marked square: a legal move must trap at least one straight line of your opponent's discs between the new disc and one of yours.
3. **Flip the trapped discs** — Every opposing disc trapped in a line — across, up, down or diagonally — turns over to your colour. One move can flip lines in several directions at once.
4. **Count the discs** — If you have no legal move, you pass. When neither player can move, the player with more discs on the board wins.

#### Frequently asked questions (15)

**How do you play Reversi?**
Two players take turns placing discs of their own colour on an 8 by 8 board, starting from four discs in the centre. Each move must outflank at least one straight line of the opponent's discs — across, down or diagonally — between the new disc and one of your own, and every disc in those lines flips to your colour. If you cannot move you pass, and when neither player can move the one with more discs wins.

**Is this Reversi game free?**
Yes. There is no sign-up, no download and no limit on how many games you play. It runs entirely in your browser.

**Can two people play Reversi on one device?**
Yes. Switch the opponent to 2 players and pass the phone, tablet or laptop between turns. Legal moves are marked for whoever is to play, and undo works the same way.

**Who goes first in Reversi?**
Black always moves first, from the standard start with two black and two white discs crossed in the centre. Against the computer you can play Black, play White, or alternate between games.

**What happens if I have no legal move?**
You must pass, and your opponent plays again; the game tells you when that happens. You may not pass while you still have a legal move. If neither player can move, usually because the board is full, the game ends.

**Is Reversi the same as Othello?**
Othello is a trademarked version of Reversi launched in Japan in the 1970s, which fixed the four-disc starting position. The rules played here are those same modern rules. Reversi itself is older: it was devised in England in the 1880s.

**What is the best strategy in Reversi?**
Take corners, because a disc in a corner can never be flipped. Avoid the squares diagonally next to an empty corner, which usually give it away. Early on, keep your options open rather than grabbing discs: the player with more possible moves is usually the one who is winning, even with fewer discs.

**Why should I avoid the squares next to the corners?**
A disc on an X-square, diagonally touching an empty corner, often lets your opponent take that corner by outflanking along the diagonal. The C-squares beside a corner on the edge carry a similar risk. Once the corner has been taken, those squares are safe.

**How strong is the computer opponent?**
Easy looks one move ahead and plays a random move about four times in ten. Medium looks three moves ahead, Hard up to five, and Expert searches as deep as it can in under a second. Near the end they stop estimating and count the finish out exactly: Medium over the last 6 empty squares, Hard over the last 10 and Expert over the last 14 when time allows.

**Is Reversi solved?**
The standard 8 by 8 game was reported solved in 2023 by researcher Hiroki Takizawa, whose computation found that perfect play by both sides ends in a draw. The smaller 6 by 6 board was solved in 1993: with perfect play White, the second player, wins 20 to 16.

**How many moves are there in a game of Reversi?**
At most 60 on the 8 by 8 board, one for each square that is empty at the start, and fewer if the game ends before the board is full. A 6 by 6 game has at most 32 moves. Passes do not count as moves.

**Can I undo a move?**
Yes, all the way back to the start. Against the computer one press also takes back the computer's reply and any passes in between, so you return to your own decision.

**Does the game save my progress?**
Yes. The game in progress is saved in your browser after every move and restored when you come back, even after closing the tab. Your score against the computer is kept as well. Nothing is uploaded.

**Can I play Reversi with the keyboard?**
Yes. The arrow keys move around the board, Enter or Space plays on the focused square, U undoes, H shows a hint and N starts a new game. Every square is a labelled button that says what is on it and, for a legal move, how many discs it would flip.

**What do square names like d3 mean?**
Columns are lettered a to h from the left and rows numbered 1 to 8 from the top, the convention used in tournament game records. Black's four possible opening moves are d3, c4, f5 and e6, and all four lead to the same position turned around, so the choice makes no difference.

### Ludo

Pass-and-play Ludo for **2, 3 or 4 players** with an optional CPU toggle that turns every seat except the first into a bot, animated 3D dice and tokens, safe squares, sound and a resumable game.

- URL: https://tooladda.online/ludo-game.html
- Page title: Ludo Game — 3D Dice, 2–4 Players, Free Online | ToolAdda
- Meta description: Play Ludo online free — a 3D-dice board game with animated tokens, captures, safe zones, 2–4 players and optional CPU opponents. In your browser, no signup.

#### How to play Ludo

Race all four of your tokens from the yard to the centre before your opponents.

1. **Roll a 6 to start** — Roll a 6 to move a token out of your yard onto its coloured start cell.
2. **Race around the board** — Move your tokens clockwise around the ring track according to each dice roll.
3. **Capture opponents** — Land exactly on an opponent to send their token home, unless they are on a safe cell.
4. **Reach the centre** — Turn into your coloured home lane and land exactly on the centre to finish a token. First to bring all four home wins.

#### Frequently asked questions (14)

**How many players can play?**
Two, three or four, all on the same device taking turns. Four is the traditional game; two is the most tactical because there are fewer tokens on the board and captures become deliberate rather than accidental.

**How do I get a token out of the yard?**
Roll a six. A token can only leave its yard on a six, which is why the opening can feel slow. Rolling a six also earns you another roll, so a good opening often releases two tokens at once.

**What happens when I land on another player's token?**
Their token is sent back to its yard and has to roll a six to start again. Capturing costs an opponent their entire journey so far, which is usually worth far more than the squares you would have gained by moving elsewhere.

**What are safe squares?**
Marked squares where a token cannot be captured. Parking on one is the safest way to hold position when you have no good move, particularly when an opponent is close behind.

**Do I need an exact roll to get home?**
Yes. You cannot overshoot the home square, so the last few steps often need a specific number. That is why games so often end with a token stuck one or two squares short.

**Is Ludo a game of luck or skill?**
Mostly luck, but not entirely. The dice are out of your control, but every roll gives you a choice of which token to move, and that choice decides most close games. Spreading tokens out and prioritising captures are the two decisions that matter most.

**What is the best Ludo strategy?**
Spread your tokens rather than bunching them, so a bad roll never leaves you without a useful move. Check which opponents are within six squares before committing. Take a capture when one is available. And do not waste rolls pushing a token that is already nearly home.

**Why does a six give another turn?**
It is what keeps the game moving. Without it, players who could not roll a six would sit out entirely. The extra roll rewards the same number that releases tokens, so a six is always good news twice over.

**Can I play Ludo against the computer?**
This version is designed for people playing together on one device. For a game against a computer opponent, try Tic Tac Toe, where the hardest setting has solved the game completely.

**Where did Ludo come from?**
It is a simplified descendant of Pachisi, an Indian cross-and-circle game documented since at least the sixteenth century and played on cloth with cowrie shells instead of dice. The modern version was patented in England in 1896 as Ludo, Latin for "I play".

**Is Ludo the same as Parcheesi?**
They are close relatives rather than the same game. Parcheesi in the United States, Mensch argere Dich nicht in Germany and Parques in Colombia are all descendants of Pachisi, each with small rule differences around safe squares and capturing.

**Does the game work on a phone?**
Yes. The board scales to the screen and the tokens stay large enough to tap accurately. Passing one phone around is the natural way to play a turn-based game like this.

**Is my game saved if I close the tab?**
The game runs in the page you have open. Closing or refreshing the tab starts a new game, so finish a game in one sitting.

**Is it free?**
Completely. No sign-up, no download and no paid tier.
